CM:001.title: A force law is incomplete until its frame and dimensions are declared
CM:001.objective: Frame-covariance and dimensional analysis distinguish a medium-relative drag law from an invariant internal pair law and expose a concrete boost error.
CM:001.statement:
A particle of mass $m$ moves in a plane. In an inertial laboratory frame tied to a stationary medium, a proposed model is
$$
m\ddot{\mathbf r}=-k\mathbf r-c\dot{\mathbf r},
$$
where the coordinate origin is also the spring anchor. First determine the SI dimensions of $k$ and $c$, and explain which pieces of the model select an origin or a preferred inertial frame.

Let another inertial frame move with constant velocity $\mathbf U$, so $\mathbf r'=\mathbf r-\mathbf U t-\mathbf a$ and $\dot{\mathbf r}'=\dot{\mathbf r}-\mathbf U$. Derive the correctly transformed equation, retaining the laboratory anchor and medium velocity in primed coordinates. Show why merely writing $-k\mathbf r'-c\dot{\mathbf r}'$ describes a different physical system.

Contrast this with two particles interacting through
$$
\mathbf F_{12}=-K(\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2)-C(\mathbf v_1-\mathbf v_2),
\qquad \mathbf F_{21}=-\mathbf F_{12},
$$
and prove that the pair law is Galilean invariant and conserves total linear momentum, although its relative damping dissipates mechanical energy.

For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k=6.00\,\mathrm{N/m}$, $c=2.00\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, $\mathbf r=(0.500,-0.200)\,\mathrm m$, and $\dot{\mathbf r}=(3.00,1.00)\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in the medium frame, compute force and acceleration. Then use $\mathbf U=(1.00,-2.00)\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to compute the spurious force change produced by the naive primed law.
permittedResults: Acceleration is unchanged under a constant-velocity Galilean boost.
A physical velocity relative to a medium is the difference between particle and medium velocities measured in the same frame.

acceptableStrategies.description: Identify every dimensional parameter and every object that defines the frame before transforming coordinates. Rewrite anchor and medium data in the primed frame, then compare with a separation-based internal law whose coordinate differences cancel boosts.

milestones.criterion: Determines $[k]=\mathrm{N/m}$ and $[c]=\mathrm{kg/s}$ while naming the anchor and medium that define the model.
Transforms both anchor position and medium velocity, rather than reusing an unqualified primed coordinate and speed.
Proves invariance and momentum conservation for the relative pair law and computes the numerical force, acceleration, and boost artifact.

commonErrors.description: Calls the laboratory drag law Galilean invariant because acceleration is invariant.
commonErrors.consequence: The preferred medium velocity is omitted, so two coordinate descriptions predict different physical forces.

commonErrors.description: Assigns force units to both $k$ and $c$ without accounting for their multiplying variables.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed equation fails dimensional homogeneity before any dynamics are solved.

hintTree.content: The spring anchor has primed position $-\mathbf U t-\mathbf a$, and the medium has primed velocity $-\mathbf U$.
The physical drag is $-c(\dot{\mathbf r}'-\mathbf v'_{\rm med})$, not automatically $-c\dot{\mathbf r}'$.
For the pair law, both $\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2$ and $\mathbf v_1-\mathbf v_2$ survive a common translation or boost unchanged.

CM:001.canonicalSolution:
Dimensional consistency requires
$$
[k]=\mathrm{N/m}=\mathrm{kg/s^2},
\qquad
[c]=\mathrm{N}/(\mathrm{m/s})=\mathrm{kg/s}.
$$
The spring term refers to the stated anchor and therefore breaks translation symmetry. The drag term refers to the medium rest frame and therefore selects a preferred inertial frame.

In primed coordinates, the laboratory anchor is
$\mathbf r'_{\rm a}=-\mathbf U t-\mathbf a$ and the medium velocity is
$\mathbf v'_{\rm med}=-\mathbf U$. Since $\ddot{\mathbf r}'=\ddot{\mathbf r}$, the same physics is
$$
m\ddot{\mathbf r}'
=-k(\mathbf r'-\mathbf r'_{\rm a})
-c(\dot{\mathbf r}'-\mathbf v'_{\rm med})
=-k(\mathbf r'+\mathbf U t+\mathbf a)-c(\dot{\mathbf r}'+\mathbf U).
$$
Replacing this expression by $-k\mathbf r'-c\dot{\mathbf r}'$ silently moves the anchor to the primed origin and makes the medium co-move with that frame. It is a new experiment, not a transformed equation.

For the pair law, common translations cancel from $\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2$ and common boosts cancel from $\mathbf v_1-\mathbf v_2$. Thus its functional form is Galilean invariant. Equal and opposite forces give
$d(m_1\mathbf v_1+m_2\mathbf v_2)/dt=0$. Its instantaneous power is
$$
\mathbf F_{12}\cdot(\mathbf v_1-\mathbf v_2)
=-K(\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2)\cdot(\mathbf v_1-\mathbf v_2)
-C|\mathbf v_1-\mathbf v_2|^2.
$$
The first term is the negative derivative of spring energy and the second is nonpositive dissipation, so momentum conservation does not imply mechanical-energy conservation.

Numerically,
$$
\mathbf F=-6(0.500,-0.200)-2(3.00,1.00)
=\boxed{(-9.00,-0.800)\,\mathrm N},
$$
and
$\boxed{\ddot{\mathbf r}=(-4.50,-0.400)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}$.
If one naively inserts $\mathbf r'$ and $\dot{\mathbf r}'$ while keeping the anchor and medium falsely at rest, the velocity part changes by
$$
\Delta\mathbf F=c\mathbf U
=\boxed{(2.00,-4.00)\,\mathrm N}
$$
at a common event with coincident origins. A coordinate change cannot create this physical force difference; it diagnoses the missing frame data.

CM:002.title: Central internal forces vanish from the total torque balance
CM:002.objective: Central-force geometry removes every internal torque from the fixed-origin angular-momentum balance and fixes the numerical torque sign.
CM:002.statement: For particles in a fixed inertial frame, suppose every internal pair force is central: $\mathbf F_{ij}=f_{ij}(\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_j)$ with $\mathbf F_{ji}=-\mathbf F_{ij}$. Prove directly that $d\mathbf L_O/dt=\boldsymbol\tau_O^{\rm ext}$ about a fixed origin $O$. At one instant two external forces act: $\mathbf r_1=(1.00,0,0)\,\mathrm m$, $\mathbf f_1=(0,3.00,0)\,\mathrm N$, $\mathbf r_2=(0,2.00,0)\,\mathrm m$, and $\mathbf f_2=(-1.00,0,0)\,\mathrm N$. Find $dL_{O,z}/dt$ and check the collinear-pair limit.
permittedResults: For a fixed origin, $\mathbf L_O=\sum_i\mathbf r_i\times m_i\dot{\mathbf r}_i$.
Parallel vectors have zero cross product.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Differentiate total angular momentum about the fixed origin. Next: Combine the two torques from each internal pair before using centrality. Finally: Compute both external $z$-torques with the right-hand rule and check torque units.

milestones.criterion: Differentiates total angular momentum about the fixed origin.
Combines the two torques from each internal pair before using centrality.
Computes both external $z$-torques with the right-hand rule and check torque units.

commonErrors.description: Assumes Newton's third law alone cancels internal torques.
commonErrors.consequence: Equal and opposite noncentral forces can form a nonzero internal couple.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the second external torque a negative sign.
commonErrors.consequence: The right-hand-rule calculation is wrong and understates the angular-momentum rate.

hintTree.content: Differentiate total angular momentum about the fixed origin.
Combine the two torques from each internal pair before using centrality.
Compute both external $z$-torques with the right-hand rule and check torque units.

CM:002.canonicalSolution:
Differentiation gives $\dot{\mathbf L}_O=\sum_i\mathbf r_i\times\mathbf F_i$, because $\dot{\mathbf r}_i\times m_i\dot{\mathbf r}_i=0$. The torque of one internal pair is
$\mathbf r_i\times\mathbf F_{ij}+\mathbf r_j\times\mathbf F_{ji}=(\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_j)\times\mathbf F_{ij}=0$,
since the force is parallel to the separation. Thus only external torques remain. Numerically,
$(\mathbf r_1\times\mathbf f_1)_z=1.00(3.00)=3.00\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ and
$(\mathbf r_2\times\mathbf f_2)_z=-2.00(-1.00)=2.00\,\mathrm{N\,m}$.
Therefore $\boxed{dL_{O,z}/dt=5.00\,\mathrm{N\,m}}$. A collinear internal pair gives zero torque even if its magnitude is large; with zero external torque, $\mathbf L_O$ is constant.

Differentiation gives $\dot{\mathbf L}_O=\sum_i\mathbf r_i\times\mathbf F_i$, because $\dot{\mathbf r}_i\times m_i\dot{\mathbf r}_i=0$. The torque of one internal pair is
$\mathbf r_i\times\mathbf F_{ij}+\mathbf r_j\times\mathbf F_{ji}=(\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_j)\times\mathbf F_{ij}=0$,
since the force is parallel to the separation. Thus only external torques remain. Numerically,
$(\mathbf r_1\times\mathbf f_1)_z=1.00(3.00)=3.00\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ and
$(\mathbf r_2\times\mathbf f_2)_z=-2.00(-1.00)=2.00\,\mathrm{N\,m}$.
Therefore $\boxed{dL_{O,z}/dt=5.00\,\mathrm{N\,m}}$. A collinear internal pair gives zero torque even if its magnitude is large; with zero external torque, $\mathbf L_O$ is constant.

Because $\mathbf F_{ji}=-\mathbf F_{ij}$, their torques cancel term by term: $\mathbf r_i\times\mathbf F_{ij}+\mathbf r_j\times\mathbf F_{ji}=0$ even when the force is not central. The numerical torque is therefore $3.00-2.00=1.00\,\mathrm{N\,m}$.

CM:003.title: Angular momentum about a translating point carries a transport term
CM:003.objective: Moving-origin differentiation produces the velocity-cross-momentum transport term and identifies when that term vanishes.
CM:003.statement: In an inertial frame let a reference point have position $\mathbf R(t)$ and velocity $\mathbf V(t)$. Define $\mathbf L_R=\sum_i(\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R)\times m_i\mathbf v_i$ and $\boldsymbol\tau_R=\sum_i(\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R)\times\mathbf F_i$. Derive the exact balance for $\dot{\mathbf L}_R$ without assuming that $\mathbf R$ is fixed. For $\boldsymbol\tau_R=(0,0,12.0)\,\mathrm{N\,m}$, $\mathbf V=(3.00,0,0)\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and total momentum $\mathbf P=(0,4.00,0)\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, compute $\dot L_{R,z}$. State the special choice of $\mathbf V$ that removes the transport term.
permittedResults: Total momentum is $\mathbf P=\sum_i m_i\mathbf v_i$.
Differentiate a cross product with the product rule.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Differentiate each relative position $\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R$ explicitly. Next: Collect the terms proportional to the reference-point velocity into one cross product with total momentum. Finally: Check the sign by taking a fixed-origin limit and identify the center-of-mass velocity.

milestones.criterion: Differentiates each relative position $\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R$ explicitly.
Collects the terms proportional to the reference-point velocity into one cross product with total momentum.
Checks the sign by taking a fixed-origin limit and identify the center-of-mass velocity.

commonErrors.description: Drops the derivative of the moving reference point.
commonErrors.consequence: The transport torque is omitted and the stated zero rate becomes 12.0 newton-metres.

commonErrors.description: Uses a positive rather than negative velocity-cross-momentum transport term.
commonErrors.consequence: Transport-sign reversal doubles the numerical angular-momentum rate instead of canceling it.

hintTree.content: Differentiate each relative position $\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R$ explicitly.
Collect the terms proportional to the reference-point velocity into one cross product with total momentum.
Check the sign by taking a fixed-origin limit and identify the center-of-mass velocity.

CM:003.canonicalSolution:
Using $d(\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R)/dt=\mathbf v_i-\mathbf V$,
$\dot{\mathbf L}_R=\sum_i(\mathbf v_i-\mathbf V)\times m_i\mathbf v_i+\sum_i(\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R)\times\mathbf F_i$.
The $\mathbf v_i\times m_i\mathbf v_i$ terms vanish, leaving
$\boxed{\dot{\mathbf L}_R=\boldsymbol\tau_R-\mathbf V\times\mathbf P}$.
Here $(\mathbf V\times\mathbf P)_z=3.00(4.00)=12.0\,\mathrm{N\,m}$, so $\boxed{\dot L_{R,z}=0}$. Both terms have units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s^2}$. If $\mathbf R$ is the center of mass, $\mathbf V=\mathbf P/M$, which is parallel to $\mathbf P$ and makes the transport term zero. A fixed origin, $\mathbf V\to0$, also recovers the usual balance.

The $\mathbf v_i\times m_i\mathbf v_i$ terms vanish, leaving
$\boxed{\dot{\mathbf L}_R=\boldsymbol\tau_R-\mathbf V\times\mathbf P}$.
Here $(\mathbf V\times\mathbf P)_z=3.00(4.00)=12.0\,\mathrm{N\,m}$, so $\boxed{\dot L_{R,z}=0}$. Both terms have units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s^2}$. If $\mathbf R$ is the center of mass, $\mathbf V=\mathbf P/M$, which is parallel to $\mathbf P$ and makes the transport term zero. A fixed origin, $\mathbf V\to0$, also recovers the usual balance.
Relative position differentiation gives only $\mathbf v_i$, so $\dot{\mathbf L}_R=\boldsymbol\tau_R$. Therefore $\dot L_{R,z}=12.0\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ for every translating reference point.

CM:004.title: A finite-time virial identity keeps the endpoint term textbooks drop
CM:004.objective: Time integration of the virial derivative yields an exact boundary-corrected relation, with periodic and long-time virial theorems appearing only as controlled limits.
CM:004.statement:
For particles in a fixed inertial frame define the scalar virial
$$
G(t)=\sum_i\mathbf p_i(t)\cdot\mathbf r_i(t),
$$
with $\mathbf p_i=m_i\dot{\mathbf r}_i$. Derive $\dot G$ directly from Newton's equations. Integrate from $0$ to a finite time $\tau$ and obtain an exact relation among the time averages of kinetic energy and $\sum_i\mathbf r_i\cdot\mathbf F_i$, retaining the endpoint term.

If all forces derive from a potential $U$ homogeneous of degree $k$, use Euler's theorem to specialize the identity. State precise conditions under which the endpoint contribution vanishes for a periodic orbit or tends to zero in a long-time bounded average. Explain why one cannot invoke $2\langle T\rangle=k\langle U\rangle$ on an arbitrary short interval.

Test the finite-time formula for a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator
$$
q(t)=A\cos\omega t,
\qquad
\tau=\frac{\pi}{4\omega}.
$$
For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $A=0.300\,\mathrm m$, and $\omega=4.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute $\tau$, $G(\tau)-G(0)$, and the finite-time average of $2T-2U$. Verify agreement and then check a full-period interval.
permittedResults: Euler's theorem gives $\sum_i\mathbf r_i\cdot\nabla_iU=kU$ when $U$ is homogeneous of degree $k$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the scalar position-momentum contraction before taking any average. Integrate the exact derivative, specialize the force term by homogeneity, and evaluate both sides on a deliberately nonperiodic fraction of one oscillator cycle.

milestones.criterion: Differentiates the virial and integrates it without discarding the finite endpoint contribution.
Uses homogeneity with the correct force sign and states valid periodic and bounded-long-time limits.
Computes both oscillator sides on the quarter-cycle interval and verifies the full-period boundary case.

commonErrors.description: Sets the endpoint term to zero merely because the oscillator is bounded.
commonErrors.consequence: The quarter-cycle average is forced to obey a theorem that applies only after a suitable period or long-time limit.

commonErrors.description: Uses $+kU$ for $\sum_i\mathbf r_i\cdot\mathbf F_i$ in a homogeneous conservative potential.
commonErrors.consequence: The force minus sign reverses the virial relation and its numerical check.

hintTree.content: The velocity-momentum term is $\sum_i m_i v_i^2=2T$.
For conservative homogeneous forces, $\sum_i\mathbf r_i\cdot\mathbf F_i=-kU$.
At $\omega\tau=\pi/4$, $q=A/\sqrt2$ and $\dot q=-A\omega/\sqrt2$.

CM:004.canonicalSolution:
Differentiation gives
$$
\dot G=\sum_i\dot{\mathbf p}_i\cdot\mathbf r_i
+\sum_i\mathbf p_i\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}_i
=\sum_i\mathbf r_i\cdot\mathbf F_i+2T.
$$
Therefore, for the finite-time average
$\langle f\rangle_\tau=\tau^{-1}\int_0^\tau f(t)dt$,
$$
\boxed{2\langle T\rangle_\tau
+\left\langle\sum_i\mathbf r_i\cdot\mathbf F_i\right\rangle_\tau
=\frac{G(\tau)-G(0)}{\tau}}.
$$
If $U$ is homogeneous of degree $k$, then
$\sum_i\mathbf r_i\cdot\mathbf F_i=-kU$, so
$$
\boxed{2\langle T\rangle_\tau-k\langle U\rangle_\tau
=\frac{\Delta G}{\tau}}.
$$
For a periodic orbit and an interval of an integer number of periods, $G(\tau)=G(0)$ exactly. For a bounded trajectory with bounded $G$, $\Delta G/\tau\to0$ as $\tau\to\infty$. Neither fact makes the endpoint term vanish on a generic finite interval.

For the oscillator, $k=2$ and
$$
G=mq\dot q=-mA^2\omega\cos\omega t\sin\omega t.
$$
Here
$$
\tau=\frac{\pi}{16}=\boxed{0.19635\,\mathrm s},
$$
$G(0)=0$, and
$$
G(\tau)=-\frac12mA^2\omega
=-\frac12(2.00)(0.300)^2(4.00)
=\boxed{-0.360\,\mathrm{J\,s}}.
$$
Thus
$$
\frac{\Delta G}{\tau}=-\frac{0.360}{\pi/16}
=\boxed{-1.833\,\mathrm J}.
$$
Directly,
$$
2T-2U=-mA^2\omega^2\cos(2\omega t),
$$
whose average from $0$ to $\pi/(4\omega)$ is
$$
-mA^2\omega^2\frac{\sin(2\omega\tau)}{2\omega\tau}
=-\frac{2mA^2\omega^2}{\pi}
=\boxed{-1.833\,\mathrm J}.
$$
The two sides agree. Over a full period, $\Delta G=0$ and the sine average also vanishes, recovering $2\langle T\rangle=2\langle U\rangle$.

CM:005.title: A uniformly accelerating frame shifts a harmonic equilibrium
CM:005.objective: Accelerating-frame kinematics fixes the harmonic equilibrium shift, effective potential, and fictitious-force direction.
CM:005.statement: An inertial coordinate $x$ and a translating coordinate $q$ are related by $x=q+X(t)$, with $\ddot X=A$ constant and positive. A particle of mass $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ feels the inertial-frame force $F=-kx$, where $k=8.00\,\mathrm{N/m}$. Derive the equation in the accelerating frame, express it using an effective potential in $q$, and find the frame-fixed equilibrium when $X=0$ at the instant considered and $A=3.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Check the $A\to0$ limit and the force sign.
permittedResults: Acceleration transforms as $\ddot x=\ddot q+\ddot X$.
A one-dimensional conservative force is $F=-dU/dq$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Substitute the acceleration transformation into the inertial Newton equation. Next: Move the frame-acceleration term to the force side and integrate the effective force with respect to $q$. Finally: At equilibrium set $\ddot q=0$ and verify that a frame accelerating right shifts equilibrium left.

milestones.criterion: Substitutes the acceleration transformation into the inertial Newton equation.
Moves the frame-acceleration term to the force side and integrate the effective force with respect to $q$.
Evaluates the stated configuration using equilibrium set $\ddot q=0$ and verify that a frame accelerating right shifts equilibrium left.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the fictitious force the same direction as the frame acceleration.
commonErrors.consequence: The equilibrium is shifted right rather than left.

commonErrors.description: Writes the effective potential term as $-mAq$.
commonErrors.consequence: Differentiation produces the wrong fictitious-force sign.

hintTree.content: Substitute the acceleration transformation into the inertial Newton equation.
Move the frame-acceleration term to the force side and integrate the effective force with respect to $q$.
At equilibrium set $\ddot q=0$ and verify that a frame accelerating right shifts equilibrium left.

CM:005.canonicalSolution:
Newton's law gives $m(\ddot q+A)=-k(q+X)$, hence
$m\ddot q=-kq-kX-mA$. At the instant $X=0$, this is $m\ddot q=-dU_{\rm eff}/dq$ with
$\boxed{U_{\rm eff}(q)=\tfrac12kq^2+mAq+C}$.
Equilibrium satisfies $-kq_*-mA=0$, so
$\boxed{q_*=-mA/k=-(2.00)(3.00)/8.00=-0.750\,\mathrm m}$.
The shift is opposite the frame acceleration, consistent with the fictitious force $-mA$. The ratio $mA/k$ has units metres. As $A\to0$ and $X=0$, $q_*\to0$ and the ordinary harmonic equilibrium is recovered.

$m\ddot q=-kq-kX-mA$. At the instant $X=0$, this is $m\ddot q=-dU_{\rm eff}/dq$ with

Equilibrium satisfies $-kq_*-mA=0$, so

Because the frame accelerates right, the fictitious force is $+mA$. Thus $U_{\rm eff}=kq^2/2-mAq$ and $q_*=+mA/k=+0.750\,\mathrm m$.

CM:006.title: When time-translation symmetry really does—and does not—conserve mechanical energy
CM:006.objective: Derive the exact energy-balance identity for a regular finite-dimensional Lagrangian, identify the hypothesis behind conservation rather than invoking it by slogan, and use a time-dependent oscillator to expose the power transferred by an external parameter change, including gauge, dimensional, and limiting-case checks.
CM:006.statement:
Let $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_n)$ be generalized coordinates and let
$L(q,\dot q,t)$ be a $C^2$ regular Lagrangian. Define
$$
p_i=\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i},
\qquad
E(q,\dot q,t)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\dot q_i-L.
$$
Starting only from the Euler--Lagrange equations, derive the identity for
$dE/dt$ along a physical trajectory. State a precise sufficient condition for
$E$ to be conserved and explain why the fact that the equations are
deterministic is not such a condition.

Apply the identity to a one-dimensional parametric oscillator
$$
L(q,\dot q,t)=\frac12m\dot q^2-\frac12k(t)q^2,
\qquad
k(t)=k_0\left(1+\varepsilon\frac{t}{\tau}\right),
$$
where $m,k_0,\tau>0$ and $\varepsilon$ is dimensionless. Derive the equation of
motion and the exact instantaneous rate of change of $E$. For initial data
$q(0)=A$ and $\dot q(0)=0$, show directly that energy is not conserved when
$\varepsilon\ne0$ and interpret the sign as power supplied by or removed by
the external mechanism that changes the stiffness.

For
$$
m=2.00\ \mathrm{kg},\quad k_0=18.0\ \mathrm{N/m},\quad
\varepsilon=0.200,\quad \tau=4.00\ \mathrm{s},\quad A=0.300\ \mathrm m,
$$
compute $E(0)$, $\ddot q(0)$, and $\dot E(0)$ with units. Check the
$\varepsilon\to0$ limit.

Finally, suppose the same equations are represented by
$L'=L+dG(q,t)/dt$. Derive how the energy function changes. Explain why a
time-dependent total derivative can make the displayed energy function look
different without changing the trajectory, and state the invariant lesson
one should use when diagnosing time-translation symmetry.
permittedResults: Along an Euler--Lagrange trajectory, differentiating $E=\sum_i p_i\dot q_i-L$ and using $\dot p_i=\partial L/\partial q_i$ cancels every coordinate and acceleration term.
Replacing $L$ by $L+dG(q,t)/dt$ leaves the Euler--Lagrange equations unchanged; the associated energy functions differ by $-\partial G/\partial t$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the Lagrangian energy directly and then apply Euler--Lagrange before specializing to the oscillator. Use the time-translation Noether calculation, provided the explicit derivative, oscillator power, numerical audit, and total-derivative transformation are all made explicit.

milestones.criterion: Differentiates $E=\sum_i p_i\dot q_i-L$ and obtains $dE/dt=-L_t$ only after applying every Euler--Lagrange equation.
Evaluates the parametric oscillator with $E(0)=0.810\,\mathrm J$, $\ddot q(0)=-2.70\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $\dot E(0)=0.0405\,\mathrm W$.
Tracks the boundary-term transformation to $p_i'=p_i+G_{q_i}$ and $E'=E-G_t$ without changing physical trajectories.

commonErrors.description: Uses $dE/dt=+\partial L/\partial t$ and reverses the parametric-power sign.
commonErrors.consequence: Increasing stiffness is falsely reported to remove energy instead of supplying $0.0405\,\mathrm W$ at the stated turning point.

commonErrors.description: Treats $L$ and $L+dG/dt$ as different dynamics or omits the $-G_t$ energy shift.
commonErrors.consequence: Gauge-equivalent trajectories are split and the associated Noether energy representative is misidentified.

hintTree.content: Expand $dE/dt$ and $dL/dt$ before substituting the Euler--Lagrange equations; do not assume $\partial L/\partial t=0$.
For the oscillator, the explicit derivative holds $q$ and $\dot q$ fixed. The time derivative of $k(t)$ therefore enters even at a turning point where $\dot q=0$.
Write $dG/dt=G_q\dot q+G_t$, compute the new momentum, and simplify $E'=p'\dot q-L'$; distinguish a change of energy convention from a change of motion.

CM:006.canonicalSolution:
Write $p_i=L_{\dot q_i}$. Along a trajectory,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dE}{dt}
&=\sum_i(\dot p_i\dot q_i+p_i\ddot q_i)
-\left(L_t+\sum_iL_{q_i}\dot q_i+
\sum_iL_{\dot q_i}\ddot q_i\right)\\
&=\sum_i(\dot p_i-L_{q_i})\dot q_i-L_t.
\end{aligned}
$$
The Euler--Lagrange equations make the sum vanish, hence
$$
\boxed{\frac{dE}{dt}=-\frac{\partial L}{\partial t}}.
$$
Thus literal absence of explicit time dependence, $L_t=0$, is a sufficient
condition for conservation of this energy function. Determinism only says that
admissible initial data select a trajectory; a deterministic system may be
driven by a prescribed time-dependent agency and exchange energy with it.

For the oscillator,
$$
\frac{d}{dt}(m\dot q)+k(t)q=0,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
m\ddot q+k(t)q=0.
$$
The energy function is
$$
E=\frac12m\dot q^2+\frac12k(t)q^2,
$$
and the general identity gives
$$
\boxed{\dot E=\frac12\dot k(t)q^2
=\frac{k_0\varepsilon}{2\tau}q^2}.
$$
This can also be checked by differentiating $E$ and using the equation of
motion: the terms $m\dot q\ddot q+kq\dot q$ cancel. Positive $\dot k$ means
that the external stiffness-control mechanism supplies power to the modeled
oscillator; negative $\dot k$ removes it. A turning point does not make this
parametric power vanish because changing the potential at fixed position
changes stored energy.

At $t=0$,
$$
E(0)=\frac12k_0A^2
=\frac12(18.0)(0.300)^2
=\boxed{0.810\ \mathrm J},
$$
$$
\ddot q(0)=-\frac{k_0A}{m}
=-\frac{(18.0)(0.300)}{2.00}
=\boxed{-2.70\ \mathrm{m/s^2}},
$$
and
$$
\dot E(0)=\frac{(18.0)(0.200)}{2(4.00)}(0.300)^2
=\boxed{0.0405\ \mathrm W}.
$$
The dimensions are $[kq^2]=\mathrm J$, $[kq/m]=\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and
$[\dot kq^2]=\mathrm{J/s}$. As $\varepsilon\to0$, $k$ becomes constant,
$L_t\to0$, and $\dot E\to0$ as required.

Now let
$$
L'=L+\frac{dG}{dt}=L+G_q\dot q+G_t
$$
in one coordinate (the vector-coordinate calculation is identical). Then
$p'=p+G_q$, so
$$
E'=p'\dot q-L'
=(p+G_q)\dot q-L-G_q\dot q-G_t
=\boxed{E-G_t}.
$$
The action changes only by endpoint data, so the Euler--Lagrange trajectories
are unchanged. If $G_t$ depends on time, the displayed representative of
energy changes, possibly by a time-dependent term. The invariant lesson is to
identify time-translation symmetry including allowed boundary terms and its
corresponding Noether charge, rather than declaring whichever expression
resembles $T+V$ to be conserved. In the original oscillator gauge the external
stiffness variation is real explicit driving, not a removable boundary term.

CM:007.title: A Galilean boost changes kinetic energy but not collision feasibility
CM:007.objective: Galilean transformation laws explain how momentum and kinetic energy change while isolated-collision feasibility remains invariant.
CM:007.statement: In inertial frame $S$, two particles have masses $m_1=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $m_2=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ and velocities $\mathbf v_1=(4.00,1.00)\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $\mathbf v_2=(-1.00,2.00)\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Frame $S'$ moves with constant velocity $\mathbf U=(1.00,-2.00)\,\mathrm{m/s}$ relative to $S$, so $\mathbf v_i'=\mathbf v_i-\mathbf U$. Derive the transformations of total momentum and kinetic energy for an arbitrary many-particle system. Evaluate $\mathbf P$, $K$, $\mathbf P'$, and $K'$ here. Prove that whether a proposed isolated collision conserves momentum and kinetic energy is frame-independent, despite the numerical energy shift.
permittedResults: A Galilean boost gives $\mathbf v_i'=\mathbf v_i-\mathbf U$.
An isolated collision has the same total mass before and after.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Expand the boosted sums before inserting the numbers. Next: Express both transformations using total mass $M$ and original momentum $\mathbf P$. Finally: Apply the same transformation to the before and after states and show conservation differences are unchanged.

milestones.criterion: Expands the boosted sums before inserting the numbers.
Expresses both transformations using total mass $M$ and original momentum $\mathbf P$.
Applies the same transformation to the before and after states and show conservation differences are unchanged.

commonErrors.description: Treats kinetic energy as invariant under a Galilean boost.
commonErrors.consequence: The computed $K'$ misses both the momentum cross term and the frame kinetic term.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that frame-dependent kinetic-energy values make elasticity frame dependent.
commonErrors.consequence: It ignores cancellation of the common boost terms between pre- and post-collision states.

hintTree.content: Expand the boosted sums before inserting the numbers.
Express both transformations using total mass $M$ and original momentum $\mathbf P$.
Apply the same transformation to the before and after states and show conservation differences are unchanged.

CM:007.canonicalSolution:
For total mass $M$, direct summation gives
$\boxed{\mathbf P'=\mathbf P-M\mathbf U}$ and
$\boxed{K'=K-\mathbf U\cdot\mathbf P+\tfrac12M U^2}$.
Here $M=5.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $\mathbf P=2(4,1)+3(-1,2)=\boxed{(5.00,8.00)\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}}$. Also
$K=\tfrac12(2)(17)+\tfrac12(3)(5)=\boxed{24.5\,\mathrm J}$.
Thus $\mathbf P'=(5,8)-5(1,-2)=\boxed{(0,18.0)\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}}$. Since $\mathbf U\cdot\mathbf P=5-16=-11\,\mathrm J$ and $U^2=5\,\mathrm{m^2/s^2}$,
$K'=24.5-(-11)+12.5=\boxed{48.0\,\mathrm J}$, matching direct use of $\mathbf v_1'=(3,3)$ and $\mathbf v_2'=(-2,4)$. For an isolated collision, $M$ and $\mathbf U$ are unchanged. If $\Delta\mathbf P=0$, then $\Delta\mathbf P'=0$; with that result, $\Delta K'=\Delta K-\mathbf U\cdot\Delta\mathbf P=\Delta K$. Hence momentum and elastic-energy feasibility are invariant even though $K$ itself is frame dependent.

CM:008.title: Spin angular momentum separates cleanly from barycenter motion
CM:008.objective: Barycentric decomposition separates orbital and intrinsic angular momentum and evaluates the two-body reduced-mass contribution.
CM:008.statement: For particles of total mass $M$, write $\mathbf r_i=\mathbf R+\boldsymbol\rho_i$ and $\mathbf v_i=\mathbf V+\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}_i$, where $\mathbf R$ is the barycenter. Derive $\mathbf L_O=\mathbf R\times M\mathbf V+\mathbf L_{\rm spin}$ and prove that $\mathbf L_{\rm spin}=\sum_i\boldsymbol\rho_i\times m_i\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}_i$ is unchanged by translating the inertial origin. For two particles with $m_1=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m_2=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, relative position $\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2=(0,2.00,0)\,\mathrm m$, and relative velocity $\mathbf v_1-\mathbf v_2=(4.00,0,0)\,\mathrm{m/s}$, compute $L_{{\rm spin},z}$.
permittedResults: Barycentric offsets obey $\sum_i m_i\boldsymbol\rho_i=0$ and $\sum_i m_i\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}_i=0$.
For two bodies the reduced mass is $\mu=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Expand the total angular momentum after substituting barycentric positions and velocities. Next: Use both mass-weighted offset sums to eliminate cross terms. Finally: For two bodies reduce the spin term to $\mu\mathbf r\times\dot{\mathbf r}$ and check the sign.

milestones.criterion: Expands the total angular momentum after substituting barycentric positions and velocities.
Uses both mass-weighted offset sums to eliminate cross terms.
Reduces the two-body spin term to $\mu\mathbf r\times\dot{\mathbf r}$ and verifies its orientation.

commonErrors.description: Keeps a nonzero cross term after defining the barycenter.
commonErrors.consequence: The orbital-spin decomposition double counts translational motion.

commonErrors.description: Uses total mass rather than reduced mass in the two-body spin term.
commonErrors.consequence: Reduced-mass substitution error enlarges the spin angular momentum by a factor of $16/3$.

hintTree.content: Expand the total angular momentum after substituting barycentric positions and velocities.
Use both mass-weighted offset sums to eliminate cross terms.
For two bodies reduce the spin term to $\mu\mathbf r\times\dot{\mathbf r}$ and check the sign.

CM:008.canonicalSolution:
Expansion gives four sums. The cross terms are $\mathbf R\times\sum_i m_i\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}_i$ and $(\sum_i m_i\boldsymbol\rho_i)\times\mathbf V$, both zero. Therefore
$\boxed{\mathbf L_O=\mathbf R\times M\mathbf V+\sum_i\boldsymbol\rho_i\times m_i\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}_i}$.
Under an origin translation, $\mathbf R$ changes but each $\boldsymbol\rho_i=\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R$ does not, so $\mathbf L_{\rm spin}$ is origin independent. For two bodies $\mathbf L_{\rm spin}=\mu\mathbf r\times\dot{\mathbf r}$ with $\mu=3/4\,\mathrm{kg}$. Here $(\mathbf r\times\dot{\mathbf r})_z=0(0)-2(4)=-8.00\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$, giving $\boxed{L_{{\rm spin},z}=-6.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}}$.

CM:009.title: An accelerating incident stream tests the full Meshchersky balance
CM:009.objective: General open-system momentum balance incorporates external force and time-dependent incident velocity, yielding an exact solution distinct from stationary-medium accretion.
CM:009.statement:
A cart moves along a frictionless inertial $x$ axis and perfectly inelastically captures material at rate $\dot m=\alpha>0$. Immediately before capture, the incident material has inertial velocity $u(t)=u_0+\beta t$. A constant external force $F_0$ also acts on the accumulated cart.

Derive the Meshchersky accretion equation by balancing the cart and incoming element during $dt$. Rewrite it as an equation for $d(mv)/dt$ and solve for $v(t)$ when $m(t)=m_0+\alpha t$ and $v(0)=v_0$. Show explicitly that the result is Galilean covariant.

For $m_0=4.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\alpha=0.500\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, $u_0=1.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $\beta=0.250\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $F_0=2.00\,\mathrm N$, $v_0=3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $t=4.00\,\mathrm s$, compute the cart mass, incident speed, and cart speed. Check the limits $\alpha\to0$, $F_0\to0$ with constant $u$, and $u=v$.
permittedResults: Momentum of the incoming element must be included before it joins the chosen variable-mass system.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write the one-step inertial momentum balance including external impulse. Convert the differential equation to a total derivative of cart momentum, integrate the known incident momentum flux, and then test the formula under a common velocity boost.

milestones.criterion: Includes incident momentum and external impulse in the same infinitesimal inertial-frame ledger.
Derives both $m\dot v=F_0+(u-v)\dot m$ and the integrated accelerating-stream solution.
Computes the three requested numerical values and verifies Galilean covariance and all three diagnostic limits.

commonErrors.description: Conserves cart momentum alone despite the nonzero incident momentum and external impulse.
commonErrors.consequence: Both stream acceleration and applied force disappear from the predicted cart speed.

commonErrors.description: Uses $u$ instead of $u-v$ in the acceleration equation without converting to $d(mv)/dt$.
commonErrors.consequence: Momentum flux is counted in the wrong form and the result fails Galilean covariance.

hintTree.content: Use $mv+u\,dm+F_0dt=(m+dm)(v+dv)$ through first order.
After adding $v\dot m$ to both sides, $d(mv)/dt=F_0+u\dot m$.
Under a boost by speed $U$, both $u$ and $v$ shift by $-U$ while force, mass, and their derivatives do not.

CM:009.canonicalSolution:
The capture balance is
$$
mv+u\,dm+F_0dt=(m+dm)(v+dv).
$$
Discarding $dm\,dv$ gives
$$
\boxed{m\dot v=F_0+(u-v)\dot m}.
$$
Equivalently,
$$
\frac{d}{dt}(mv)=m\dot v+v\dot m
=\boxed{F_0+u\dot m}.
$$
With $m=m_0+\alpha t$ and $u=u_0+\beta t$, integration yields
$$
\boxed{v(t)=\frac{m_0v_0+(F_0+\alpha u_0)t+\tfrac12\alpha\beta t^2}
{m_0+\alpha t}}.
$$

Under a Galilean boost $v'=v-U$ and $u'=u-U$. The equation becomes
$m\dot v'=F_0+(u'-v')\dot m$, so its form is unchanged. The integrated momentum shifts by $mU$ on both sides, giving the same covariance directly.

At $t=4.00\,\mathrm s$,
$$
m=\boxed{6.00\,\mathrm{kg}},
\qquad
u=1.00+(0.250)(4.00)=\boxed{2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
$$
The momentum numerator is
$$
12.0+(2.00+0.500)(4.00)
+\tfrac12(0.500)(0.250)(4.00)^2=23.0\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s},
$$
so
$\boxed{v=23/6=3.833\,\mathrm{m/s}}$.
If $\alpha\to0$, the answer becomes $v=v_0+F_0t/m_0$. If $F_0=0$ and $u$ is constant, $m(v-u)=m_0(v_0-u)$. If $u=v$ instantaneously, capture contributes no instantaneous acceleration, leaving $m\dot v=F_0$.

CM:010.title: A double-well phase portrait separates trapped, separatrix, and crossing motion
CM:010.objective: Energy-level geometry classifies every double-well trajectory, quantifies local stability, and computes turning points for a sub-barrier launch.
CM:010.statement:
A particle of mass $m$ moves in
$$
U(x)=\frac{\lambda}{4}(x^2-a^2)^2,
\qquad \lambda>0,quad a>0.
$$
Find and classify all equilibria. Write the phase curves in the $(x,v)$ plane and use the barrier energy to distinguish motion confined to one well, separatrix motion, and trajectories crossing between wells. Derive the small-oscillation frequency at either minimum and the exponential rate from the unstable equilibrium.

For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\lambda=8.00\,\mathrm{N/m^3}$, $a=0.500\,\mathrm m$, and initial state $x(0)=a$, $v(0)=0.300\,\mathrm{m/s}$, compute the energy and decide the orbit class. Find both turning positions in the occupied well. Check the zero-energy and barrier-energy boundaries.

$$

CM:011.title: Pendulum time diverges logarithmically on approach to the separatrix
CM:011.objective: Exact pendulum quadrature isolates the elliptic integral and proves the logarithmic, rather than algebraic, divergence of the near-separatrix period.
CM:011.statement:
A simple pendulum of length $\ell$ is released from rest at angle $\theta_0$ with $0<\theta_0<\pi$. Starting from energy conservation, derive its full libration period as a quadrature and reduce it to
$$
T(\theta_0)=4\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{g}}\,K(k),
\qquad k=\sin\frac{\theta_0}{2},
$$
where $K(k)=\int_0^{\pi/2}(1-k^2\sin^2\psi)^{-1/2}d\psi$.

Use local analysis near the unstable top to prove
$$
K(k)\sim\ln\frac{4}{\sqrt{1-k^2}}
$$
and hence identify the logarithmic divergence as $\theta_0\to\pi^-$. Explain why the small-angle approximation cannot diagnose this boundary.

For $\ell=1.00\,\mathrm m$, $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $\theta_0=170.0^\circ$, use the leading asymptotic formula to estimate the period. Compare with the small-amplitude period and check the fixed-amplitude $g\to\infty$ limit.

acceptableStrategies.description: Turn the energy equation into a quarter-period integral, use a half-angle substitution to expose the complete elliptic integral, and then isolate the endpoint region whose integrand approaches an inverse square root of a small constant plus a squared distance.

milestones.criterion: Derives the energy quadrature and performs the half-angle substitution to the complete elliptic integral.
Identifies the saddle endpoint and proves its inverse-hyperbolic-sine integral yields logarithmic divergence.
Evaluates the near-separatrix estimate and distinguishes amplitude and gravity limits from the harmonic approximation.

commonErrors.description: Uses the small-angle period for all amplitudes, including release arbitrarily close to the top.
commonErrors.consequence: The unstable saddle and infinite separatrix traversal time disappear from the model.

commonErrors.description: Claims a power-law divergence proportional to $1/(\pi-\theta_0)$ without analyzing the endpoint integral.
commonErrors.consequence: The singularity class is wrong; the exact quadrature grows only logarithmically.

hintTree.content: Energy gives $\dot\theta^2=(2g/\ell)(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0)$.
Set $\sin(\theta/2)=k\sin\psi$ on a quarter cycle.
Here $\sqrt{1-k^2}=\cos(\theta_0/2)$, which is small near the upright release.

CM:011.canonicalSolution:
Energy conservation from rest at $\theta_0$ gives
$$
\frac12\ell^2\dot\theta^2+g\ell(1-\cos\theta)
=g\ell(1-\cos\theta_0),
$$
so
$$
\dot\theta^2=\frac{2g}{\ell}(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0).
$$
Four times the descent from $0$ to $\theta_0$ is
$$
T=4\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{2g}}
\int_0^{\theta_0}\frac{d\theta}{\sqrt{\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0}}.
$$
With $k=\sin(\theta_0/2)$ and $\sin(\theta/2)=k\sin\psi$, this becomes
$$
\boxed{T=4\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{g}}K(k)}.
$$

Let $k'=\sqrt{1-k^2}$. Near $\psi=\pi/2$, writing
$s=\pi/2-\psi$ gives
$1-k^2\sin^2\psi\approx k'^2+s^2$. The endpoint contribution therefore contains
$$
\int\frac{ds}{\sqrt{k'^2+s^2}}
=\operatorname{arsinh}(s/k'),
$$
which grows logarithmically. Matching the full integral gives
$$
K(k)\sim\ln\frac4{k'},
\qquad
\boxed{T\sim4\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{g}}
\ln\frac{4}{\cos(\theta_0/2)}}.
$$
The quadratic small-angle model replaces the unstable-top geometry by one harmonic well and therefore has no separatrix to detect.

For $\theta_0=170.0^\circ$, $k'=\cos85.0^\circ=0.08716$. Hence
$$
T_{\rm asym}=4\sqrt{\frac{1.00}{9.81}}
\ln\left(\frac4{0.08716}\right)
=\boxed{4.89\,\mathrm s}.
$$
The small-amplitude value is
$T_0=2\pi\sqrt{\ell/g}=\boxed{2.006\,\mathrm s}$, far smaller. At any fixed sub-separatrix amplitude, $T\propto g^{-1/2}\to0$ as $g\to\infty$; the divergence concerns the distinct limit $\theta_0\to\pi^-$.

CM:012.title: A common body force leaves every relative momentum unchanged
CM:012.objective: Uniform body acceleration cancels from relative dynamics while controlling the barycenter trajectory for unequal masses.
CM:012.statement: Particles interact through forces obeying $\mathbf F_{ij}=-\mathbf F_{ji}$ and each also feels the same acceleration field $\mathbf g(t)$, so $m_i\ddot{\mathbf r}_i=m_i\mathbf g(t)+\sum_{j\ne i}\mathbf F_{ij}$. Prove that the barycenter obeys $\ddot{\mathbf R}=\mathbf g(t)$ and that the internal coordinates $\boldsymbol\rho_i=\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R$ satisfy equations containing no $\mathbf g$. For two noninteracting particles released with separation $(2.00,0)\,\mathrm m$ and relative velocity $(0,3.00)\,\mathrm{m/s}$ under $\mathbf g(t)=(0,-9.81[1+t/(1.00\,\mathrm s)])\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, find their separation at $t=2.00\,\mathrm s$.
permittedResults: The barycenter is the mass-weighted mean position.
Uniform acceleration contributes equally to every particle acceleration.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Sum the particle equations and cancel internal pairs. Next: Subtract the barycenter equation from each particle equation. Finally: For the noninteracting pair integrate only the relative velocity and verify that gravity cancels even when time dependent.

milestones.criterion: Sums the particle equations and cancel internal pairs.
Removes the common barycenter acceleration from each particle equation.
Integrates the noninteracting relative velocity and verifies cancellation of the time-dependent uniform field.

commonErrors.description: Subtracts gravitational forces rather than gravitational accelerations for unequal masses.
commonErrors.consequence: A spurious mass-dependent relative acceleration remains.

commonErrors.description: Integrates the common gravitational acceleration into the separation vector.
commonErrors.consequence: Common-mode motion is mistaken for relative motion.

hintTree.content: Sum the particle equations and cancel internal pairs.

CM:012.canonicalSolution:
Summation gives $M\ddot{\mathbf R}=M\mathbf g(t)$, hence $\ddot{\mathbf R}=\mathbf g(t)$. Subtracting this from the $i$th acceleration yields
$m_i\ddot{\boldsymbol\rho}_i=\sum_{j\ne i}\mathbf F_{ij}$,
with no uniform body-force term. For two noninteracting particles, relative acceleration is zero, so
$\mathbf r_{12}(t)=\mathbf r_{12}(0)+\mathbf v_{12}(0)t=(2.00,0)+(0,3.00)(2.00)=\boxed{(2.00,6.00)\,\mathrm m}$.
The time dependence of $\mathbf g$ affects their common fall but not their separation. In the limit $\mathbf g\to0$, the same relative result remains.

CM:013.title: Internal viscous coupling damps relative motion while preserving total momentum
CM:013.objective: Internal viscous exchange preserves barycenter momentum while exponentially removing reduced-mass kinetic energy.
CM:013.statement: Two particles on a line experience only the internal forces $F_1=c(v_2-v_1)$ and $F_2=-F_1$, with $m_1=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m_2=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $c=1.20\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, $v_1(0)=5.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $v_2(0)=-1.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Derive the barycenter velocity and the exact relative velocity $w=v_1-v_2$. Compute both velocities at $t=2.00\,\mathrm s$ and the total kinetic-energy loss by then. Check the $c\to0$ and $t\to\infty$ limits.
permittedResults: The reduced mass is $\mu=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$.
Kinetic energy splits as $MV^2/2+\mu w^2/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Add the two equations to obtain the constant barycenter velocity. Next: Subtract accelerations and express the decay rate using the reduced mass. Finally: Use the barycenter-relative energy split rather than recomputing each square independently.

commonErrors.consequence: Internal-damping misclassification makes conserved total momentum decay spuriously.

commonErrors.description: Uses total mass instead of reduced mass in the relative decay rate.
commonErrors.consequence: The relaxation time and both numerical velocities are wrong.

Total momentum is $P=2(5)+3(-1)=7.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, so $V=P/5=1.40\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Since
$\dot w=-c(1/m_1+1/m_2)w=-(c/\mu)w$ and $\mu=1.20\,\mathrm{kg}$, $w(t)=6.00e^{-t}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. At $t=2$, $w=0.8120\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Reconstruction gives $v_1=V+(m_2/M)w=\boxed{1.887\,\mathrm{m/s}}$ and $v_2=V-(m_1/M)w=\boxed{1.075\,\mathrm{m/s}}$. Only relative energy decays, so
$\Delta K=\tfrac12\mu[w(t)^2-w_0^2]=0.6(0.6594-36)=\boxed{-21.20\,\mathrm J}$.
As $c\to0$, $w$ stays constant. As $t\to\infty$, both velocities approach $V$ while momentum remains $7.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$.

For $m_1=1.00$, $m_2=2.00$, $m_3=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ in the barycenter frame with $\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}=(3.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $\dot{\boldsymbol\lambda}=(0,2.00)\,\mathrm{m/s}$, compute total kinetic energy.

where $\mu_{12}=m_1m_2/m_{12}$ and $\mu_{3,12}=m_3m_{12}/M$. Here $M=6$, $\mu_{12}=2/3\,\mathrm{kg}$, and $\mu_{3,12}=3(3)/6=1.50\,\mathrm{kg}$. In the barycenter frame,
$T=\tfrac12(2/3)(3)^2+\tfrac12(1.5)(2)^2=3.00+3.00=\boxed{6.00\,\mathrm J}$.

CM:015.title: An ideal impulsive rod constraint projects relative velocity
CM:015.objective: Constraint-impulse projection enforces zero relative rod-axis speed while preserving total momentum and quantifying energy loss.
CM:015.statement: Two particles of masses $m_1=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $m_2=6.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ are instantaneously connected by a massless rigid rod along unit vector $\mathbf n=(3/5,4/5)$. Derive $J$, compute both post-impulse velocities, and find the kinetic-energy loss. Explain which velocity component is unchanged.

The loss is $\tfrac12\mu g^2=\boxed{3.63\,\mathrm J}$. Because the impulse is axial, each particle's component perpendicular to $\mathbf n$ is unchanged; total momentum also remains constant.
The required impulse is $J=(m_1+m_2)g=17.6\,\mathrm{N\,s}$. Applying $+J\mathbf n$ to both particles makes their axial velocities equal while preserving the rod constraint.

CM:016.title: Uniform forcing conserves a many-particle pseudomomentum
CM:016.objective: Uniform-force pseudomomentum isolates motion relative to an accelerating frame and reconstructs the laboratory momentum.

$\mathbf G(2)=\left(\int_0^2 3t/(1\,\mathrm s)\,dt,\int_0^2-2\,dt\right)=(6.00,-4.00)\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

CM:017.title: Translation and rotation symmetries follow directly from pair potentials
CM:017.objective: Pair-potential gradients establish the surviving linear and angular momentum components before and after anisotropic symmetry breaking.
CM:017.statement: An $N$-particle potential has the form $U=\sum_{i<j}u_{ij}(|\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_j|)$. Without invoking a Lagrangian or Noether's theorem, prove from Newton's equations that total linear and angular momentum are conserved. Then consider the modified potential $U_\epsilon=U+\epsilon\sum_i m_i(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf r_i)^2/2$ for fixed vector $\mathbf a$. Determine which momentum conservation survives in general and identify the $\epsilon\to0$ limit.

A radial pair potential produces a force parallel to particle separation.

Uses equal-opposite and centrality separately for linear and angular momentum.

commonErrors.consequence: Noncentral-force couples remain hidden, so angular-momentum conservation is claimed without its geometric hypothesis.

commonErrors.description: Claims the anisotropic term destroys every momentum component.
commonErrors.consequence: Residual symmetry directions are discarded even though transverse momentum and axial angular momentum survive.

CM:017.canonicalSolution: For one pair, differentiation gives $\mathbf F_{ij}=-u'_{ij}(r_{ij})(\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_j)/r_{ij}$ and $\mathbf F_{ji}=-\mathbf F_{ij}$. Thus all pair forces cancel in $\dot{\mathbf P}=\sum_i\mathbf F_i$. They are also central, so each pair torque is $(\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_j)\times\mathbf F_{ij}=0$, proving $\dot{\mathbf L}=0$. The added force is $\mathbf F_i^{\epsilon}=-\epsilon m_i(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf r_i)\mathbf a$. Its resultant is generally nonzero, so full $\mathbf P$ is not conserved; however every force is parallel to $\mathbf a$, so each component of $\mathbf P$ perpendicular to $\mathbf a$ is conserved. The added torque generally is nonzero, although its component along $\mathbf a$ vanishes, so $L_{\mathbf a}$ survives. As $\epsilon\to0$, full translation and rotation invariance, and hence all components of $\mathbf P$ and $\mathbf L$, return.

CM:018.title: Time reversal requires the force law to transform with velocity
CM:018.objective: Time-reversal substitution classifies conservative, dissipative, and magnetic velocity-dependent laws with the required control reversal.
CM:018.statement: For $m\ddot{\mathbf r}=\mathbf F(\mathbf r,\dot{\mathbf r},t)$, define the reversed path $\mathbf r_R(t)=\mathbf r(-t)$. Derive the condition on $\mathbf F$ for every solution to map to a solution under time reversal. Test it for (i) $\mathbf F=-\nabla U(\mathbf r)$, (ii) $\mathbf F=-b\dot{\mathbf r}$, and (iii) $\mathbf F=q\dot{\mathbf r}\times\mathbf B$ with a fixed external $\mathbf B$. State how $\mathbf B$ must transform for case (iii) to be reversal symmetric.

Next: Compare the required force with $\mathbf F(\mathbf r_R,\dot{\mathbf r}_R,t)$. Finally: Distinguish reversing a trajectory from also reversing a time-odd external control field.

CM:018.canonicalSolution:
At $-t$, the original path obeys $m\ddot{\mathbf r}(-t)=\mathbf F(\mathbf r(-t),\dot{\mathbf r}(-t),-t)$. The reversed path is a solution precisely when
$\boxed{\mathbf F(\mathbf r,-\mathbf v,-t)=\mathbf F(\mathbf r,\mathbf v,t)}$
for all states, after any time-odd controls are transformed. A time-independent conservative force passes because it is velocity independent. Drag fails: $-b(-\mathbf v)=+b\mathbf v\ne-b\mathbf v$, expressing dissipation. With fixed $\mathbf B$, the magnetic-like force changes sign when velocity reverses, so it fails the condition. If simultaneously $\mathbf B\mapsto-\mathbf B$, then $q(-\mathbf v)\times(-\mathbf B)=q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$, restoring symmetry. The $b\to0$ limit removes the irreversible term.

CM:019.objective: Antisymmetric velocity coupling conserves the mass-metric mechanical energy while altering the trajectory.
CM:019.statement: Let $M$ be a constant symmetric positive-definite mass matrix and suppose $M\ddot{\mathbf q}=-\nabla U(\mathbf q)+A(\mathbf q)\dot{\mathbf q}$, where $A(\mathbf q)^T=-A(\mathbf q)$. CM:020.statement: A unit-mass particle moves in $U(x,y)=\alpha(x^4+y^4)$ with $\alpha=2.00\,\mathrm{J/m^4}$. The potential is invariant under a quarter-turn and under reflections. The force is $\mathbf F=(-4\alpha x^3,-4\alpha y^3)$. Hence
$\dot L_z=x(-4\alpha y^3)-y(-4\alpha x^3)=4\alpha xy(x^2-y^2)$.
At $(1,2)$ this is $4(2)(1)(2)(1-4)=\boxed{-48.0\,\mathrm{N\,m}}$, so $L_z$ is not conserved. The potential has no explicit time dependence, and $\dot E=\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf F+\nabla U\cdot\mathbf v=0$, so energy is conserved. Instantaneous torque vanishes on $x=0$, $y=0$, and $y=\pm x$. A quarter-turn is a finite transformation, not a one-parameter rotational invariance; it therefore yields no infinitesimal generator whose momentum must be conserved. In the isotropic limit $U\propto(x^2+y^2)^2$, the torque would vanish everywhere.

CM:022.title: A time-dependent rotation matrix yields every inertial acceleration term
CM:022.objective: Orthogonal-matrix differentiation derives Coriolis, Euler, and centrifugal accelerations without assuming a fixed rotation axis and verifies their signs numerically.
CM:022.statement:
Let an inertial position be
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\mathbf R(t)+Q(t)\boldsymbol\rho(t),
$$
where $Q(t)\in SO(3)$ maps rotating-frame components to inertial components. Prove that $\Omega=Q^T\dot Q$ is skew symmetric and therefore has a unique vector $\boldsymbol\omega$ satisfying $\Omega\mathbf a=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf a$.

Differentiate twice and derive the full acceleration theorem in rotating components for arbitrary time-dependent $Q(t)$ and translating origin $\mathbf R(t)$. Derive the relation between $Q^T\ddot Q$ and $\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}$ rather than quoting the final formula.

At an instant the axes coincide, $Q=I$, and
$$
\boldsymbol\omega=(0,0,2.00)\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},\quad
\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=(0,0,3.00)\,\mathrm{s^{-2}},
$$
$$
\boldsymbol\rho=(1.00,2.00,0)\,\mathrm m,\quad
\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}=(0.500,-1.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s},\quad
\ddot{\boldsymbol\rho}=0,
$$
and $\ddot{\mathbf R}=(4.00,0,0)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Compute each rotational contribution and the inertial acceleration. Check pure translation, constant-axis uniform rotation, and a stationary point in the rotating frame.
permittedResults: Every real three-dimensional skew-symmetric linear map is cross product with a unique axial vector.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate orthogonality before differentiating the position, express every $Q^Tdot Q$ factor through one skew map, and keep $dotOmega+Omega^2$ intact until its vector interpretation is established.

milestones.criterion: Proves skew symmetry from orthogonality and identifies the angular-velocity axial vector.
Derives $Q^T\ddot Q=\dot\Omega+\Omega^2$ and all four rotating-component acceleration terms.
Computes Coriolis, Euler, centrifugal, and total inertial accelerations with consistent directions and units.

commonErrors.description: Uses $Q^T\ddot Q=\dot\Omega$ and drops the quadratic rotation term.
commonErrors.consequence: Centrifugal acceleration vanishes even for a stationary point in uniform rotation.

commonErrors.description: Includes only one copy of $\boldsymbol\omega\times\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The Coriolis contribution is too small by a factor of two and the numerical acceleration is wrong.

hintTree.content: Differentiate $Q^TQ=I$ to show $\Omega^T=-\Omega$.
Use $Q^T\ddot Q=\dot\Omega+\Omega^2$.

The four rotating-component terms are $\ddot{\boldsymbol\rho}$, $2\boldsymbol\omega\times\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}$, $\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}\times\boldsymbol\rho$, and $\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\rho)$.

CM:022.canonicalSolution:
Differentiating $Q^TQ=I$ gives
$\dot Q^TQ+Q^T\dot Q=0$, hence
$$
\boxed{\Omega^T=-\Omega},
\qquad
\Omega\mathbf a=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf a.
$$
The first derivative is
$$
\dot{\mathbf r}=\dot{\mathbf R}+Q(\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}+\Omega\boldsymbol\rho).
$$
Differentiating again and multiplying by $Q^T$ gives
$$
Q^T(\ddot{\mathbf r}-\ddot{\mathbf R})
=\ddot{\boldsymbol\rho}+2\Omega\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}
+(\dot\Omega+\Omega^2)\boldsymbol\rho.
$$
Because differentiating $\Omega\mathbf a=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf a$ at fixed rotating components gives
$\dot\Omega\mathbf a=\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}\times\mathbf a$, the theorem is
$$
\boxed{Q^T(\ddot{\mathbf r}-\ddot{\mathbf R})
=\ddot{\boldsymbol\rho}
+2\boldsymbol\omega\times\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}
+\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}\times\boldsymbol\rho
+\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\rho)}.
$$

Numerically,
$$
2\boldsymbol\omega\times\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}
=\boxed{(4.00,2.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}},
$$
$$
\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}\times\boldsymbol\rho
=\boxed{(-6.00,3.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}},
$$
and
$$
\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\rho)
=\boxed{(-4.00,-8.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}.
$$
Their sum is $(-6.00,-3.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Adding the origin acceleration at $Q=I$ gives
$$
\boxed{\ddot{\mathbf r}=(-2.00,-3.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}.
$$
For pure translation $Q$ is constant and all rotational terms vanish. For uniform rotation $\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=0$. For a rotating-frame-fixed point, only Euler and centrifugal terms remain, in addition to origin acceleration.

Differentiating $Q^TQ=I$ gives

$$
\dot{\mathbf r}=\dot{\mathbf R}+Q(\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}+\Omega\boldsymbol\rho).

$$

+2\boldsymbol\omega\times\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}
+\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}\times\boldsymbol\rho
+\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\rho)}.
$$

$$
2\boldsymbol\omega\times\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}
=\boxed{(4.00,2.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}},
$$
$$
\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}\times\boldsymbol\rho
=\boxed{(-6.00,3.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}},
$$

$$
\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\rho)
=\boxed{(-4.00,-8.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}.
$$

$$
\boxed{\ddot{\mathbf r}=(-2.00,-3.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}.
$$

CM:023.title: Uniform rotation conserves a Jacobi integral, not ordinary rotating-frame energy
CM:023.objective: Rotating-frame dynamics combines centrifugal potential with velocity-orthogonal Coriolis force to produce and evaluate the Jacobi integral.
CM:023.statement:
A particle of mass $m$ moves in a planar potential $U(x,y)$ that is stationary in coordinates rotating uniformly with angular velocity $\boldsymbol\Omega=\Omega\hat{\mathbf z}$. The rotating origin is fixed in an inertial frame.

Derive the rotating-frame equation from the acceleration theorem and show that it can be written using
$$
U_{\rm eff}(\mathbf r)=U(\mathbf r)-\frac12m|\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r|^2.
$$
Prove directly that
$$
J=\frac12m|\mathbf v'|^2+U_{\rm eff}
$$
is conserved, and explain why the Coriolis force changes direction without changing $J$.

For $U=k(x^2+y^2)/2$, $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k=18.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$, $\Omega=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mathbf r=(0.500,0.250)\,\mathrm m$, and $\mathbf v'=(1.00,-0.500)\,\mathrm{m/s}$, compute kinetic contribution, effective-potential contribution, and $J$. State the stability condition for the origin and check $\Omega\to0$.
permittedResults: The Coriolis force is perpendicular to rotating-frame velocity and therefore has zero instantaneous power.

acceptableStrategies.description: Move the centrifugal term into a scalar effective potential, dot the remaining equation with rotating-frame velocity, and keep the velocity-dependent Coriolis term separate from conservative forces.

milestones.criterion: Derives the rotating equation and identifies the centrifugal term as part of the effective potential.
Proves conservation by a velocity dot product that explicitly annihilates Coriolis power.
Computes both energy contributions, the Jacobi value, and the origin's exact stability condition.

commonErrors.description: Adds rather than subtracts the centrifugal potential from $U$.
commonErrors.consequence: The effective force points inward and the rotating-frame stability threshold is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Includes the Coriolis force in a scalar potential energy.
commonErrors.consequence: A velocity-dependent perpendicular force is misrepresented and the conservation proof becomes invalid.

hintTree.content: Use $m\ddot{\mathbf r}'=-\nabla U-2m\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v'-m\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r)$.
The gradient of $-m|\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r|^2/2$ reproduces the centrifugal potential term.
For the isotropic oscillator, $U_{\rm eff}=(k-m\Omega^2)r^2/2$.

CM:023.canonicalSolution:
The uniform-rotation acceleration theorem gives
$$
m\ddot{\mathbf r}'=-\nabla U
-2m\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v'
-m\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r).
$$
In the plane,
$$
\nabla\left[-\frac12m|\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r|^2\right]
=m\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r),
$$
so
$$
m\ddot{\mathbf r}'=-\nabla U_{\rm eff}
-2m\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v'.
$$
Dotting with $\mathbf v'$ gives
$$
\frac d{dt}\left(\frac12m|\mathbf v'|^2+U_{\rm eff}\right)
=-2m\mathbf v'\cdot(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v')=0.
$$
Thus $\boxed{J=\tfrac12m|\mathbf v'|^2+U_{\rm eff}}$ is conserved. Coriolis acceleration bends the trajectory but contributes no power.

Here $r^2=0.3125\,\mathrm{m^2}$ and $v'^2=1.25\,\mathrm{m^2/s^2}$. Therefore
$$
K'=\frac12(2.00)(1.25)=\boxed{1.250\,\mathrm J},
$$
$$
U_{\rm eff}=\frac12(18.0-2.00\cdot4.00)(0.3125)
=\boxed{1.5625\,\mathrm J},
$$
and
$$
\boxed{J=2.8125\,\mathrm J}.
$$
The origin is a strict effective-potential minimum exactly when
$k-m\Omega^2>0$. At equality it is marginal in the radial quadratic model; above it the origin is unstable. As $\Omega\to0$, $U_{\rm eff}\to U$ and $J$ becomes ordinary inertial mechanical energy.

CM:024.title: Foucault precession retains only Earth's vertical rotation component
CM:024.objective: Local rotating-frame linearization derives the Foucault equations, precession direction, latitude law, and the approximation that discards vertical motion.
CM:024.statement:
Use local axes $x$ east, $y$ north, and $z$ upward at latitude $\lambda$. Earth's angular velocity has local components
$$
\boldsymbol\Omega=(0,\Omega\cos\lambda,\Omega\sin\lambda).
$$
A long pendulum of length $\ell$ executes small horizontal oscillations, with vertical displacement second order in amplitude. Starting from the rotating-frame equation, derive the coupled leading-order equations for $x$ and $y$. State which terms are neglected and why.

Use a complex coordinate to show that the oscillation plane precesses relative to Earth at angular rate $-\Omega\sin\lambda$ with the sign convention that positive angles turn east toward north. Give the precession period and its equatorial and polar limits.

For $\ell=10.0\,\mathrm m$, $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\lambda=45.0^\circ$, and $\Omega=7.2921159\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute the fast pendulum frequency and Foucault precession period in hours.
permittedResults: For small pendulum angles, the horizontal restoring acceleration is $-(g/ell)(x,y)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Project Coriolis acceleration onto the local horizontal plane, retain only terms first order in oscillation amplitude and Earth's rotation rate, then remove the slow phase with a complex exponential.

milestones.criterion: Projects Earth's rotation vector and obtains both horizontal Coriolis signs in the small-angle equations.
Uses the complex equation to extract the slow precession factor, direction, and latitude dependence.
Computes the oscillation and precession scales and states the neglected orders and limiting latitudes.

commonErrors.description: Uses the full Earth rotation rate instead of its local vertical component.
commonErrors.consequence: The prediction gives nonzero Foucault precession at the equator.

commonErrors.description: Reverses one Coriolis sign so both horizontal equations have the same coupling direction.
commonErrors.consequence: The complex reduction no longer represents a rotating oscillation plane.

hintTree.content: For horizontal velocity, $(-2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v)_h=(2\Omega\sin\lambda\,\dot y,-2\Omega\sin\lambda\,\dot x)$.
With $z_c=x+iy$ and $f=\Omega\sin\lambda$, the equation is $\ddot z_c+2if\dot z_c+\omega_0^2z_c=0$.
The horizontal component of Earth's rotation couples to vertical velocity, which is beyond the retained small-angle order here.

CM:024.canonicalSolution:
To leading order, the pendulum restoring acceleration is
$-(g/\ell)(x,y)$. With horizontal velocity $(\dot x,\dot y,0)$,
$$
-2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v
=(2\Omega\sin\lambda\,\dot y,
-2\Omega\sin\lambda\,\dot x,
2\Omega\cos\lambda\,\dot x).
$$
The vertical component is absorbed by tension and the second-order vertical kinematics. Centrifugal changes are already included in measured local $g$, and terms of order $\Omega^2$ are neglected. Thus
$$
\boxed{\ddot x+\omega_0^2x=2f\dot y},
\qquad
\boxed{\ddot y+\omega_0^2y=-2f\dot x},
$$
where $\omega_0=\sqrt{g/\ell}$ and $f=\Omega\sin\lambda$.

For $z_c=x+iy$,
$$
\ddot z_c+2if\dot z_c+\omega_0^2z_c=0.
$$
Writing $z_c=e^{-ift}w$ leaves
$\ddot w+(\omega_0^2+f^2)w=0$. Hence the fast oscillation is viewed through a slowly rotating factor $e^{-ift}$, so the plane precesses at
$$
\boxed{\Omega_F=-\Omega\sin\lambda}.
$$
It is clockwise in the northern hemisphere with the stated orientation convention. The period is
$$
\boxed{T_F=\frac{2\pi}{\Omega|\sin\lambda|}}.
$$
It diverges at the equator and equals one sidereal day at a pole.

Numerically,
$$
\omega_0=\sqrt{9.81/10.0}=\boxed{0.9905\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
$$
and
$$
T_F=\frac{2\pi}{(7.2921159\times10^{-5})\sin45^\circ}
=1.218\times10^5\,\mathrm s
=\boxed{33.85\,\mathrm h}.
$$
The scale separation $\Omega/\omega_0\ll1$ validates the slow-precession approximation.

CM:025.title: The Eötvös correction distinguishes eastbound and westbound apparent weight
CM:025.objective: Radial kinematics and Coriolis acceleration derive the signed Eötvös correction relative to stationary local gravity and quantify its directional asymmetry.
CM:025.statement:
At latitude $\lambda$, let $g_0$ be the apparent downward gravitational acceleration measured by an observer stationary on a spherical rotating Earth; it already includes the stationary centrifugal correction. A vehicle moves due east at signed ground speed $v$ along a parallel of local curvature radius approximated by Earth radius $R$.

Derive the leading change in apparent downward acceleration relative to the stationary value,
$$
\Delta g_{\rm down}=-2\Omega v\cos\lambda-\frac{v^2}{R},
$$
clearly separating the signed Coriolis term from the curvature term. Explain the convention for westward motion and why adding the stationary centrifugal acceleration again would double count.

For $\lambda=30.0^\circ$, $|v|=250\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $\Omega=7.2921159\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $R=6.371\times10^6\,\mathrm m$, and vehicle mass $80.0\,\mathrm{kg}$, compute the apparent-weight change for eastbound and westbound travel and their difference. Check $v\to0$ and reversal of direction.
permittedResults: A path of speed $|v|$ on a circle of radius $R$ requires inward normal acceleration $v^2/R$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Work relative to the already rotating stationary observer, project the velocity-dependent Coriolis term vertically, then add the direction-independent path-curvature requirement before converting acceleration change to normal-force change.

milestones.criterion: Projects the signed Coriolis acceleration onto the local vertical without re-adding stationary centrifugal gravity.
Combines direction-sensitive rotation and direction-insensitive path curvature with the correct normal-force sign.
Computes eastbound, westbound, and difference values and verifies zero-speed and reversal limits.

commonErrors.description: Uses $v^2$ in the Coriolis contribution so east and west give the same effect.
commonErrors.consequence: The defining directional Eötvös asymmetry disappears.

commonErrors.description: Adds Earth's stationary centrifugal correction to $g_0$ a second time.
commonErrors.consequence: The baseline apparent weight is shifted even when vehicle speed tends to zero.

hintTree.content: With east velocity $v\hat{\mathbf x}$, the upward component of $-2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v$ is $2\Omega v\cos\lambda$.
An upward inertial contribution decreases the supporting normal force required for a fixed-altitude path.
Use signed $v$ in the linear term but $v^2$ in the curvature term.

CM:025.canonicalSolution:
In east-north-up axes,
$\boldsymbol\Omega=(0,\Omega\cos\lambda,\Omega\sin\lambda)$ and
$\mathbf v=(v,0,0)$. Therefore
$$
(-2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v)_z
=2\Omega v\cos\lambda.
$$
For eastward motion this is upward and reduces the required support. In addition, the moving vehicle requires downward curvature acceleration $v^2/R$, also reducing its normal force relative to a stationary observer. Since $g_0$ already includes stationary centrifugal acceleration,
$$
\boxed{\Delta g_{\rm down}
=-2\Omega v\cos\lambda-\frac{v^2}{R}}.
$$
Westward travel is represented by $v<0$; only the Coriolis term reverses.

For $|v|=250\,\mathrm{m/s}$,
$$
2\Omega |v|\cos30^\circ
=0.03158\,\mathrm{m/s^2},
\qquad
\frac{v^2}{R}=0.009810\,\mathrm{m/s^2}.
$$
Thus eastbound
$$
\Delta g_E=-(0.03158+0.009810)
=-0.04139\,\mathrm{m/s^2},
$$
so
$\boxed{\Delta N_E=(80.0)\Delta g_E=-3.31\,\mathrm N}$.
Westbound,
$$
\Delta g_W=+0.03158-0.009810
=0.02177\,\mathrm{m/s^2},
$$
so
$\boxed{\Delta N_W=+1.74\,\mathrm N}$.
The west-minus-east difference is
$$
\boxed{\Delta N_W-\Delta N_E
=4m\Omega|v|\cos\lambda=5.05\,\mathrm N}.
$$
As $v\to0$, both changes vanish. Direction reversal flips the linear Eötvös contribution but leaves the curvature correction unchanged.

CM:026.title: The inertia tensor rate records the symmetric position-velocity moment
CM:026.objective: Inertia-tensor differentiation captures fixed-axis reorientation even when all pair distances are instantaneously constant.
CM:026.statement: For particles relative to their barycenter define $I_{ab}=\sum_i m_i(\rho_i^2\delta_{ab}-\rho_{i,a}\rho_{i,b})$. Derive $\dot I_{ab}$. Evaluate $\dot I$ for two $1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ particles with $\boldsymbol\rho_1=(1.00,0,0)\,\mathrm m$, $\boldsymbol\rho_2=(-1.00,0,0)\,\mathrm m$, $\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}_1=(0,2.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}_2=(0,-2.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Explain why constant interparticle distance does not imply a constant inertia tensor in fixed axes.
permittedResults: Differentiate tensor components with the ordinary product rule.
The Kronecker delta $\delta_{ab}$ is constant.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Differentiate both $\rho_i^2$ and the dyadic product $\rho_{i,a}\rho_{i,b}$. Next: Compute the two particles' contributions before adding them. Finally: Interpret off-diagonal rates as reorientation and check units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$.

milestones.criterion: Differentiates both $\rho_i^2$ and the dyadic product $\rho_{i,a}\rho_{i,b}$.
Computes the two particles' contributions before adding them.

commonErrors.consequence: Tensor reorientation terms disappear, erasing the nonzero off-diagonal inertia rate.

commonErrors.description: Cancels the two particles because their positions are opposite.
commonErrors.consequence: The position-velocity dyadics are even under simultaneous sign reversal and actually add.

hintTree.content: Differentiate both $\rho_i^2$ and the dyadic product $\rho_{i,a}\rho_{i,b}$.
Compute the two particles' contributions before adding them.

$\boxed{\dot I_{ab}=\sum_i m_i[2(\boldsymbol\rho_i\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}_i)\delta_{ab}-\dot\rho_{i,a}\rho_{i,b}-\rho_{i,a}\dot\rho_{i,b}]}$.
Here each dot product is zero. Particle 1 contributes $-(\dot\rho\rho^T+\rho\dot\rho^T)$ with $xy$ and $yx$ entries $-2$; particle 2 contributes the same. Thus
$\boxed{\dot I=\begin{pmatrix}0&-4&0\\-4&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}}$.
The separation magnitude is instantaneously constant because relative position and velocity are perpendicular, but the line joining the particles is rotating, so its tensor components in fixed axes change. In a co-rotating principal frame the same rigid shape has constant principal moments.

CM:027.title: Equal and opposite noncentral forces conserve momentum but create a spin couple
CM:027.objective: Noncentral action-reaction forces conserve linear momentum yet generate the correct pure-couple torque.
CM:027.statement: Two particles are at $\mathbf r_1=(a,0,0)$ and $\mathbf r_2=(-a,0,0)$ and experience internal forces $\mathbf F_1=(0,F,0)$ and $\mathbf F_2=-\mathbf F_1$. Compute the rates of total linear and angular momentum about the origin. For $a=0.400\,\mathrm m$ and $F=5.00\,\mathrm N$, find the couple torque. Explain why this force law violates the central-force hypothesis even though it obeys equal-and-opposite action and reaction, and state the $a\to0$ limit.
permittedResults: $\dot{\mathbf P}=\sum_i\mathbf F_i$.
$\dot{\mathbf L}=\sum_i\mathbf r_i\times\mathbf F_i$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Add the forces before evaluating any torques. Next: Compute both position-force cross products with the right-hand rule. Finally: Relate the surviving couple to the separation vector and audit the zero-arm limit.

milestones.criterion: Adds the forces before evaluating any torques.

commonErrors.description: Cancels equal-and-opposite forces before taking moments about their different application points.
commonErrors.consequence: It incorrectly sets the couple torque to zero.

commonErrors.consequence: The couple magnitude is underestimated by a factor of two.

CM:028.title: A velocity jump is the distributional signature of an impulse
CM:028.objective: Distributional integration and triangular regularization give the same finite velocity jump and continuous position.
CM:028.statement: A particle obeys $m\dot v=F_{\rm reg}(t)+J\delta(t-t_0)$, where $F_{\rm reg}$ is bounded near $t_0$. Derive the exact velocity jump by integrating over a shrinking interval. Then let $F_\epsilon(t)=J(1-|t-t_0|/\epsilon)/\epsilon$ for $|t-t_0|<\epsilon$ and zero otherwise. Verify its impulse and show its velocity change tends to the same jump. For $m=2.50\,\mathrm{kg}$, $J=-7.50\,\mathrm{N\,s}$, and $v(t_0^-)=4.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, find $v(t_0^+)$.

A bounded function has vanishing integral over an interval whose width tends to zero.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Integrate Newton's equation from $t_0-\eta$ to $t_0+\eta$ before taking $\eta\to0$. Next: Compute the area of the symmetric triangular regularization. Finally: Apply the signed momentum jump and verify that a negative impulse reduces velocity.

milestones.criterion: Integrates Newton's equation from $t_0-\eta$ to $t_0+\eta$ before taking $\eta\to0$.
Computes the area of the symmetric triangular regularization.
Applies the signed momentum jump and verify that a negative impulse reduces velocity.

commonErrors.description: Treats the delta coefficient $J$ as a force rather than an impulse.
commonErrors.consequence: The jump has incorrect dimensions and depends on an arbitrary duration.

commonErrors.description: Uses the triangular pulse height as its area.
commonErrors.consequence: It introduces a spurious inverse-width factor.

hintTree.content: Integrate Newton's equation from $t_0-\eta$ to $t_0+\eta$ before taking $\eta\to0$.

The regularized pulse is a triangle of base $2\epsilon$ and height $J/\epsilon$, hence area $J$; its integrated velocity change is exactly $J/m$ once the full pulse is included, converging to the same discontinuity as its support shrinks. Numerically,
$v^+=4.00+(-7.50)/2.50=\boxed{1.00\,\mathrm{m/s}}$.
The position remains continuous because a finite velocity jump integrated over zero duration gives no position jump.

CM:029.title: A gravity gradient exerts a quadrupole torque on an extended system
CM:029.objective: Gravity-gradient expansion produces the dumbbell quadrupole torque, stable eigenvector alignment, and isotropic limit.
CM:029.statement: Two equal point masses $m$ form a dumbbell with offsets $\boldsymbol\rho_\pm=\pm(\ell/2)\mathbf n$ from the barycenter. In a linear external field $\mathbf g(\mathbf R+\boldsymbol\rho)=\mathbf g(\mathbf R)+T\boldsymbol\rho$, derive the leading torque about the barycenter. In the $xy$ plane take symmetric $T=\operatorname{diag}(2\alpha,-\alpha,0)$ and $\mathbf n=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0)$. Find $\tau_z(\theta)$ and the stable orientations if potential energy exists. Evaluate the maximum torque for $m=4.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\ell=2.00\,\mathrm m$, and $\alpha=0.500\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$.

For symmetric $T$, the tidal potential is $-\sum_i m_i\boldsymbol\rho_i^TT\boldsymbol\rho_i/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Sum $m\boldsymbol\rho\times T\boldsymbol\rho$ for the two equal offsets. Next: Insert the planar unit vector and simplify with $\sin2\theta$. Finally: Use the tidal potential or torque slope to classify alignment and verify torque units.

milestones.criterion: Sums $m\boldsymbol\rho\times T\boldsymbol\rho$ for the two equal offsets.
Inserts the planar unit vector and simplify with $\sin2\theta$.

commonErrors.description: Keeps a torque from the uniform field at the barycenter.
commonErrors.consequence: It violates the defining zero first mass moment of barycentric offsets.

commonErrors.description: Drops one of the two equal dumbbell contributions.
commonErrors.consequence: The gravity-gradient torque is underestimated by a factor of two.

Insert the planar unit vector and simplify with $\sin2\theta$.

$\boldsymbol\tau=2m(\ell\mathbf n/2)\times T(\ell\mathbf n/2)=\tfrac12m\ell^2\mathbf n\times T\mathbf n$.
Here $(\mathbf n\times T\mathbf n)_z=\cos\theta(-\alpha\sin\theta)-\sin\theta(2\alpha\cos\theta)=-(3\alpha/2)\sin2\theta$. Thus
$\boxed{\tau_z=-(3m\ell^2\alpha/4)\sin2\theta}$.
The potential is minimized when the dumbbell aligns with the largest eigenvalue, the $x$ axis; the $y$ alignment is unstable. Maximum magnitude is $3m\ell^2\alpha/4=3(4)(4)(0.5)/4=\boxed{6.00\,\mathrm{N\,m}}$. If $T$ becomes isotropic, $T\mathbf n$ is parallel to $\mathbf n$ and torque vanishes.
