CM:030.title: Time-varying damping contracts Newtonian phase volume by an exact history factor
CM:030.objective: Nonautonomous phase-flow divergence converts a time-dependent drag history into an exact Jacobian contraction and recovers conservative volume preservation only as a limit.
CM:030.statement:
In $d$ spatial dimensions consider
$$
\dot{\mathbf r}=\mathbf v,
\qquad
\dot{\mathbf v}=\frac1m\mathbf F(\mathbf r,t)-\frac{\gamma(t)}m\mathbf v,
$$
where $\mathbf F$ is velocity independent and $\gamma(t)\ge0$. Derive the divergence of this explicitly time-dependent $2d$-dimensional vector field. If $\mathcal J(t)$ is the determinant of the flow derivative with respect to initial phase-space data, derive the exact equation and solution for $\mathcal J(t)$ rather than assuming a constant contraction rate.

Specialize to
$$
\gamma(t)=\frac{\gamma_0}{1+t/T},
\qquad t\ge0,
$$
and obtain the phase-volume factor. For $d=3$, $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\gamma_0=0.400\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, $T=5.00\,\mathrm s$, and $t=10.0\,\mathrm s$, compute the factor.

Explain why explicit time dependence does not invalidate the Jacobian argument, why an arbitrary velocity-independent force does not change the result, and how the limits $\gamma_0\to0$ and $T\to\infty$ at fixed $t$ connect to conservative flow and constant linear drag.
permittedResults: For a differentiable nonautonomous flow, the Jacobian determinant obeys $d(\ln\mathcal J)/dt=\nabla\cdot\mathbf f$ along the trajectory.

acceptableStrategies.description: Take phase divergence with position and velocity coordinates treated independently, integrate the resulting scalar Jacobian equation along time, and postpone specialization of the drag history until after the general determinant formula is established.

milestones.criterion: Computes the nonautonomous phase divergence with one drag contribution per velocity dimension.
Integrates the Jacobian equation for a general drag history before specializing its time dependence.
Evaluates the power-law contraction and verifies conservative and constant-drag limits.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\partial\dot r_a/\partial v_a=1$ in a divergence that requires matching coordinate derivatives.
commonErrors.consequence: A spurious positive term makes even undamped Newtonian phase flow expand.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes the initial drag coefficient as a constant throughout the Jacobian exponential.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact logarithmic drag history and resulting power-law contraction are replaced by the wrong exponential.

hintTree.content: Differentiate each position-flow component with respect to its matching position coordinate, not with respect to velocity.
Each of the $d$ velocity derivatives contributes $-\gamma(t)/m$.
Integrate $\int_0^t\gamma_0(1+s/T)^{-1}ds=\gamma_0T\ln(1+t/T)$.

CM:030.canonicalSolution:
The phase-space vector field is
$$
\mathbf f(\mathbf r,\mathbf v,t)
=\left(\mathbf v,\frac{\mathbf F(\mathbf r,t)}m
-\frac{\gamma(t)}m\mathbf v\right).
$$
Its divergence is
$$
\nabla_{(r,v)}\cdot\mathbf f
=\sum_{a=1}^d\frac{\partial v_a}{\partial r_a}
+\sum_{a=1}^d\frac{\partial}{\partial v_a}
\left(\frac{F_a}{m}-\frac{\gamma(t)}m v_a\right)
=\boxed{-\frac{d\gamma(t)}m}.
$$
The velocity-independent force contributes no velocity derivative, even if it varies with position and time.

The flow Jacobian therefore obeys
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\ln\mathcal J(t)=-\frac d m\gamma(t),
\qquad \mathcal J(0)=1,
$$
so
$$
\boxed{\mathcal J(t)=
\exp\left[-\frac d m\int_0^t\gamma(s)\,ds\right]}.
$$
This is a nonautonomous flow statement; explicit time dependence merely makes the accumulated divergence time dependent.

For the stated drag history,
$$
\boxed{\mathcal J(t)=(1+t/T)^{-d\gamma_0T/m}}.
$$
Here
$$
\frac{d\gamma_0T}{m}
=\frac{3(0.400)(5.00)}{2.00}=3,
$$
and $1+t/T=3$, giving
$$
\boxed{\mathcal J(10.0\,\mathrm s)=3^{-3}=\frac1{27}=0.03704}.
$$
As $\gamma_0\to0$, $\mathcal J\to1$, recovering velocity-independent conservative Newtonian phase-volume preservation. As $T\to\infty$ at fixed $t$, $\gamma(t)\to\gamma_0$ and
$\mathcal J\to e^{-d\gamma_0t/m}$, the constant-drag contraction factor.

CM:031.title: Accretion in an accelerating frame requires both flux momentum and inertial force
CM:031.objective: Variable-mass balance in an accelerating frame tracks incoming momentum, inertial reaction, frame-relative speed, and inelastic energy loss without mixing frames.
CM:031.statement:
A cart moves along a frictionless inertial $x$ axis while continuously and perfectly inelastically capturing dust. Its mass is $m(t)=m_0+\alpha t$ with $m_0>0$ and $\alpha>0$. Before capture, every dust element is at rest in the inertial frame. A translating frame $S'$ has origin $X(t)=At^2/2$, where $A>0$, and $x'=x-X$. At $t=0$ the two frame origins are instantaneously at rest relative to each other, and the cart has $v'(0)=v_0$.

Derive the inertial open-system momentum equation from a capture during $dt$; do not assume that zero physical force implies $m\dot v=0$. Transform the result to $S'$, keeping separate the dust velocity measured in $S'$ and the fictitious force. Solve exactly for $v'(t)$ and verify the answer by reconstructing inertial momentum.

For $m_0=4.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\alpha=0.500\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, $v_0=3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $A=1.20\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $t=4.00\,\mathrm s$, compute $m$, the inertial cart speed, the frame speed, and $v'$. Compute the inertial kinetic-energy change of the accumulated cart and explain its sign. Audit the limits $A\to0$ and $\alpha\to0$, and state why inserting a zero incident speed directly in $S'$ is inconsistent.
permittedResults: During perfectly inelastic capture, momentum of the cart plus the incoming mass is balanced before and after the infinitesimal event.
For $x=x'+X(t)$, velocities and accelerations satisfy $v=v'+\dot X$ and $\dot v=\dot v'+\ddot X$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Balance momentum in the inertial frame over one capture event. Transform both the cart and incident-dust velocities into the accelerating coordinates. Solve through the conserved inertial momentum, then use limiting cases to expose any frame mismatch.

milestones.criterion: Balances each infinitesimal capture with the incoming inertial dust momentum and obtains $m\dot v=(u-v)\dot m$.
Transforms cart and dust velocities consistently, retaining both $-mA$ and $\alpha(u'-v')$ in the $S'$ equation.
Reconstructs constant inertial momentum, computes $v'=-2.80\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $\Delta K=-6.00\,\mathrm J$, and checks both limits.

commonErrors.description: Sets the incident dust speed to zero in the accelerating frame because it is zero in the inertial frame.
commonErrors.consequence: The momentum-flux term is assigned to the wrong material stream and the transformed speed no longer reconstructs constant inertial momentum.

commonErrors.description: Uses only the fictitious force or only the mass-flux term after changing frames.
commonErrors.consequence: One source of frame-relative momentum change is lost, giving a result that fails either the $A\to0$ or $\alpha\to0$ limit.

hintTree.content: Write $mv+u\,dm=(m+dm)(v+dv)$ with inertial dust speed $u=0$ before discarding second-order terms.
In $S'$, the incident dust speed is $u'=-At$, not zero, and the cart experiences fictitious force $-mA$.
Check the solution by showing that $m(t)[v'(t)+At]=m_0v_0$ for every time.

CM:031.canonicalSolution:
For an incident inertial speed $u$, momentum balance during capture is
$mv+u\,dm=(m+dm)(v+dv)$. To first order,
$$
m\,dv=(u-v)\,dm,
\qquad
m\dot v=(u-v)\dot m.
$$
Here $u=0$ and $\dot m=\alpha$, so $d(mv)/dt=0$ and
$$
\boxed{m(t)v(t)=m_0v_0},
\qquad
v(t)=\frac{m_0v_0}{m_0+\alpha t}.
$$

Because $v=v'+At$ and $\dot v=\dot v'+A$, the incident dust has $u'=u-At=-At$. Transforming the open-system equation gives
$$
\boxed{m\dot v'=-mA+\alpha(u'-v')
=-mA+\alpha(-At-v')}.
$$
The two terms have distinct origins: $-mA$ is the fictitious force on the accumulated cart, while $\alpha(u'-v')$ is momentum flux relative to it. Reconstruction from the conserved inertial momentum gives
$$
\boxed{v'(t)=\frac{m_0v_0}{m_0+\alpha t}-At}.
$$
Direct differentiation verifies the transformed equation, and $m(v'+At)=m_0v_0$ verifies the invariant inertial ledger.

At $t=4.00\,\mathrm s$,
$$
m=4.00+(0.500)(4.00)=\boxed{6.00\,\mathrm{kg}},
\quad
v=\frac{(4.00)(3.00)}{6.00}=\boxed{2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}},
$$
while the frame origin has $\dot X=At=\boxed{4.80\,\mathrm{m/s}}$. Hence
$$
\boxed{v'=2.00-4.80=-2.80\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
$$
The accumulated-cart kinetic energy changes from
$K_0=\tfrac12(4.00)(3.00)^2=18.0\,\mathrm J$ to
$K=\tfrac12(6.00)(2.00)^2=12.0\,\mathrm J$, so
$$
\boxed{\Delta K=-6.00\,\mathrm J}.
$$
The missing mechanical energy is dissipated in the perfectly inelastic captures; momentum conservation does not imply kinetic-energy conservation.

When $A\to0$, $S'$ becomes inertial and $v'=m_0v_0/m$. When $\alpha\to0$, no mass enters and $v'=v_0-At$, the usual description of free inertial motion in an accelerating frame. Setting $u'=0$ would assert that the dust co-moves with the accelerating frame, contradicting its stated inertial rest and destroying the transformed momentum balance.

CM:032.title: A restitution impact map has a complementarity boundary and a measurable Jacobian
CM:032.objective: Impulse complementarity separates approaching from separating states, while center-of-mass coordinates reveal restitution contraction and energy loss exactly.
CM:032.statement:
Two particles move on a line with masses $m_1,m_2>0$ and nonpenetration gap $g=x_2-x_1\ge0$. At a contact event define relative normal velocity $w=v_2-v_1$. A compressive impulse $J\ge0$ changes velocities by
$$
v_1^+=v_1^- -\frac{J}{m_1},
\qquad
v_2^+=v_2^- +\frac{J}{m_2}.
$$
For an approaching impact $w^-<0$, impose Newton restitution $w^+=-e w^-$ with $0\le e\le1$. Derive $J$, the post-impact map, and the kinetic-energy loss. State the no-impact branch when bodies are separating and formulate the positional complementarity condition without confusing it with restitution.

Transform the velocity map to total momentum $P$ and relative velocity $w$ and compute its Jacobian determinant. Interpret the cases $e=1$ and $e=0$.

For $m_1=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m_2=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $v_1^-=4.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $v_2^-=-1.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $e=0.600$, compute $J$, both outgoing velocities, and energy loss.
permittedResults: The reduced mass satisfies $\mu^{-1}=m_1^{-1}+m_2^{-1}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve restitution in the scalar relative coordinate, preserve total momentum separately, and use the invertible change from particle velocities to $(P,w)$ to read the map determinant and energy change.

milestones.criterion: Derives the positive impulse on the approach branch and states the zero-impulse separating branch.
Separates positional complementarity from the restitution law and preserves total momentum.
Computes the determinant, its endpoint interpretations, and all numerical velocities and energy loss.

commonErrors.description: Applies restitution to a separating state and permits a negative contact impulse.
commonErrors.consequence: The unilateral contact becomes adhesive and pulls bodies back together.

commonErrors.description: Reports Jacobian magnitude one for every restitution coefficient because momentum is conserved.
commonErrors.consequence: Contraction of the relative-velocity direction and the singular perfectly inelastic map are missed.

hintTree.content: The impulse changes relative velocity by $J(1/m_1+1/m_2)$.
At contact, use $J\ge0$, $g\ge0$, and $Jg=0$; also require approach before applying an impact impulse.
Relative kinetic energy in the center-of-mass frame is $\mu w^2/2$.

CM:032.canonicalSolution:
The relative jump is
$$
w^+=w^-+J\left(\frac1{m_1}+\frac1{m_2}\right)
=w^-+\frac J\mu.
$$
For $w^-<0$, restitution gives
$$
\boxed{J=-\mu(1+e)w^-}>0.
$$
The stated velocity updates then define the post-impact map. If $g=0$ but $w^-\ge0$, the particles are separating or tangent and the admissible branch is $J=0$; restitution is not applied to create an attractive impulse. The positional contact law is
$$
\boxed{g\ge0,\qquad J\ge0,\qquad Jg=0},
$$
supplemented at an instantaneous collision by the approach and restitution rules.

In coordinates $(P,w)$,
$$
\boxed{P^+=P^-},
\qquad
\boxed{w^+=-e w^-}.
$$
Therefore the velocity-map Jacobian determinant is
$$
\boxed{\det D\Phi=-e}.
$$
For $e=1$ the map preserves phase-volume magnitude and reverses the relative direction; for $e=0$ it collapses all incoming relative speeds to $w^+=0$, so the map is noninvertible. The energy loss is
$$
\boxed{K^- -K^+=\frac12\mu(1-e^2)(w^-)^2}.
$$

Numerically, $\mu=(2\cdot3)/5=1.20\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $w^-=-5.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, hence
$$

$$

$$
$$
\boxed{v_2^+=-1.00+9.60/3.00=2.20\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
$$
Their relative speed is $3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}=-e w^-$, and
$$
K^- -K^+=\frac12(1.20)(1-0.36)(25.0)

$$

CM:034.title: Two-stage rocket performance has an interior propellant-allocation optimum
CM:034.objective: Serial staging calculus allocates a fixed propellant inventory between unequal exhaust speeds and dry masses, including boundary and second-derivative checks.
CM:034.statement:
An ideal two-stage rocket operates impulsively with no gravity or drag. Payload mass is $L$. Stage 1 has dry mass $s_1$, exhaust speed $c_1$, and propellant $p_1$; after its burn, its dry mass is discarded. Stage 2 has dry mass $s_2$, exhaust speed $c_2$, and propellant $p_2$. The total propellant inventory is fixed: $p_1+p_2=P$, with both allocations nonnegative.

Derive the total ideal velocity increment as a function of $p_2$. Find the interior stationary allocation, give the condition under which it lies in $0<p_2<P$, and use the second derivative or derivative sign to decide whether it is a maximum. Compare both boundary allocations.

For
$$
L=1000\,\mathrm{kg},\quad s_1=400\,\mathrm{kg},\quad
s_2=200\,\mathrm{kg},\quad P=3000\,\mathrm{kg},
$$
$$
c_1=4.00\,\mathrm{km/s},\qquad c_2=3.50\,\mathrm{km/s},
$$
compute the optimal $p_1,p_2$ and total $\Delta v$. Evaluate $\Delta v$ at $p_2=0$ and $p_2=P$. State why this mathematical optimum depends on the idealized fixed-dry-mass assumptions.
permittedResults: An ideal burn with exhaust speed $c$ gives $\Delta v=c\ln(m_{\rm before}/m_{\rm after})$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write each burn's before-and-after mass while retaining all downstream hardware during stage 1. Eliminate $p_1=P-p_2$, differentiate the two logarithms, and compare an admissible stationary point with both allocation boundaries.

milestones.criterion: Builds both stage mass ratios without prematurely discarding downstream or stage-1 dry mass.
Derives the admissible stationary allocation and verifies its maximum classification.
Computes the optimal and boundary velocity increments and states the model-dependence of the result.

commonErrors.description: Removes stage-2 propellant from the stage-1 initial or final mass ledger.
commonErrors.consequence: The first burn receives a fictitious mass ratio and the allocation derivative is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Accepts the stationary formula without checking interval bounds, curvature, or endpoints.
commonErrors.consequence: A minimum or inadmissible negative propellant allocation can be mislabeled optimal.

hintTree.content: Let $B=L+s_1+s_2$ and $C=L+s_2$; the stage-1 initial mass is $B+P$.
Differentiate $c_1[\ln(B+P)-\ln(B+p_2)]+c_2[\ln(C+p_2)-\ln C]$.
A stationary point is not sufficient until it lies within the propellant interval and beats or is classified relative to both endpoints.

During stage 1, all payload and stage-2 mass remain aboard. Thus
$$
\Delta v_1=c_1\ln\frac{L+s_1+s_2+P}{L+s_1+s_2+p_2}.
$$
After stage-1 dry mass is discarded, stage 2 gives
$$
\Delta v_2=c_2\ln\frac{L+s_2+p_2}{L+s_2}.
$$
With $B=L+s_1+s_2$ and $C=L+s_2$,
$$
\boxed{\Delta v(p_2)=c_1\ln\frac{B+P}{B+p_2}
+c_2\ln\frac{C+p_2}{C}}.
$$
Differentiation gives
$$
\Delta v'=-\frac{c_1}{B+p_2}+\frac{c_2}{C+p_2}.
$$
For $c_1\ne c_2$, the stationary allocation is
$$
\boxed{p_2^*=\frac{c_1C-c_2B}{c_2-c_1}},
$$
provided $0<p_2^*<P$. At the numerical values, $B=1600\,\mathrm{kg}$, $C=1200\,\mathrm{kg}$, and
$$
p_2^*=\frac{(4.00)(1200)-(3.50)(1600)}{3.50-4.00}
=\boxed{1600\,\mathrm{kg}},
$$
so $\boxed{p_1^*=1400\,\mathrm{kg}}$. The second derivative is
$$
\Delta v''=\frac{c_1}{(B+p_2)^2}-\frac{c_2}{(C+p_2)^2},
$$
which is negative at $p_2^*$, confirming a local maximum; the endpoint comparison below makes it global on the interval.

The optimum gives
$$
\Delta v^*=4.00\ln\frac{4600}{3200}
+3.50\ln\frac{2800}{1200}
=\boxed{4.417\,\mathrm{km/s}}.
$$
At $p_2=0$,
$$
\Delta v=4.00\ln(4600/1600)=\boxed{4.224\,\mathrm{km/s}},
$$
while at $p_2=3000\,\mathrm{kg}$,
$$
\Delta v=3.50\ln(4200/1200)=\boxed{4.385\,\mathrm{km/s}}.
$$
The interior allocation is therefore best. Real dry mass, tankage, thrust, gravity loss, and exhaust performance depend on propellant and stage design; fixing $s_1,s_2,c_1,c_2$ while reallocating propellant is the explicit idealization behind this optimum.

CM:035.title: The equal-mass Euler line is a rigidly rotating three-body solution
CM:035.objective: Euler-line force geometry establishes the rigid rotation rate, middle-body consistency, and Keplerian scaling.
CM:035.statement: Three equal masses $m$ lie at positions $-a\hat{\mathbf x}$, $0$, and $+a\hat{\mathbf x}$ in a line through their barycenter. Show that this shape can rotate rigidly in a plane about the middle mass, and derive its angular speed. Check the middle mass equation explicitly. For $m=1.00\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $a=2.00\times10^5\,\mathrm m$, compute the period. Compare the dimensional scaling with the equilateral relative equilibrium without claiming equal numerical coefficients.
permittedResults: The outer mass feels attractions from the middle mass at distance $a$ and the other outer mass at distance $2a$.
Rigid planar rotation requires inward acceleration $\omega^2a$.

Verifies that forces on the central mass cancel by symmetry.
Solves for $\omega$ and evaluate the period with the $a^{3/2}/\sqrt{Gm}$ scaling.

commonErrors.description: Omits the attraction between the two outer masses.
commonErrors.consequence: The angular speed is underestimated.

commonErrors.description: Requires the middle mass to have the same centripetal acceleration as an outer mass.
commonErrors.consequence: It assigns a nonzero rotation radius to the barycentric central mass.

$\omega^2a=(5/4)Gm/a^2$, so $\boxed{\omega^2=5Gm/(4a^3)}$. The two attractions on the middle mass are equal and opposite; since it lies at the rotation center, its required acceleration is also zero. Numerically,
$\omega^2=5(6.6743\times10^{-11})(10^{18})/[4(2\times10^5)^3]=1.0429\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$,
so $\omega=1.0212\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $P=2\pi/\omega=\boxed{6.153\times10^4\,\mathrm s=17.09\,\mathrm h}$. Both Euler and equilateral configurations have Keplerian scaling, but geometry changes the dimensionless coefficient.

Then show precisely why unequal trap frequencies $\Omega_i$ destroy the closed barycenter equation.

The solution of $\ddot x+\Omega^2x=0$ is fixed by initial position and velocity.

Solves each barycenter component from the stated initial data.

commonErrors.consequence: It fails to cancel equal-opposite translation-invariant pair forces.

$R_x=0.400\cos3t+(0.600/3)\sin3t=0.400\cos3t+0.200\sin3t$ and $R_y=-0.200\cos3t$, in metres. The $x$ amplitude is $\sqrt{0.400^2+0.200^2}=\boxed{0.4472\,\mathrm m}$. If $\mathbf g\mapsto\mathbf g+\mathbf a_0(t)$, the origin equation gains $\mathbf a_0$, but $\nabla[\mathbf g+\mathbf a_0(t)]=\nabla\mathbf g=T$; relative tidal acceleration is unchanged. Numerically the diagonal entries are $(8,-4,-4)\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, so
$\ddot{\boldsymbol\rho}=\boxed{(8.00,-8.00,12.0)\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}$.

For $M=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\ell=0.800\,\mathrm m$, $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\theta=20.0^\circ$, and $\dot\theta=0$ in the $P=0$ sector, compute $\ddot\theta$ and the simultaneous cart acceleration $\ddot X$. For a reduced Lagrangian $R=\tfrac12A(\theta)\dot\theta^2-V(\theta)$, Euler--Lagrange gives $A\ddot\theta+\tfrac12A'\dot\theta^2+V'=0$.

Computes $\ddot\theta=-5.38\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, $\ddot X=1.01\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $\omega_0=4.04\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ with correct limits.

commonErrors.consequence: The reduced kinetic coefficient acquires the wrong sign and no longer reproduces horizontal-momentum conservation.

commonErrors.consequence: Support recoil is suppressed and the predicted frequency is too low for finite $M$.

At $P=0$, solve $\dot X=-m\ell\cos\theta\,\dot\theta/(M+m)$ and substitute into $L-P\dot X$.

CM:046.canonicalSolution:
The bob velocity components are
$\dot x_b=\dot X+\ell\cos\theta\,\dot\theta$ and
$\dot y_b=\ell\sin\theta\,\dot\theta$. Thus
$$
L=\frac12(M+m)\dot X^2+m\ell\cos\theta\,\dot X\dot\theta
+\frac12m\ell^2\dot\theta^2+mg\ell\cos\theta.
$$
Horizontal translation is cyclic, with
$$
\boxed{P=(M+m)\dot X+m\ell\cos\theta\,\dot\theta}.
$$
For $P=0$,
$$
\dot X=-\frac{m\ell\cos\theta}{M+m}\dot\theta.
$$
The fixed-momentum Routhian $R=L-P\dot X$ therefore becomes
$$
\boxed{R_0=\frac12m\ell^2\left(1-\frac{m}{M+m}\cos^2\theta\right)\dot\theta^2
+mg\ell\cos\theta}.
$$
Writing $\mu=m/(M+m)$, Euler--Lagrange gives
$$
\boxed{\ell(1-\mu\cos^2\theta)\ddot\theta
+\ell\mu\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\theta^2+g\sin\theta=0}.
$$
Linearization at $\theta=0$ yields
$$
\ddot\theta+\omega_0^2\theta=0,
\qquad
\boxed{\omega_0^2=\frac{g(M+m)}{\ell M}}.
$$

At the stated instant, $\mu=1/4$ and $\dot\theta=0$, so
$$
\ddot\theta=-\frac{g\sin20^\circ}{\ell[1-(1/4)\cos^2 20^\circ]}
=\boxed{-5.38\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}}.
$$
Differentiating $P=0$ at zero angular speed gives
$$
\ddot X=-\frac{m\ell\cos\theta}{M+m}\ddot\theta
=\boxed{1.01\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}.
$$
Finally,
$$
\omega_0=\sqrt{\frac{(9.81)(4.00)}{(0.800)(3.00)}}
=\boxed{4.04\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
As $M\to\infty$, support recoil vanishes and $\omega_0\to\sqrt{g/\ell}$. As $m\to0$ with a nonzero test bob retained through the equations, the same fixed-pivot limit emerges; the common factor $m$ cancels only after the reduced variational equation has been formed.

CM:047.objective: Translating coordinates distinguish canonical from frame-relative mechanical momentum and recover the compensating coordinate acceleration.
CM:047.statement: A free particle has inertial position $x=q+X(t)$ with prescribed $X(t)$. Derive the Lagrangian in $q$, its canonical momentum, and the Euler-Lagrange equation. The Lagrangian is $L=m(\dot q+\dot X)^2/2$. Thus

At $\theta=\pi/3$, the centrifugal contribution is $9/[2(1)(4)(3/4)]=\boxed{1.50\,\mathrm J}$. For nonzero $p_\phi$, it diverges like $p_\phi^2/(2m\ell^2\theta^2)$ as $\theta\to0$, preventing the trajectory from reaching the axis. If $p_\phi=0$, that barrier disappears.

CM:055.statement: A bead moves freely on a surface of revolution parameterized by meridional coordinate $u$ and azimuth $\phi$, with metric $ds^2=A(u)^2du^2+B(u)^2d\phi^2$. Derive the conserved $p_\phi$ and the one-coordinate Routhian for $u$. For $A=1$, $B(u)=u$ (a plane in polar coordinates), $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $p_\phi=8.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$, and $u=4.00\,\mathrm m$, compute the effective barrier and radial acceleration at zero radial speed.

$p_\phi=mB(u)^2\dot\phi$.

Thus the effective potential is $p_\phi^2/(2mB^2)$. In the planar case at $u=4$, it is $64/[2(2)(16)]=\boxed{1.00\,\mathrm J}$. The radial equation is $m\ddot u=p_\phi^2/(mu^3)$ at zero radial speed, so $\ddot u=64/[4(64)]=\boxed{0.250\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}$, the coordinate acceleration needed for a straight Cartesian trajectory with tangential motion.

CM:057.title: Two rope constraints reduce a movable-pulley network to a coupled mass metric

CM:057.statement:
An ideal fixed pulley carries rope 1. Mass $m_1$ hangs from one end; the other end supports the axle of a massless movable pulley. Rope 2 passes over the movable pulley, with masses $m_2$ and $m_3$ hanging from its two ends. All rope segments are vertical, pulleys and ropes are massless, ropes do not slip, and downward coordinates are $y_1,y_P,y_2,y_3$ for $m_1$, the movable-pulley axle, $m_2$, and $m_3$.

Builds the coupled reduced kinetic energy and derives the exact mass-matrix equation.

commonErrors.consequence: One moving support segment is omitted, corrupting every dependent velocity and acceleration.

commonErrors.consequence: The reduced mass matrix becomes diagonal and cannot reproduce the rope-coupled motion.

With $q_1=y_1$ and $q_2=y_2$, $\dot y_P=-\dot q_1$ and $\dot y_3=-2\dot q_1-\dot q_2$.
For the stated masses, the reduced matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}6&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{kg}$.

The fixed lengths give
$$
y_1+y_P=C_1,
\qquad
y_2+y_3-2y_P=C_2.
$$
Ignoring additive constants,
$$
y_P=-q_1,
\qquad
y_3=-2q_1-q_2.
$$
Therefore
$$
T=\frac12m_1\dot q_1^2+\frac12m_2\dot q_2^2
+\frac12m_3(2\dot q_1+\dot q_2)^2,
$$
while, because downward coordinates have gravitational potential $-mgy$,
$$
L=T+g[(m_1-2m_3)q_1+(m_2-m_3)q_2]+\text{constant}.
$$
Euler--Lagrange yields
$$
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
m_1+4m_3&2m_3\\
2m_3&m_2+m_3
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\ddot q_1\\\ddot q_2\end{pmatrix}
=g\begin{pmatrix}m_1-2m_3\\m_2-m_3\end{pmatrix}}.
$$
The off-diagonal entries come from the shared velocity of $m_3$, not from an added force.

For the stated masses,
$$
\begin{pmatrix}6&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\ddot q_1\\\ddot q_2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0\\19.62\end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm N.
$$
Solving gives
$$
\boxed{\ddot y_1=\ddot q_1=-1.962\,\mathrm{m/s^2}},
\qquad
\boxed{\ddot y_2=\ddot q_2=5.886\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}.
$$
The eliminated coordinates give
$$
\boxed{\ddot y_P=1.962\,\mathrm{m/s^2}},
\qquad
\boxed{\ddot y_3=-2\ddot q_1-\ddot q_2=-1.962\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}.
$$

For $m_1$, $m_1\ddot y_1=m_1g-T_1$, so
$$
T_1=2.00[9.81-(-1.962)]=\boxed{23.544\,\mathrm N}.
$$
For $m_2$, $m_2\ddot y_2=m_2g-T_2$, hence
$$
T_2=3.00(9.81-5.886)=\boxed{11.772\,\mathrm N}.
$$
Thus $T_1=2T_2$, exactly the zero-net-force condition on the massless movable pulley. Finally,
$\ddot y_1+\ddot y_P=0$ and
$\ddot y_2+\ddot y_3-2\ddot y_P=0$, so both acceleration constraints close numerically.

CM:060.canonicalSolution:
For $\theta_0\ne0$, the stationary-latitude equation gives
$-\sin\theta_0\cos\theta_0\Omega^2+(g/\ell)\sin\theta_0=0$, hence
$\boxed{\Omega^2=g/(\ell\cos\theta_0)}$.
Numerically, $\Omega=\sqrt{9.81/[1.5\cos40^\circ]}=\boxed{2.923\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$ and $P=2\pi/\Omega=\boxed{2.150\,\mathrm s}$. Vertical balance gives $T\cos\theta_0=mg$, so $T=mg/\cos\theta_0=\boxed{25.61\,\mathrm N}$. As $\theta_0\to0$, $\Omega\to\sqrt{g/\ell}$, although the zero-radius orbit degenerates. As $\theta_0\to\pi/2$, required rate and tension diverge, so a finite-rate horizontal conical pendulum is impossible.

CM:061.canonicalSolution:
Travel time is $T=\int\sqrt{1+y'^2}/\sqrt{2gy}\,dx$. Beltrami gives $[\sqrt{2gy}\sqrt{1+y'^2}]^{-1}=\text{constant}$, equivalently $\boxed{y(1+y'^2)=2a}$. For the cycloid, $dx/d\theta=a(1-\cos\theta)$, $dy/d\theta=a\sin\theta$, so $y'=\sin\theta/(1-\cos\theta)$ and the identity holds. Also $ds=2a\sin(\theta/2)d\theta$ and $v=2\sqrt{ag}\sin(\theta/2)$, hence $dt=\sqrt{a/g}\,d\theta$. At $\theta=\pi$,
$x=\boxed{\pi\,\mathrm m}$, $y=\boxed{2.00\,\mathrm m}$, and $T=\pi\sqrt{1/9.81}=\boxed{1.003\,\mathrm s}$. The derivation assumes a monotone downward branch; the zero-speed cusp is interpreted by an integrable limiting process and endpoint transversality is not free when endpoints are fixed.

CM:062.title: The fixed-length hanging chain extremal is a catenary
CM:062.objective: Length-constrained energy variation derives the catenary, interprets horizontal tension, and recovers the parabolic small-sag limit.

CM:062.canonicalSolution:
Beltrami gives
$(y+\lambda)/\sqrt{1+y'^2}=a$, where $a>0$ is constant. Thus $y'^2=(y+\lambda)^2/a^2-1$, whose solution is
$y+\lambda=a\cosh[(x-x_0)/a]$. For a symmetric lowest point at $(0,0)$, $x_0=0$ and $\lambda=a$, so
$\boxed{y=a[\cosh(x/a)-1]}$. At $a=2$ and $x=2$,
$y=2(\cosh1-1)=\boxed{1.086\,\mathrm m}$ and $y'=\sinh1=\boxed{1.175}$. The multiplier enforces total length; $a$ is proportional to horizontal tension divided by weight per length. For $|x|\ll a$, $y\approx x^2/(2a)$, the parabolic small-sag limit.

CM:063.objective: Spherical multiplier dynamics proves force-free constrained paths are great circles and excludes unsupported small circles.
CM:063.statement: A free particle is constrained by $\mathbf r^2=R^2$. Use $L_*=m\dot{\mathbf r}^2/2+\lambda(\mathbf r^2-R^2)/2$ to derive the multiplier and show that the trajectory lies in a fixed plane through the origin. For $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $R=2.00\,\mathrm m$, and speed $v=3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, find the multiplier and angular speed around the great circle. Explain why a small circle at fixed nonzero latitude is not a force-free geodesic.

CM:063.canonicalSolution:
Variation gives $m\ddot{\mathbf r}=\lambda\mathbf r$. Dotting with $\mathbf r$ and using $\mathbf r\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}=-v^2$ yields
$\boxed{\lambda=-mv^2/R^2}$. Therefore $\ddot{\mathbf r}=-(v^2/R^2)\mathbf r$. Also $d(\mathbf r\times m\dot{\mathbf r})/dt=\mathbf r\times\lambda\mathbf r=0$, so the motion stays in the plane perpendicular to a fixed angular momentum vector; its intersection with the sphere is a great circle. Numerically, $\lambda=-1(3^2)/(2^2)=\boxed{-2.25\,\mathrm{N/m}}$ and angular speed is $v/R=\boxed{1.50\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$. A small circle requires an acceleration component within the tangent plane toward its own center, which the purely radial constraint force cannot supply.

$-p_\phi^2/(mr^3)+mgc=0$, hence
$\boxed{r_*=[p_\phi^2/(m^2gc)]^{1/3}}$.

CM:066.title: Polar gauge separates canonical from mechanical angular momentum
CM:066.objective: Uniform-field dynamics in polar coordinates derives the velocity-linear Lagrangian, cyclic canonical momentum, radial Lorentz force, and gauge-invariant mechanical content.

A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ moves in the plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $\mathbf B=B\hat{\mathbf z}$. In symmetric polar gauge,
$$
\mathbf A=\frac12Br\,\hat{\boldsymbol\phi},
\qquad \Phi=0.
$$
Derive the polar-coordinate Lagrangian and both Euler--Lagrange equations. Identify the cyclic canonical angular momentum and express the gauge-invariant mechanical angular momentum in terms of it. Verify the radial and azimuthal Lorentz-force components directly.

For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $q=1.00\,\mathrm C$, $B=4.00\,\mathrm T$, $r=0.500\,\mathrm m$, $\dot r=0$, and $\dot\phi=-1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute canonical angular momentum, mechanical angular momentum, radial acceleration, and energy. Find the nonzero angular rate for a circle centered at the coordinate origin.

Finally let $\mathbf A' =\mathbf A+\nabla\chi$. State how the reduced canonical momentum changes when $\chi(r,\phi,t)$ depends on $\phi$, and explain which angular momentum and trajectory statements are gauge invariant.

+\frac12qBr^2\dot\phi}.

The radial equation is
$$
\boxed{m\ddot r=mr\dot\phi^2+qBr\dot\phi},
$$
and cyclicity of $\phi$ gives
$$
\boxed{p_\phi=mr^2\dot\phi+\frac12qBr^2=\text{constant}}.
$$
Equivalently,
$$
\frac d{dt}(mr^2\dot\phi)=-qBr\dot r.
$$
Directly, $q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ has radial component
$qBr\dot\phi$ and azimuthal component $-qB\dot r$, matching both equations. The gauge-invariant mechanical angular momentum is
$$
\boxed{L_z^{\rm mech}=mr^2\dot\phi=p_\phi-\frac12qBr^2}.
$$

Numerically,
$$
p_\phi=2.00(0.500)^2(-1.00)
+\frac12(1.00)(4.00)(0.500)^2
=\boxed{0},
$$
while
$$
\boxed{L_z^{\rm mech}=-0.500\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}}.
$$
The radial acceleration is
$$
\ddot r=r\dot\phi^2+\frac{qB}{m}r\dot\phi
=0.500-1.000
=\boxed{-0.500\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}.
$$
The energy contains no velocity-linear term:
$$
E=\frac12m(\dot r^2+r^2\dot\phi^2)
=\boxed{0.250\,\mathrm J}.
$$
For a centered circle with $\dot r=\ddot r=0$, the nonzero branch is
$$
\boxed{\dot\phi=-qB/m=-2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$

Under $\mathbf A' =\mathbf A+\nabla\chi$, the Lagrangian changes by
$q\,d\chi/dt$, so
$$
\boxed{p_\phi'=p_\phi+q\frac{\partial\chi}{\partial\phi}}.
$$
Canonical momentum can therefore shift with gauge. Mechanical momentum, Lorentz force, energy for the static scalar-potential choice, and physical trajectories remain gauge invariant when all potentials and boundary terms are transformed consistently.

CM:067.title: Galilean boosts are quasi-symmetries of the free-particle action
CM:067.objective: Boost quasi-symmetry and its boundary term generate the correct center-of-mass Noether charge.
CM:067.statement: For a free particle $L=m\dot q^2/2$, consider the infinitesimal boost $\delta q=\epsilon t$. Show that $\delta L$ is a total time derivative rather than zero, and derive the corresponding Noether conserved quantity. For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $q(0)=3.00\,\mathrm m$, and $\dot q=4.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, evaluate the conserved quantity and verify it at $t=5.00\,\mathrm s$. Explain why omitting the boundary term gives the wrong result.
permittedResults: For a quasi-symmetry with $\delta L=dF/dt$, Noether charge is $p\,\delta q-F$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Vary velocity under the time-dependent coordinate displacement. Next: Express the Lagrangian variation as the derivative of a coordinate-dependent boundary function. Finally: Construct the charge, choose a sign convention, and verify it along the explicit straight trajectory.

milestones.criterion: Varies velocity under the time-dependent coordinate displacement.
Expresses the Lagrangian variation as the derivative of a coordinate-dependent boundary function.
Constructs the charge, choose a sign convention, and verify it along the explicit straight trajectory.

commonErrors.description: Requires the free Lagrangian to be strictly invariant under a boost.
commonErrors.consequence: It rejects a valid action quasi-symmetry whose variation is a boundary term.

commonErrors.description: Uses momentum times time alone as the Noether charge.
commonErrors.consequence: Boundary-term omission leaves momentum times time, which grows along the free trajectory.

hintTree.content: Vary velocity under the time-dependent coordinate displacement.
Express the Lagrangian variation as the derivative of a coordinate-dependent boundary function.
Construct the charge, choose a sign convention, and verify it along the explicit straight trajectory.

CM:067.canonicalSolution:
The boost gives $\delta\dot q=\epsilon$, so $\delta L=m\dot q\epsilon=d(mq\epsilon)/dt$. Thus $F=mq\epsilon$. Dividing the Noether charge by $-\epsilon$ gives the equivalent conserved quantity
$\boxed{K=mq-tp=m(q-t\dot q)}$.
Initially $K=2(3)=\boxed{6.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m}}$. At $t=5$, $q=3+4(5)=23\,\mathrm m$ and $p=8\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, so $K=2(23)-5(8)=6.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m}$. If the boundary term were omitted, one would use $pt$, which is not conserved. The charge fixes the intercept of the inertial worldline.

Since $\delta L=m\dot q\epsilon$ is nonzero, a boost is not a symmetry and there is no conserved charge.

CM:068.title: Horizontal pivot acceleration drives a pendulum through a cosine torque
CM:068.objective: Horizontal support acceleration supplies the pendulum cosine torque and the opposite-leaning static equilibrium.
CM:068.statement: A pendulum support has prescribed horizontal coordinate $X(t)$, with $x=X+\ell\sin\theta$ and $y=-\ell\cos\theta$. Derive the exact equation for $\theta$. For $\ell=1.00\,\mathrm m$, $\theta=30.0^\circ$, $\dot\theta=0$, and support acceleration $\ddot X=+4.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, compute $\ddot\theta$. Determine the static angle in a frame with constant support acceleration and check both zero-drive and zero-gravity limits.
permittedResults: Terms depending only on prescribed support motion may be dropped after the full kinetic energy is expanded.
A constant-acceleration frame has effective gravity vector opposite the frame acceleration plus downward gravity.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Retain the kinetic cross term between support speed and angular velocity. Next: Apply Euler-Lagrange so support acceleration appears after differentiating that cross term. Finally: Solve static balance from the sine-cosine equation and inspect limiting force directions.

milestones.criterion: Retains the kinetic cross term between support speed and angular velocity.
Applies Euler-Lagrange so support acceleration appears after differentiating that cross term.
Solves static balance from the sine-cosine equation and inspect limiting force directions.

commonErrors.description: Uses a sine rather than cosine factor for the horizontal inertial torque.
commonErrors.consequence: The equation gives zero drive torque when the pendulum hangs vertically.

commonErrors.description: Makes the bob lean in the direction of support acceleration.
commonErrors.consequence: The fictitious-force direction is reversed.

hintTree.content: Retain the kinetic cross term between support speed and angular velocity.
Apply Euler-Lagrange so support acceleration appears after differentiating that cross term.
Solve static balance from the sine-cosine equation and inspect limiting force directions.

CM:068.canonicalSolution:
Up to time-only terms,
$L=\tfrac12m\ell^2\dot\theta^2+m\ell\dot X\cos\theta\dot\theta+mg\ell\cos\theta$.
Euler-Lagrange gives
$\boxed{\ell\ddot\theta+g\sin\theta+\ddot X\cos\theta=0}$.
At the stated instant,
$\ddot\theta=-[9.81(0.5)+4(\sqrt3/2)]/1=\boxed{-8.369\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}}$. Static balance satisfies $\tan\theta_*=-\ddot X/g$, so for positive rightward support acceleration the bob leans left. If $\ddot X\to0$, $\theta_*=0$. If $g\to0$ with nonzero acceleration, the stable string direction becomes horizontal opposite the frame acceleration.

CM:069.title: A spherical holonomic constraint, its multiplier force, and the contact model it cannot hide
CM:069.objective: Derive constrained Euler--Lagrange motion for a particle on a sphere from an augmented action, solve the multiplier from the differentiated constraint, interpret its sign and dimensions as a bilateral reaction, and identify when the same state is impossible for a unilateral string or contact model.
CM:069.statement:
A particle of mass $m$ moves in a uniform gravitational field near Earth's
surface. Use an inertial Cartesian frame with upward unit vector
$\hat{\mathbf z}$, position $\mathbf r=(x,y,z)$, and potential
$V=mgz$. The particle is trapped by an ideal, fixed, frictionless,
bilateral spherical guide of radius $a$ centered at the origin:
$$
f(\mathbf r)=\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf r-a^2=0.
$$
The guide may push or pull normally; this assumption is deliberate.

Starting from an augmented action with
$$
L_\lambda=\frac12m\dot{\mathbf r}^{2}-mgz
+\lambda(t)(\mathbf r^2-a^2),
$$
perform the independent variations in $\mathbf r$ and $\lambda$. Derive the
equation of motion and both velocity- and acceleration-level constraint
relations. Eliminate the unknown radial acceleration to obtain $\lambda$ in
terms of $z$ and $v=|\dot{\mathbf r}|$. Identify the physical constraint force,
its direction, and the SI dimensions of $\lambda$.

Prove that the constraint force does no instantaneous work on an admissible
trajectory and that the mechanical energy is conserved. Explain why setting
$\delta\mathbf r$ tangent to the sphere from the beginning loses the normal
force but still gives the same tangential dynamics.

At an instant when
$$
z=\frac a2,
\qquad
v^2=\frac{ga}{4},
$$
compute $\lambda$ and the magnitude and direction of the guide force. Then use
$m=2.00\ \mathrm{kg}$, $a=0.800\ \mathrm m$, and
$g=9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ for numerical values.

Finally replace the bilateral guide by a massless taut string of length $a$
attached to the origin. The string can pull inward but cannot push outward.
Decide whether the same instantaneous state can satisfy that model. State the
correct consequence if the required multiplier has the forbidden sign rather
than silently continuing the constrained equations.
permittedResults: Variation of $L+\lambda f(q)$ gives $dL_{\dot q}/dt-L_q=\lambda\nabla f$ in the sign convention used here, together with $f(q)=0$.
Differentiating $\mathbf r^2=a^2$ twice gives $\mathbf r\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}=0$ and $\mathbf r\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}=-\dot{\mathbf r}^{2}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use Cartesian multiplier variation exactly as posed, then differentiate the spherical constraint to eliminate radial acceleration. Project Newton's law into tangent and normal components, provided the augmented-action derivation, multiplier normalization, energy proof, and unilateral boundary are also supplied.

milestones.criterion: Varies the augmented action independently in $\mathbf r$ and $\lambda$, retaining the reaction $2\lambda\mathbf r$.
Differentiates the spherical constraint twice and obtains $\lambda=m(gz-v^2)/(2a^2)$ with zero guide power.
Computes $\lambda=3.065625\,\mathrm{N/m}$ and $|\mathbf R|=4.905\,\mathrm N$ outward, then enforces string slackness.

commonErrors.description: Drops the factor $2$ from $\nabla(\mathbf r^2-a^2)$ or reverses the reaction sign relative to the stated augmented action.
commonErrors.consequence: The guide force normalization and its outward numerical direction are both wrong.

commonErrors.description: Interprets the required outward guide reaction as an admissible positive string tension.
commonErrors.consequence: The unilateral string is allowed to push, so the necessary slack-detachment transition is missed.

hintTree.content: The gradient of the chosen constraint is $2\mathbf r$, so keep the factor of two when identifying the physical reaction.
Dot the vector equation of motion with $\mathbf r$ and use the second derivative of the constraint to solve for $\lambda$.
A string tension has force $-T\mathbf r/a$ with $T\ge0$. Compare that allowed direction with the sign of $2\lambda\mathbf r$ at the specified state.

CM:069.canonicalSolution:
Varying the augmented action with endpoint-fixed
$\delta\mathbf r$ gives
$$
\delta S=\int\left[-m\ddot{\mathbf r}-mg\hat{\mathbf z}
+2\lambda\mathbf r\right]\cdot\delta\mathbf r\,dt
+\int(\mathbf r^2-a^2)\,\delta\lambda\,dt.
$$
Independent variations therefore imply
$$
\boxed{m\ddot{\mathbf r}=-mg\hat{\mathbf z}+2\lambda\mathbf r},
\qquad
\boxed{\mathbf r^2=a^2}.
$$
With this normalization of $f$, the physical guide reaction is
$$
\mathbf R=2\lambda\mathbf r.
$$

Differentiating the constraint once and twice yields
$$
\mathbf r\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}=0,
\qquad
\dot{\mathbf r}^{2}+\mathbf r\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}=0.
$$
Thus $\mathbf r\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}=-v^2$. Dotting the equation of motion
with $\mathbf r$ gives
$$
-mv^2=-mgz+2\lambda a^2,
$$
and hence
$$
\boxed{\lambda=\frac{m(gz-v^2)}{2a^2}},
\qquad
\boxed{\mathbf R=\frac{m(gz-v^2)}{a^2}\mathbf r}.
$$
Positive $\lambda$ is outward in this convention and negative $\lambda$ is
inward. Since $\lambda f$ has energy dimensions and $f$ has dimensions
$\mathrm m^2$, $[\lambda]=\mathrm{J/m^2}=\mathrm{N/m}$; multiplying by
$2\mathbf r$ gives force.

The instantaneous constraint power is
$$
\mathbf R\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}
=2\lambda\mathbf r\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}=0.
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac d{dt}\left(\frac12mv^2+mgz\right)
=\dot{\mathbf r}\cdot(m\ddot{\mathbf r}+mg\hat{\mathbf z})
=\dot{\mathbf r}\cdot\mathbf R=0.
$$
If variations are restricted to the tangent plane, then
$\mathbf r\cdot\delta\mathbf r=0$ and the normal reaction disappears from
the virtual-work equation. The remaining projected equation determines the
same tangential acceleration, but it cannot determine the force needed to
enforce the embedding constraint; the multiplier method retains that
information.

At the specified state,
$$
gz-v^2=\frac{ga}{2}-\frac{ga}{4}=\frac{ga}{4},
$$
so
$$
\boxed{\lambda=\frac{mg}{8a}},
\qquad
\boxed{\mathbf R=\frac{mg}{4a}\mathbf r},
\qquad
\boxed{|\mathbf R|=\frac{mg}{4}}.
$$
The reaction points radially outward. Numerically,
$$
\lambda=\frac{(2.00)(9.81)}{8(0.800)}
=\boxed{3.065625\ \mathrm{N/m}},
\qquad
|\mathbf R|=\frac{(2.00)(9.81)}4
=\boxed{4.905\ \mathrm N}.
$$

A taut string supplies
$$
\mathbf R_{\rm string}=-T\frac{\mathbf r}{a},\qquad T\ge0,
$$
which is inward only. The state above requires an outward force and therefore
would correspond to $T<0$, impossible for a string. The equality-constrained
string model must stop at the loss-of-tension boundary: the string goes slack
and the particle thereafter follows unconstrained ballistic motion until a
later geometric event. One may not preserve $\mathbf r^2=a^2$ by allowing an
unphysical compressive string.

CM:070.title: A nonintegrable velocity constraint conserves energy without defining a surface
CM:070.objective: Nonintegrable velocity constraints require d'Alembert reactions that do no work without defining a configuration surface.
CM:070.statement: A particle of mass $m$ has free kinetic Lagrangian $m(\dot x^2+\dot y^2+\dot z^2)/2$ and nonholonomic constraint $\dot y-(x/\ell_0)\dot z=0$, where $\ell_0$ is a fixed length. Apply Lagrange-d'Alembert to derive the multiplier and accelerations. Show the reaction does zero power and that the constraint is not the derivative of $y-(x/\ell_0)z=\text{constant}$. At a state with $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\ell_0=1.00\,\mathrm m$, $x=1.00\,\mathrm m$, $\dot x=2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $\dot z=3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, compute the required $\dot y$, multiplier, and acceleration.
permittedResults: The multiplier force is proportional to the constraint covector $(0,1,-x/\ell_0)$.
Differentiate the velocity constraint along a valid motion.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Write the three multiplier equations and differentiate the velocity constraint. Next: Solve the resulting scalar equation for the multiplier. Finally: Dot reaction with velocity and compare the actual constraint with the derivative of the tempting positional expression.

milestones.criterion: Writes the three multiplier equations and differentiate the velocity constraint.
Solves the resulting scalar equation for the multiplier.
Dots reaction with velocity and compare the actual constraint with the derivative of the tempting positional expression.

commonErrors.description: Integrates the velocity constraint as if the coefficient $x$ were constant.
commonErrors.consequence: It imposes an extra position restriction and changes the dynamics.

commonErrors.description: Claims nonzero multiplier force must change kinetic energy.
commonErrors.consequence: It overlooks zero virtual power along admissible velocities.

hintTree.content: Write the three multiplier equations and differentiate the velocity constraint.
Solve the resulting scalar equation for the multiplier.
Dot reaction with velocity and compare the actual constraint with the derivative of the tempting positional expression.

CM:070.canonicalSolution:
Lagrange-d'Alembert gives $m\ddot x=0$, $m\ddot y=\lambda$, and $m\ddot z=-\lambda x/\ell_0$. Differentiating $\dot y-(x/\ell_0)\dot z=0$ gives $\ddot y-(\dot x/\ell_0)\dot z-(x/\ell_0)\ddot z=0$, hence
$\boxed{\lambda=\dfrac{m\dot x\dot z/\ell_0}{1+x^2/\ell_0^2}}$.
At the stated state, $\dot y=(x/\ell_0)\dot z=\boxed{3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}}$, $\lambda=6/2=\boxed{3.00\,\mathrm N}$, and
$(\ddot x,\ddot y,\ddot z)=\boxed{(0,3.00,-3.00)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}$. Reaction power is $\lambda[\dot y-(x/\ell_0)\dot z]=0$, so kinetic energy is conserved. But $d[y-(x/\ell_0)z]/dt=\dot y-(x/\ell_0)\dot z-(\dot x/\ell_0)z$, which is not generally zero; the velocity constraint does not define that positional surface.

The constraint integrates to $y-(x/\ell_0)z=C$, so ordinary holonomic elimination applies. The multiplier is $m\dot x\dot z/\ell_0$ and necessarily dissipates energy.

CM:071.objective: Tangent-space second variation gives the true constrained stability threshold and small-oscillation frequency.
CM:071.statement: A particle of mass $m$ is constrained to a circle $x=R\sin\theta$, $y=-R\cos\theta$ and has potential $U=mgy+\kappa x^2/2$, where $\kappa$ may be negative. Derive the exact reduced potential and the small-oscillation stability criterion at the bottom. For $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $R=1.00\,\mathrm m$, and $\kappa=-5.00\,\mathrm{N/m}$, compute the small-oscillation frequency. Explain why inspecting the unconstrained Cartesian Hessian alone can give the wrong answer.

The kinetic coefficient is $mR^2$.

The reduced potential is

At $\theta=0$, $U'(0)=0$ and
$U''(0)=mgR+\kappa R^2$. Stability requires
$\boxed{mgR+\kappa R^2>0}$, and the small-oscillation frequency is
$\omega^2=U''(0)/(mR^2)=g/R+\kappa/m$.
For the data, $\omega^2=9.81-5.00=4.81\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, so $\boxed{\omega=2.193\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$. The Cartesian Hessian tests displacements normal as well as tangent to the circle; normal variations are forbidden and their curvature is irrelevant. $\boxed{p_1\sin\theta_1=p_2\sin\theta_2}$, where $p_i=\sqrt{2m(E-U_i)}$. Thus

so $\boxed{\theta_2=45.0^\circ}$. Momentum and speed are lower in the higher-potential region, so the path bends away from the normal. CM:073.title: Two coupled rod constraints require two interacting multipliers
CM:073.objective: Cartesian multiplier variation for a double pendulum derives coupled constraint reactions, acceleration-level conditions, zero reaction power, and bottom-state tensions.
CM:073.statement:
A planar double pendulum consists of masses $m_1,m_2$ at Cartesian positions $\mathbf r_1,\mathbf r_2$ in an inertial frame with upward unit vector $\hat{\mathbf y}$. Massless rigid rods have lengths $\ell_1,\ell_2$ and impose
$$
f_1=\mathbf r_1^2-\ell_1^2=0,
\qquad
f_2=(\mathbf r_2-\mathbf r_1)^2-\ell_2^2=0.
$$
Use the augmented Lagrangian
$$
L_*=\frac12m_1\dot{\mathbf r}_1^2+\frac12m_2\dot{\mathbf r}_2^2
-m_1g y_1-m_2g y_2+\frac12\lambda_1f_1+\frac12\lambda_2f_2.
$$
Vary all coordinates and multipliers independently. Derive both vector equations, the velocity- and acceleration-level constraints, and the linear system that determines $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ from an admissible instantaneous state. Prove that total constraint power is zero.

At the bottom configuration
$$
\mathbf r_1=(0,-\ell_1),
\qquad
\mathbf r_2-\mathbf r_1=(0,-\ell_2),
$$
with both velocities zero, take $m_1=m_2=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\ell_1=\ell_2=1.00\,\mathrm m$, and $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Compute both multipliers, physical rod tensions, and accelerations. Explain the multiplier dimensions and sign convention.
permittedResults: Twice differentiating $\mathbf d^2=\ell^2$ gives $\mathbf d\cdot\ddot{\mathbf d}=-|\dot{\mathbf d}|^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Keep the two constraint gradients separate in each particle equation. Differentiate both geometric equalities to acceleration level, substitute the vector dynamics, and interpret multiplier signs only after reconstructing the physical rod forces.

milestones.criterion: Varies both constraint terms with their correct equal-and-opposite lower-rod forces.
Uses both acceleration constraints to define the coupled multiplier solve and proves zero reaction power.
Computes multiplier signs, units, physical tensions, and bottom-state accelerations consistently.

commonErrors.description: Applies the lower-rod multiplier in the same direction to both masses.
commonErrors.consequence: The internal rod force creates net external momentum and the multiplier system is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Sets both second derivatives of the length vectors perpendicular to the rods without the velocity-squared curvature terms.
commonErrors.consequence: Moving configurations receive incorrect radial accelerations and tensions.

hintTree.content: Let $\mathbf d=\mathbf r_2-\mathbf r_1$; variation gives forces $-\lambda_2\mathbf d$ on mass 1 and $+\lambda_2\mathbf d$ on mass 2.
The constraints imply $\mathbf r_1\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}_1=-|\dot{\mathbf r}_1|^2$ and $\mathbf d\cdot(\ddot{\mathbf r}_2-\ddot{\mathbf r}_1)=-|\dot{\mathbf d}|^2$.
At the stationary bottom state, the lower rod supports only mass 2 while the upper rod supports both masses.

CM:073.canonicalSolution:
Independent variation gives the constraints and
$$
\boxed{m_1\ddot{\mathbf r}_1=-m_1g\hat{\mathbf y}
+\lambda_1\mathbf r_1-\lambda_2\mathbf d},
$$
$$
\boxed{m_2\ddot{\mathbf r}_2=-m_2g\hat{\mathbf y}
+\lambda_2\mathbf d},
\qquad
\mathbf d=\mathbf r_2-\mathbf r_1.
$$
The first derivatives are
$$
\mathbf r_1\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}_1=0,
\qquad
\mathbf d\cdot\dot{\mathbf d}=0,
$$
and the acceleration constraints are
$$
\boxed{\mathbf r_1\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}_1=-|\dot{\mathbf r}_1|^2},
\qquad
\boxed{\mathbf d\cdot(\ddot{\mathbf r}_2-\ddot{\mathbf r}_1)=-|\dot{\mathbf d}|^2}.
$$
Substituting the two vector equations into these scalar relations produces a $2\times2$ linear system for $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ at any regular admissible state; its coefficients are the mass-weighted dot products of the two constraint gradients. This construction retains their coupling automatically.
Explicitly,
$$
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
\ell_1^2&-\mathbf r_1\cdot\mathbf d\\
-(\mathbf r_1\cdot\mathbf d)/m_1&
\ell_2^2(1/m_1+1/m_2)
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_1\\\lambda_2\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
m_1(g y_1-|\dot{\mathbf r}_1|^2)\\
-|\dot{\mathbf d}|^2
\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

Constraint power is
$$
(\lambda_1\mathbf r_1-\lambda_2\mathbf d)\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}_1
+(\lambda_2\mathbf d)\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}_2
=\lambda_1\mathbf r_1\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}_1
+\lambda_2\mathbf d\cdot\dot{\mathbf d}=0.
$$
Thus ideal rods exchange forces but perform no net instantaneous work.

At the stationary collinear bottom state with unit lengths and masses, the equations are purely vertical. The acceleration constraints require zero acceleration along both rods. Writing downward as negative $y$, they yield
$$
\lambda_1-\lambda_2=-g,
\qquad
\lambda_1=2\lambda_2.
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{\lambda_2=-g=-9.81\,\mathrm{N/m}},
\qquad
\boxed{\lambda_1=-2g=-19.62\,\mathrm{N/m}}.
$$
Because each multiplier multiplies a length vector to give force, its units are $\mathrm{N/m}$. Negative $\lambda_i$ in the stated $+\lambda_i f_i/2$ convention gives tensile force. The physical tensions are
$$
\boxed{T_2=-\lambda_2\ell_2=9.81\,\mathrm N},
\qquad
\boxed{T_1=-\lambda_1\ell_1=19.62\,\mathrm N}.
$$
They balance the lower mass's weight and the combined weight transmitted through the upper rod, so
$\boxed{\ddot{\mathbf r}_1=\ddot{\mathbf r}_2=\mathbf0}$ at that instant.

CM:074.title: A singular Lagrangian hides an arbitrary gauge function
CM:074.objective: Singular-Hessian equations reveal an arbitrary-function gauge orbit and the failure of initial-data uniqueness without fixing.
CM:074.statement: Consider $L=(\dot q_1-q_2)^2/2$. Derive both Euler-Lagrange equations and show that one is the time derivative of the other. Prove invariance under $q_1\mapsto q_1+\epsilon(t)$ and $q_2\mapsto q_2+\dot\epsilon(t)$ for arbitrary smooth $\epsilon$. Characterize all solutions and compute the velocity Hessian rank. Explain why specifying $q_1(0)$ and $\dot q_1(0)$ cannot determine a unique trajectory without gauge fixing.
permittedResults: The velocity Hessian has entries $\partial^2L/\partial\dot q_i\partial\dot q_j$.
A transformation that leaves the combination $\dot q_1-q_2$ unchanged leaves $L$ unchanged.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Vary each coordinate separately, noting that the second has no velocity in the Lagrangian. Next: Check the arbitrary-function transformation on the single combination appearing in $L$. Finally: Solve the algebraic Euler-Lagrange constraint first and count the Hessian rank and free function.

commonErrors.consequence: It overdetermines a system whose singular Hessian carries gauge freedom.

commonErrors.consequence: Arbitrary-function gauge freedom is reduced to constants, producing false uniqueness.

CM:074.canonicalSolution:
For $q_1$, Euler-Lagrange gives $d(\dot q_1-q_2)/dt=0$. For $q_2$, it gives the stronger algebraic equation
$\boxed{\dot q_1-q_2=0}$; its derivative is the first equation, so they are dependent. Under the stated transformation,
$\dot q_1+\dot\epsilon-(q_2+\dot\epsilon)=\dot q_1-q_2$, proving gauge invariance. Every smooth function $f(t)$ defines a solution
$\boxed{q_1=f(t),\quad q_2=\dot f(t)}$.
The velocity Hessian is $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and has rank one rather than two. Initial $q_1$ and $\dot q_1$ fix only $f(0)$ and $\dot f(0)$; higher behavior remains arbitrary because different gauge functions share those values. A gauge condition is needed for uniqueness, and it must not be mistaken for a new physical equation.

CM:075.statement: For a natural system $L=m|\dot{\mathbf q}|^2/2-U(\mathbf q)$ at fixed energy $E>U$, eliminate time from Maupertuis' abbreviated action and derive the Jacobi line element. CM:075.canonicalSolution:
Along a fixed-energy path, $|\mathbf p|=mv=\sqrt{2m(E-U)}$, so
$W=\int\sqrt{2m(E-U)}\,ds$. Its stationary paths are geodesics of the Jacobi metric
$\boxed{d\ell_J^2=2m(E-U)\,d\mathbf q^2}$.
Once the oriented path is known, physical time follows from
$\boxed{dt=\sqrt{m/[2(E-U)]}\,ds}$. For $U=kq^2/2$, allowed motion has $|q|\le\sqrt{2E/k}$. The data give
$q_\pm=\pm\sqrt{32/8}=\boxed{\pm2.00\,\mathrm m}$. At a turning point $E-U=0$, the Jacobi metric vanishes and the time integrand diverges like an integrable inverse square root. The geometric parameterization degenerates there, but the oscillator reverses smoothly with finite acceleration.

CM:076.objective: Inverse-square scaling leaves the action invariant and produces the conserved dilation charge with correct time weight.
CM:076.statement: Let $L=T-U$ with constant mass matrix and a potential homogeneous of degree $-2$. For a state with $\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf p=18.0\,\mathrm{J\,s}$, energy $E=3.00\,\mathrm J$, and $t=2.00\,\mathrm s$, compute the charge. Explain what changes when the potential degree differs from $-2$.

Finally: Differentiate the candidate charge and apply both Euler's theorem and the energy definition.

The finite scaling is $\mathbf q\mapsto\lambda\mathbf q$, $t\mapsto\lambda^2t$. Then velocity scales as $\lambda^{-1}$, so both $T$ and degree-$-2$ $U$ scale as $\lambda^{-2}$, while $dt$ scales as $\lambda^2$; the action is invariant. Noether gives
$\boxed{D=\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf p-2tE}$.
Directly, $d(\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf p)/dt=2T+\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf F=2T-\mathbf q\cdot\nabla U=2T+2U=2E$, hence $\dot D=0$. Numerically, $D=18.0-2(2)(3)=\boxed{6.00\,\mathrm{J\,s}}$. For another homogeneity degree, kinetic and potential terms do not scale with the same action weight under this transformation, leaving a virial-type evolution law rather than a conserved dilation charge.

Evaluate canonical and mechanical quantities separately and compare their time weights.

CM:077.canonicalSolution:
Euler-Lagrange gives
$d(e^{\gamma t}m\dot q)/dt+e^{\gamma t}kq=0$, hence
$\boxed{m\ddot q+m\gamma\dot q+kq=0}$. Canonical momentum is $p=e^{\gamma t}m\dot q$, not mechanical momentum $m\dot q$. Mechanical power is
$\dot E_{\rm mech}=\dot q(m\ddot q+kq)=-m\gamma\dot q^2\le0$.
Numerically, $p=e^1(2)(-0.4)=\boxed{-2.175\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}}$, while
$\dot E_{\rm mech}=-2(0.5)(0.4)^2=\boxed{-0.160\,\mathrm W}$. The canonical Hamiltonian is $e^{-\gamma t}p^2/(2m)+e^{\gamma t}kq^2/2=e^{\gamma t}E_{\rm mech}$ and is explicitly time dependent. Without that time dependence, a regular one-coordinate natural Lagrangian would conserve its energy and could not reproduce ordinary damping in this form.

CM:078.title: A rolling sphere conserves energy on a nonintegrable constraint distribution
CM:078.objective: Coordinate-free rolling constraints connect translation and rotation, prove ideal zero-power dynamics, and expose nonintegrability through Lie brackets.
CM:078.statement:
A homogeneous sphere of mass $m$, radius $R$, and isotropic center inertia $I=2mR^2/5$ rolls without slipping on a fixed horizontal plane. Let $\mathbf v_C=(\dot x,\dot y,0)$ be center velocity and let $\boldsymbol\omega$ be angular velocity in space components. The contact point relative to the center is $-R\hat{\mathbf z}$.

Derive the no-slip constraints from zero contact velocity. Let the horizontal contact force be $\mathbf F$. Using Newton--Euler equations, prove that in force-free horizontal motion both $\boldsymbol\omega$ and $\mathbf v_C$ are constant and that the ideal contact force does zero power, without setting the force to zero prematurely.

On the configuration manifold $\mathbb R^2\times SO(3)$, let $E_x,E_y,E_z$ denote infinitesimal space-rotation vector fields with $[E_z,E_x]=E_y$. Show that the allowed fields include
$$
A=E_x-R\partial_y,
\qquad
B=E_y+R\partial_x,
\qquad
C=E_z,
$$
and use $[C,A]$ to prove the rank-three rolling distribution is not integrable.

For $m=5.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $R=0.200\,\mathrm m$, and $\boldsymbol\omega=(3.00,-4.00,2.00)\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute center velocity, speed, translational energy, rotational energy, and total energy.
permittedResults: For an isotropic sphere, angular momentum about its center is $I\boldsymbol\omega$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Start from contact-point kinematics, retain the unknown reaction through the Newton--Euler solve, and treat nonintegrability as failure of bracket closure rather than failure to solve a single differential equation.

milestones.criterion: Derives both no-slip component constraints and the combined zero-power identity for contact reaction.
Solves Newton--Euler equations to obtain constant angular and center velocities without equating zero power to zero force.
Demonstrates bracket nonclosure and computes all requested velocity and energy values.

commonErrors.description: Sets static friction to zero solely because its contact point has zero velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: Zero reaction power is confused with zero reaction force before the dynamics are solved.

commonErrors.description: Treats the two component rolling constraints as derivatives of two global position-orientation equations.
commonErrors.consequence: The nonclosing Lie bracket is ignored and a nonholonomic distribution is falsely declared holonomic.

hintTree.content: No slip gives $\mathbf v_C+\boldsymbol\omega\times(-R\hat{\mathbf z})=0$.
Use $m\dot{\mathbf v}_C=\mathbf F$ and $I\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=(-R\hat{\mathbf z})\times\mathbf F$.
Although $[C,A]=E_y$, the pure field $E_y$ is not in $\operatorname{span}\{A,B,C\}$ because $B$ necessarily carries $R\partial_x$.

CM:078.canonicalSolution:
Zero contact velocity gives
$$
\boxed{\mathbf v_C=R\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat{\mathbf z}},
$$
or
$$
\boxed{\dot x=R\omega_y,
\qquad
\dot y=-R\omega_x}.
$$
The contact power is
$$
\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v_C
+[(-R\hat{\mathbf z})\times\mathbf F]\cdot\boldsymbol\omega
=\mathbf F\cdot[\mathbf v_C+\boldsymbol\omega\times(-R\hat{\mathbf z})]=0.
$$
Thus ideal static friction may be nonzero while doing zero total power.

Differentiate the constraint and use the dynamics:
$$
mR\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}\times\hat{\mathbf z}=\mathbf F,
\qquad
I\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=(-R\hat{\mathbf z})\times\mathbf F.
$$
Substitution gives
$$
(I+mR^2)\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}_h=0,
\qquad
I\dot\omega_z=0.
$$
Hence $\boxed{\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=0}$, then
$\boxed{\dot{\mathbf v}_C=0}$ and in this free case $\mathbf F=0$ follows from the solved dynamics rather than from zero power alone.

The rolling distribution is spanned by $A,B,C$. Because
$$
[C,A]=[E_z,E_x]=E_y,
$$
and pure $E_y$ cannot be written as a combination of $A,B,C$ without also introducing the translation $R\partial_x$, the distribution is not closed under Lie brackets. Frobenius integrability therefore fails: rolling velocities do not arise as tangents to a three-dimensional family of configuration submanifolds.

Numerically,
$$
\mathbf v_C=0.200(-4.00,-3.00,0)
=\boxed{(-0.800,-0.600,0)\,\mathrm{m/s}},
$$
so $\boxed{|\mathbf v_C|=1.00\,\mathrm{m/s}}$ and
$$
T_{\rm trans}=\frac12(5.00)(1.00)^2=\boxed{2.50\,\mathrm J}.
$$
The inertia is
$I=(2/5)(5.00)(0.200)^2=0.0800\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, hence
$$
T_{\rm rot}=\frac12(0.0800)(3^2+(-4)^2+2^2)
=\boxed{1.16\,\mathrm J}.
$$
Therefore $\boxed{T=3.66\,\mathrm J}$, constant in the free rolling motion.

CM:079.title: The harmonic-action second variation changes sign at the first conjugate time
CM:079.objective: Fixed-endpoint second variation locates the first oscillator conjugate time and distinguishes minima from saddles.
CM:079.statement: For the harmonic oscillator action $S=\int_0^T m(\dot q^2-\omega^2q^2)/2\,dt$ with fixed endpoints, derive the second variation about a classical path. Use the sharp fixed-endpoint inequality to prove that the action is a strict local minimum for $T<\pi/\omega$, has a zero direction at $T=\pi/\omega$, and has a negative direction for larger $T$. For $\omega=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute the first conjugate time and give the explicit zero mode. Explain why satisfying Euler-Lagrange alone does not determine minimum versus saddle.
permittedResults: For $\eta(0)=\eta(T)=0$, $\int_0^T\dot\eta^2dt\ge(\pi/T)^2\int_0^T\eta^2dt$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Expand the quadratic action to second order in a fixed-endpoint variation. Next: Apply the sharp inequality to bound the quadratic form by its lowest sine mode. Finally: Evaluate the threshold and test the first sine mode on both sides of it.

milestones.criterion: Expands the quadratic action to second order in a fixed-endpoint variation.
Applies the sharp inequality to bound the quadratic form by its lowest sine mode.
Evaluates the threshold and test the first sine mode on both sides of it.

commonErrors.description: Assumes every classical path minimizes action for every duration.
commonErrors.consequence: It ignores negative directions appearing beyond a conjugate point.

commonErrors.description: Uses a constant variation despite fixed endpoints.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed test direction is inadmissible and gives the wrong threshold.

hintTree.content: Expand the quadratic action to second order in a fixed-endpoint variation.
Apply the sharp inequality to bound the quadratic form by its lowest sine mode.
Evaluate the threshold and test the first sine mode on both sides of it.

CM:079.canonicalSolution:
Because the action is quadratic and the first variation vanishes on a classical path,
$\boxed{\delta^2S=m\int_0^T(\dot\eta^2-\omega^2\eta^2)dt}$.
The fixed-endpoint inequality gives
$\delta^2S\ge m[(\pi/T)^2-\omega^2]\int\eta^2dt$. It is strictly positive for $T<\pi/\omega$. At $T=\pi/\omega$, the mode $\eta(t)=\sin(\pi t/T)=\sin(\omega t)$ has zero second variation. For $T>\pi/\omega$, that same lowest sine mode makes the quadratic form negative. With $\omega=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, the first conjugate time is
$\boxed{T_c=\pi/2=1.571\,\mathrm s}$ and zero mode is $\boxed{\eta(t)=\sin2t}$ on $[0,\pi/2]$. Euler-Lagrange supplies stationarity; the second variation determines whether the stationary path is locally minimizing or saddle-like.

The second variation is always $m\int(\dot\eta^2+\omega^2\eta^2)dt>0$, so every oscillator trajectory is a minimum for arbitrary time.

CM:080.title: A translating magnetic ring exposes gauge shifts in reduced mechanics
CM:080.objective: Moving-constraint reduction and electromagnetic gauge transformation produce the same bead dynamics while shifting canonical momentum and energy representatives by explicit boundary terms.
CM:080.statement:
A bead of mass $m$ and charge $q$ is constrained to a circular ring of radius $a$ whose center has prescribed inertial position $(X(t),0)$. Use
$$
x=X(t)+a\cos\theta,
\qquad
y=a\sin\theta.
$$
A uniform magnetic field $B\hat{\mathbf z}$ is represented first in symmetric gauge
$$
\mathbf A_S=\frac B2(-y,x),
$$
with zero scalar potential. Derive the reduced one-coordinate Lagrangian, canonical momentum, and exact equation for $\theta$. Interpret separately the support-acceleration term and magnetic term.

Landau gauge $\mathbf A_L=(0,Bx)$ satisfies $\mathbf A_L=\mathbf A_S+\nabla\chi$ with $\chi=Bxy/2$. Reduce this gauge on the moving ring and prove
$$
L_L=L_S+q\frac d{dt}\chi(\theta,t).
$$
Derive the shifts in canonical momentum and reduced energy, emphasizing the partial time derivative at fixed $\theta$.

For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $q=1.00\,\mathrm C$, $B=3.00\,\mathrm T$, $a=0.500\,\mathrm m$, $X=1.00\,\mathrm m$, $\dot X=4.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $\ddot X=1.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\theta=60.0^\circ$, and $\dot\theta=0.200\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute $\ddot\theta$, $p_\theta^S$, the gauge momentum shift, and $E_L-E_S$. Check $B\to0$ and $\dot X\to0$.
permittedResults: For $L'=L+dG(q,t)/dt$, $p'=p+G_q$ and $E'=E-G_t$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Reduce kinetic and vector-potential terms in one gauge, derive the physical equation before changing gauge, then reduce the scalar gauge function itself so all momentum and energy shifts follow from one total derivative.

milestones.criterion: Reduces both kinetic and symmetric-gauge couplings and derives the exact physical angular equation.
Shows the Landau-gauge reduction differs by the reduced total derivative and obtains both canonical shifts.
Computes acceleration, momentum, gauge momentum shift, energy shift, and both diagnostic limits.

commonErrors.description: Drops the prescribed translation from the vector-potential coupling because the ring shape is unchanged.
commonErrors.consequence: The tangential magnetic drive and gauge energy shift both disappear from a physically moving constraint.

commonErrors.description: Calls canonical momentum and reduced energy gauge invariant after adding $q\,d\chi/dt$.
commonErrors.consequence: Boundary-term shifts are ignored even though the physical equation remains unchanged.

hintTree.content: The bead speed squared is $\dot X^2-2a\dot X\sin\theta\dot\theta+a^2\dot\theta^2$.
In symmetric gauge, $\mathbf A_S\cdot\mathbf v=B[-a\dot X\sin\theta+a^2\dot\theta+aX\cos\theta\dot\theta]/2$.
On the constraint, $\chi=(B/2)(X+a\cos\theta)(a\sin\theta)$.

CM:080.canonicalSolution:
The constrained velocity gives
$$
v^2=\dot X^2-2a\dot X\sin\theta\dot\theta+a^2\dot\theta^2.
$$
Also
$$
\mathbf A_S\cdot\mathbf v
=\frac B2[-a\dot X\sin\theta+a^2\dot\theta
+aX\cos\theta\dot\theta].
$$
Thus
$$
\boxed{L_S=\frac m2(\dot X^2-2a\dot X\sin\theta\dot\theta+a^2\dot\theta^2)
+\frac{qB}{2}[-a\dot X\sin\theta+a^2\dot\theta+aX\cos\theta\dot\theta]}.
$$
The canonical momentum is
$$
\boxed{p_\theta^S=m(a^2\dot\theta-a\dot X\sin\theta)
+\frac{qB}{2}(a^2+aX\cos\theta)}.
$$
Euler--Lagrange cancellations leave
$$
\boxed{ma^2\ddot\theta-ma\ddot X\sin\theta
+qBa\dot X\cos\theta=0}.
$$
The middle term is the tangential inertial effect of support acceleration; the last is the tangential Lorentz force generated by translating the charged bead through the field. Tangential bead motion around a stationary ring produces only a normal magnetic force.

Since $\mathbf A_L-\mathbf A_S=\nabla(Bxy/2)$,
$$
\chi(\theta,t)=\frac B2(X+a\cos\theta)(a\sin\theta),
$$
and substitution gives
$\boxed{L_L=L_S+q\,d\chi/dt}$. Therefore
$$
\boxed{p_\theta^L-p_\theta^S=q\chi_\theta},
\qquad
\boxed{E_L-E_S=-q\chi_t},
$$
where $\chi_t=(Ba/2)\dot X\sin\theta$ holds $\theta$ fixed.

Numerically,
$$
\ddot\theta=\frac{\ddot X}{a}\sin\theta
-\frac{qB\dot X}{ma}\cos\theta
=2(0.8660)-3(4.00)(0.500)
=\boxed{-4.268\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}}.
$$
The symmetric-gauge momentum is
$$
p_\theta^S=2[0.25(0.200)-0.5(4.00)(0.8660)]
+\frac32[0.25+0.5(1.00)(0.500)]
=\boxed{-2.614\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}}.
$$
Furthermore,
$$
\chi_\theta=\frac{Ba}{2}[X\cos\theta+a(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)]
=0.1875\,\mathrm{T\,m^2},
$$
so
$\boxed{p_\theta^L-p_\theta^S=0.1875\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}}$.
Finally,
$$
\boxed{E_L-E_S=-\frac{qBa\dot X\sin\theta}{2}
=-2.598\,\mathrm J}.
$$
When $B\to0$, only moving-support inertial dynamics remain. When $\dot X\to0$ at the instant, the tangential magnetic term and explicit-time gauge-energy shift vanish, while a nonzero $\ddot X$ may still drive the bead.

CM:081.title: Zero central torque fixes an orbital plane
CM:081.objective: Use the torque equation to prove angular-momentum conservation and identify the geometric edge case of purely radial motion.
CM:081.statement: A particle of mass $m$ moves under a central force $\mathbf F(\mathbf r)=f(r)\hat{\mathbf r}$, with $r>0$. Starting from $d\mathbf L/dt=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F$, prove that the motion lies in a fixed plane when $\mathbf L\ne0$. State carefully what remains true when $\mathbf L=0$.
permittedResults: Angular momentum about the force center is $\mathbf L=\mathbf r\times m\dot{\mathbf r}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First identify the torque direction, then use the constant normal vector supplied by nonzero angular momentum, and finally separate the radial zero-angular-momentum case.

milestones.criterion: Shows that the central torque vanishes and hence that $\mathbf L$ is a constant vector.
Uses $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf L=0$ to identify the fixed plane perpendicular to nonzero $\mathbf L$.
Treats $\mathbf L=0$ separately as radial motion and does not claim that a unique orbital plane is determined.

commonErrors.description: Claims that a radial force is parallel to the velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: Central means parallel to position, so the torque conclusion is lost by an unjustified velocity assumption.

commonErrors.description: Uses a plane normal to $\mathbf L$ even when $\mathbf L=0$.
commonErrors.consequence: The zero vector supplies no unique normal; the radial trajectory can be embedded in infinitely many planes.

hintTree.content: Evaluate $\mathbf r\times f(r)\hat{\mathbf r}$ before discussing the trajectory.
For nonzero $\mathbf L$, compute $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf L$.
If $\mathbf L=0$, ask whether one unique plane is selected or whether the motion is radial.

CM:081.canonicalSolution: Because $\mathbf r=r\hat{\mathbf r}$, $d\mathbf L/dt=\mathbf r\times f(r)\hat{\mathbf r}=\mathbf0$. Thus $\mathbf L$ is constant. Also $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf L=\mathbf r\cdot(\mathbf r\times m\dot{\mathbf r})=0$, so if $\mathbf L\ne0$, every position lies in the fixed plane through the force center perpendicular to $\mathbf L$. If $\mathbf L=0$, then $\mathbf r\times\dot{\mathbf r}=0$: away from $r=0$ the velocity is radial and the path lies on a fixed radial line, but no unique plane is selected.

If $\mathbf L=0$, then $\mathbf r\times\dot{\mathbf r}=0$: away from $r=0$ the velocity is radial and the path lies on a fixed radial line, but no unique plane is selected.
A central force is always tangent to the orbit, so $\mathbf r\times\mathbf F=0$. Therefore every orbit, including one with $\mathbf L=0$, has a unique plane perpendicular to $\mathbf L$.

CM:082.title: The centripetal sign is radial, not optional
CM:082.objective: Compute the signed radial acceleration and central force for uniform circular motion with a declared outward convention.
CM:082.statement: A $4.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle moves counterclockwise at constant speed $3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$ on a circle of radius $2.00\,\mathrm m$ centered at the force origin. Take $\hat{\mathbf r}$ outward. Find $a_r$, the central force vector, and the torque about the origin. Check the units and explain why the direction of motion does not change the force direction.
permittedResults: For uniform circular motion, $\mathbf a=-(v^2/r)\hat{\mathbf r}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the outward-positive radial component, multiply by the mass, and then evaluate the moment arm cross the radial force.

milestones.criterion: Computes $a_r$ with the correct inward sign and SI acceleration units.
Gives the force as a signed vector with magnitude and newton units.
Finds zero torque and explains that clockwise versus counterclockwise motion leaves the inward acceleration unchanged.

commonErrors.description: Reports $a_r=+v^2/r$ with outward positive.
commonErrors.consequence: The acceleration would point away from the circle center and could not maintain the orbit.

u_3=|\Omega|\sqrt{(I_3-I_1)(I_3-I_2)/(I_1I_2)}$. Both squared frequencies are positive. For moments $(1,2,3)I_0$, $
u_1=|\Omega|/\sqrt3$ and $
u_3=|\Omega|$. This checks stability about both extreme axes without implying stability about the intermediate axis.

CM:173.title: Two branches of steady heavy-top precession
CM:173.objective: Find both exact steady-precession branches of a heavy symmetric top and identify the discriminant separating allowed constant-tilt motion from nutation.
CM:173.statement: A symmetric top with fixed point has transverse moment $I_1$, axial moment $I_3$, center-of-mass distance $\ell$, and axial body component $\omega_3$. Take gravitational potential $V=Mg\ell\cos\theta$. For constant nonvertical tilt $\theta$ and steady precession $\dot\phi=\Omega_p$, derive the quadratic condition for $\Omega_p$. For $I_1=0.200\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, $I_3=0.100\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, $\omega_3=10.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $Mg\ell=0.500\,\mathrm J$, and $\theta=60^\circ$, calculate both branches.
permittedResults: Use the $\theta$ Euler-Lagrange equation with $\dot\theta=0$ and $\omega_3=\dot\psi+\Omega_p\cos\theta$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Write the heavy-top Lagrangian in the declared potential convention. Next: Set the nutation rate and acceleration to zero while retaining the coupling through $\omega_3$. Finally: Solve both quadratic roots and check the discriminant and torque dimensions.

milestones.criterion: The constant-tilt Euler-Lagrange equation retains inertial, gyroscopic, and gravitational torque terms.
Solving the resulting quadratic gives the slow and fast rates near $0.528$ and $9.47\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
The discriminant and units of every term are checked under the stated potential convention.

commonErrors.description: Drops the $I_1\Omega_p^2\cos\theta$ term and therefore finds only one precession branch.
commonErrors.consequence: Dropping the quadratic inertial term collapses two physical precession branches into an approximation valid only in a restricted regime.

commonErrors.description: Uses the opposite gravity sign without changing the declared potential convention.
commonErrors.consequence: Changing the gravity sign moves the stationary condition to a different orientation convention and invalidates the numerical roots.

hintTree.content: Write the heavy-top Lagrangian in the declared potential convention.
Set the nutation rate and acceleration to zero while retaining the coupling through $\omega_3$.
Solve both quadratic roots and check the discriminant and torque dimensions.

CM:173.canonicalSolution: The constant-tilt equation is $I_1\Omega_p^2\cos\theta-I_3\omega_3\Omega_p+Mg\ell=0$. Numerically it is $0.100\Omega_p^2-1.00\Omega_p+0.500=0$, so $\Omega_p=5(1\pm\sqrt{0.8})\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, or approximately $0.528$ and $9.47\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. These are the slow and fast precession branches. The discriminant condition $(I_3\omega_3)^2\ge4I_1Mg\ell\cos\theta$ is satisfied. Each term in the quadratic has units of torque.
