CM:174.title: Nutation effective potential of a symmetric top
CM:174.objective: Reduce heavy-top nutation to a one-dimensional energy problem using its two cyclic momenta and expose the polar centrifugal barrier.
CM:174.statement: For the heavy symmetric top with $V=Mg\ell\cos\theta$, eliminate the cyclic rates using $p_\psi=I_3(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)$ and $p_\phi=I_1\dot\phi\sin^2\theta+p_\psi\cos\theta$. Derive the one-dimensional nutation energy and its effective potential. Evaluate the effective potential at $\theta=\pi/2$ for $I_1=1$, $I_3=1/2$, $p_\phi=2$, $p_\psi=1$, and $Mg\ell=1/2$ in consistent units.
permittedResults: Solve first for $\dot\phi$ and use energy rather than substituting into the Lagrangian with the wrong sign.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Solve the two conserved-momentum relations for the cyclic rates. Next: Insert the rates into the conserved energy and isolate the positive nutation kinetic term. Finally: Evaluate the stated angle and interpret turning points and polar barriers.

milestones.criterion: The cyclic relations are inverted to give $\dot\phi=(p_\phi-p_\psi\cos\theta)/(I_1\sin^2\theta)$.
The effective potential contains the squared momentum combination, the axial constant, and the declared gravity term with correct signs.
Its value at $\pi/2$ is three energy units, and turning points and polar exclusions follow from the same expression.

commonErrors.description: Forms an effective potential by substituting cyclic rates directly into the Lagrangian without a Routh or energy construction.
commonErrors.consequence: Naive substitution into the Lagrangian gives the wrong reduced sign structure because cyclic elimination is a partial Legendre problem.

commonErrors.description: Omits the factor $\sin^2\theta$ and loses the polar barrier.
commonErrors.consequence: Removing $\sin^2\theta$ eliminates the coordinate barrier and permits generically impossible passage through the Euler poles.

hintTree.content: Solve the two conserved-momentum relations for the cyclic rates.
Insert the rates into the conserved energy and isolate the positive nutation kinetic term.

CM:174.canonicalSolution: Elimination gives $\dot\phi=(p_\phi-p_\psi\cos\theta)/(I_1\sin^2\theta)$. At $\theta=\pi/2$, this is $4/2+1/(1)+0=3$ in energy units. Nutation turning points satisfy $E=U_{eff}$; the centrifugal denominator also shows why generic nonzero momenta prevent the symmetry axis from reaching $\theta=0$ or $\pi$.

CM:175.title: Rolling disk on a circular track without slip
CM:175.objective: Enforce no slip for an upright disk following a horizontal circle and separate axle spin from vertical yaw in both contact kinematics and energy.
CM:175.statement: A thin disk of mass $M$ and radius $R$ rolls upright without slip while its center follows a horizontal circle of radius $\rho$ at constant speed $v$. The disk plane is tangent to the circle. Decompose its angular velocity into axle spin and vertical yaw, prove the instantaneous contact point has zero velocity, and derive the kinetic energy. Evaluate $|\boldsymbol\omega|$ and $T$ for $M=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $R=0.300\,\mathrm m$, $\rho=1.20\,\mathrm m$, and $v=1.50\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
permittedResults: For a thin disk, the axle moment is $MR^2/2$ and any diameter moment is $MR^2/4$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Resolve spin and yaw about their distinct instantaneous axes. Next: Apply $\mathbf v_P=\mathbf v_C+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{P/C}$ at the contact point. Finally: Use the correct principal moment for each component and check the straight-track limit.

milestones.criterion: The axle component cancels center velocity at contact while the yaw component is shown to contribute no contact velocity.
Spin and yaw use their distinct principal moments in the rotational-energy sum.
The numerical angular speed and $3.410$ J energy agree with the straight-track limit as $\rho$ grows.

commonErrors.description: Imposes $v=R|\boldsymbol\omega|$ on the total angular speed and therefore counts yaw as rolling spin.
commonErrors.consequence: Applying $v=R|\boldsymbol\omega|$ to yaw as well as axle spin imposes a false no-slip constraint.

commonErrors.description: Uses the axle moment for the vertical yaw component.
commonErrors.consequence: Using the axle moment for vertical yaw overcounts the yaw energy by a factor of two.

hintTree.content: Resolve spin and yaw about their distinct instantaneous axes.
Apply $\mathbf v_P=\mathbf v_C+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{P/C}$ at the contact point.
Use the correct principal moment for each component and check the straight-track limit.

CM:175.canonicalSolution: Choose $\mathbf e_\theta$ along the center velocity, $\mathbf e_r$ outward, and $\mathbf e_z$ upward. No slip requires axle spin $\boldsymbol\omega_s=-(v/R)\mathbf e_r$ because $\boldsymbol\omega_s\times(-R\mathbf e_z)=-v\mathbf e_\theta$. The disk also yaws with $\boldsymbol\omega_y=(v/\rho)\mathbf e_z$; this contributes no contact velocity because it is parallel to the center-to-contact vector. Thus $|\boldsymbol\omega|=v\sqrt{R^{-2}+\rho^{-2}}=5.154\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The energy is $T=Mv^2/2+(MR^2/2)(v/R)^2/2+(MR^2/4)(v/\rho)^2/2=3Mv^2/4+MR^2v^2/(8\rho^2)=3.410\,\mathrm J$. The straight-track limit $\rho\to\infty$ removes yaw energy.

CM:176.title: A rolling sphere on a translating incline

CM:177.title: Center of percussion cancels the pivot impulse
CM:177.objective: Derive the center-of-percussion distance from coupled linear and angular impulse balances and verify the result for a uniform rod.
CM:177.statement: A planar rigid body is pinned at $O$, with center of mass a distance $d$ from the pin and moment of inertia $I_O$ about it. Starting from rest, it receives a transverse impulse $J$ at a point a distance $b$ from $O$ along the line from $O$ to the center of mass. Let the pin's transverse impulse be $R$, positive in the direction of $J$. Derive $R(b)$ and the center-of-percussion distance for which $R=0$. Then take a uniform rod of mass $M=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ and length $L=1.20\,\mathrm m$, pinned at one end, with $J=9.00\,\mathrm{N\,s}$. Find the required strike distance, angular speed, center-of-mass speed, kinetic energy, and an impulse-work check.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Write angular impulse about the pin and linear impulse for the center of mass. Next: Eliminate the post-impact velocities using rigid-body kinematics and set the pin impulse to zero. Finally: Evaluate the uniform-rod case and close it with an energy-versus-impulse-work check.

milestones.criterion: Angular and linear impulse balances are combined with $v_C=\omega d$ to obtain $R=J(Mdb/I_O-1)$.

The center-of-mass speed, zero pin impulse, $18.0$ J kinetic energy, and impulse-work check are mutually consistent.

commonErrors.consequence: Replacing $I_O$ by $I_C$ predicts the false rod result $b=L/6$ and fails to cancel the pin impulse.

commonErrors.description: Treats the struck point as a particle of mass $M$ and omits the body's rotation.
commonErrors.consequence: Using only $J/M$ cannot enforce both rigid-body kinematics and angular impulse, so it misses the center-of-percussion condition.

hintTree.content: Take angular impulse about $O$, where the ideal pin impulse has zero moment.
Use $v_C=\omega d$ only after relating $I_O\omega$ to $Jb$.

CM:178.title: A reaction wheel slews its spacecraft without external torque
CM:178.objective: Use angular-momentum exchange to relate spacecraft attitude to a reaction wheel's relative rotation and audit the coupled kinetic energy.
CM:178.statement: An axisymmetric spacecraft bus has moment of inertia $I_b$ about its slew axis, excluding a coaxial reaction wheel of inertia $I_w$. milestones.criterion: Total inertial angular momentum is written as $(I_b+I_w)\dot\theta+I_w\dot\phi$ and set to its initial zero value.
The integrated relation gives $\Delta\theta=-\pi/2$, while the coast rates are $-2.00$ and $18.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ for bus and wheel inertially.

commonErrors.description: Calls $\dot\phi$ the wheel's inertial rate and uses it directly in the wheel energy.
commonErrors.consequence: Ignoring the bus rate gives the wrong wheel angular momentum and overstates the kinetic energy.

CM:184.title: Local hyperbolic map near intermediate-axis rotation
CM:184.objective: Construct the signed linear hyperbolic flow near intermediate-axis rotation, including its growth eigenvector and its finite-amplitude boundary.

If $\psi$ is held constant, they do integrate, which is a restricted special case rather than a contradiction.

CM:188.title: A sphere rolling on a rotating table
CM:188.objective: Solve the instantaneous no-slip constraint for a sphere whose center is fixed above a rotating table and minimize energy over the unconstrained spin.
CM:188.statement: A sphere of radius $R$ has center instantaneously fixed at $\mathbf r=r\mathbf e_x$ above a horizontal table rotating with $\boldsymbol\Omega=\Omega\mathbf e_z$. Impose no slip at contact and find the required horizontal angular-velocity component of the sphere. Identify the unconstrained component. For a homogeneous sphere of mass $M$, find the minimum rotational kinetic energy compatible with no slip.
permittedResults: The table velocity is $\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r$ and the contact vector from the center is $-R\mathbf e_z$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Equate the material velocities of the two surfaces at their common point. Next: Solve the cross product for the horizontal spin and identify the null direction. Finally: Minimize over the free vertical spin and check the $r=0$ limit.

milestones.criterion: Rigid contact kinematics fixes the required horizontal angular-velocity component $\omega_x=\Omega r/R$.
Vertical spin is correctly left free because it creates no velocity at the bottom contact.
Setting that free component to zero gives $T_{min}=M\Omega^2r^2/5$ and the axis limit is consistent.

commonErrors.description: Sets the sphere angular velocity equal to the table angular velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: Copying the table's vertical angular velocity onto the sphere fails to match the table's tangential contact velocity.

commonErrors.description: Treats vertical spin as fixed by no slip even though it has zero contact velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: No slip cannot determine a spin parallel to the contact radius, so assigning one removes a genuine free degree of freedom.

hintTree.content: Equate the material velocities of the two surfaces at their common point.
Solve the cross product for the horizontal spin and identify the null direction.
Minimize over the free vertical spin and check the $r=0$ limit.

CM:188.canonicalSolution: No slip requires $\mathbf v_C+\boldsymbol\omega\times(-R\mathbf e_z)=\Omega r\mathbf e_y$. Since $\mathbf v_C=0$, this is satisfied by $\omega_x=\Omega r/R$ and $\omega_y=0$. The vertical spin $\omega_z$ is unconstrained because it produces no contact velocity. Minimum energy sets that free spin to zero. With $I=2MR^2/5$, $T_{min}=I(\Omega r/R)^2/2=M\Omega^2r^2/5$. The result vanishes at the table axis and is independent of sphere radius after substitution.

graderFixtures.proofText: No slip requires $\mathbf v_C+\boldsymbol\omega\times(-R\mathbf e_z)=\Omega r\mathbf e_y$. Since $\mathbf v_C=0$, this is satisfied by $\omega_x=\Omega r/R$ and $\omega_y=0$. The vertical spin $\omega_z$ is unconstrained because it produces no contact velocity. Minimum energy sets that free spin to zero. With $I=2MR^2/5$, $T_{min}=I(\Omega r/R)^2/2=M\Omega^2r^2/5$. The result vanishes at the table axis and is independent of sphere radius after substitution.
No slip requires $\boldsymbol\omega=\Omega\mathbf e_z$, giving energy $MR^2\Omega^2/5$.

CM:189.title: Intermediate-axis instability from full Euler dynamics
CM:189.objective: Unify Euler-equation derivation, invariant checks, all three principal-axis linearizations, and a numerical intermediate-axis e-folding time.
CM:189.statement: For a torque-free body with $I_1<I_2<I_3$, derive Euler's equations, prove conservation of energy and $L^2$, and linearize about each principal-axis rotation. Show the extreme axes are stable and the intermediate axis has growth rate $\sigma=|\Omega|\sqrt{(I_2-I_1)(I_3-I_2)/(I_1I_3)}$. For $(I_1,I_2,I_3)=(1,2,3)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ and $\Omega=12.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, find the e-folding time. Explain the linear-regime boundary.
permittedResults: Use the rotating-basis angular-momentum balance and retain moment-difference signs through every linearization.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Derive the body equations from space angular-momentum balance. Next: Use two separate cyclic cancellations for the invariants, then linearize all three axes. Finally: Evaluate the intermediate growth time and state when the linear approximation ceases to apply.

milestones.criterion: The transport theorem produces the torque-free Euler equations and both quadratic conservation laws.
Extreme-axis perturbations are oscillatory while axis 2 has the stated real growth rate.
For moments $(1,2,3)$ and $12\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, the e-folding time is $0.144$ s and its linear domain is explicit.

commonErrors.description: Reverses one Euler-equation moment difference and predicts an imaginary intermediate growth rate.
commonErrors.consequence: One reversed moment difference turns a real saddle eigenvalue imaginary and falsely stabilizes the intermediate axis.

commonErrors.description: Extends the exponential perturbation solution beyond the invariant-bounded linear regime.
commonErrors.consequence: Invariant-bounded nonlinear motion invalidates an indefinitely extrapolated linear exponential after perturbations become large.

hintTree.content: Derive the body equations from space angular-momentum balance.
Use two separate cyclic cancellations for the invariants, then linearize all three axes.
Evaluate the intermediate growth time and state when the linear approximation ceases to apply.

CM:189.canonicalSolution: Euler's equations are $I_1\dot\omega_1=(I_2-I_3)\omega_2\omega_3$ and cyclic permutations. Multiplication by $\omega_i$ and by $I_i\omega_i$ gives the two cyclic cancellations proving conservation of $2T$ and $L^2$. The extreme-axis perturbations have negative second-order coefficients and oscillate. About $\Omega\mathbf e_2$, the transverse coefficient is positive, giving the stated $\sigma$. For moments $1,2,3$ and $\Omega=12$, $\sigma=12/\sqrt3=6.928\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $\tau=1/\sigma=0.144\,\mathrm s$. Exponential growth applies only while transverse components remain small relative to $|\Omega|$; the exact invariants bound the subsequent nonlinear motion.

The extreme-axis perturbations have negative second-order coefficients and oscillate. About $\Omega\mathbf e_2$, the transverse coefficient is positive, giving the stated $\sigma$. CM:190.title: Two-plane rotor balancing cancels force and rocking couple
CM:190.objective: Solve a two-plane dynamic-balancing problem with complex unbalance phasors and verify simultaneous cancellation of force and couple.
CM:190.statement: Represent each rotating unbalance by the complex phasor $U_j=m_jr_j e^{i\phi_j}$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m}$. Two existing unbalances are $U_1=0.0200\,\mathrm{kg\,m}$ at axial coordinate $z_1=+0.300\,\mathrm m$ and $U_2=0.0100i\,\mathrm{kg\,m}$ at $z_2=-0.200\,\mathrm m$. Correction masses may be placed at radius $r_c=0.100\,\mathrm m$ in planes $z_A=-0.500\,\mathrm m$ and $z_B=+0.500\,\mathrm m$. Find the two correction phasors, masses, and phases measured counterclockwise from the positive real axis so that both $\sum U$ and $\sum zU$ vanish. At $\Omega=300\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute the original rotating-force and rocking-couple amplitudes and verify their corrected values.
permittedResults: A rotating unbalance produces force phasor $\Omega^2U$ and couple phasor $\Omega^2zU$ about the reference plane.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Form the existing force and couple unbalance phasors. Next: solve the two complex linear balance equations for the correction planes. Finally: convert phasors to physical masses and phases and evaluate the before-and-after amplitudes.

milestones.criterion: Both complex balance equations are formed with the correct axial signs and solved as $U_A=-0.00400-0.00700i$ and $U_B=-0.0160-0.00300i$.
Phasor moduli and quadrants give masses $0.0806$ kg and $0.1628$ kg at $240.3^\circ$ and $190.6^\circ$.
Original force and couple amplitudes evaluate to $2.01$ kN and $569$ N m, and direct substitution verifies both corrected sums vanish.

commonErrors.description: Balances only $\sum U$ with one correction and ignores the axial couple $\sum zU$.
commonErrors.consequence: Static balance can remove the net rotating force while leaving a nonzero rocking couple.

commonErrors.description: Uses phasor components as unsigned mass values and discards their phases.
commonErrors.consequence: Correction masses placed without the computed quadrants reinforce rather than cancel some unbalance components.

hintTree.content: Static balance requires $U_A+U_B=-(U_1+U_2)$.
Dynamic balance also requires $z_AU_A+z_BU_B=-(z_1U_1+z_2U_2)$.
After solving for each complex phasor, divide its modulus by $r_c$ and use its quadrant to report the phase.

CM:190.canonicalSolution: The original sums are $U_1+U_2=0.0200+0.0100i\,\mathrm{kg\,m}$ and $z_1U_1+z_2U_2=0.00600-0.00200i\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$. The correction equations are $U_A+U_B=-0.0200-0.0100i$ and $-0.500U_A+0.500U_B=-0.00600+0.00200i$. Solving gives $U_A=-0.00400-0.00700i$ and $U_B=-0.0160-0.00300i\,\mathrm{kg\,m}$. Thus $m_A=|U_A|/r_c=0.0806\,\mathrm{kg}$ at $240.3^\circ$ and $m_B=0.1628\,\mathrm{kg}$ at $190.6^\circ$. Before correction the force amplitude is $\Omega^2|\sum U|=2.01\times10^3\,\mathrm N$ and the couple amplitude is $\Omega^2|\sum zU|=5.69\times10^2\,\mathrm{N\,m}$. Substitution gives both corrected phasor sums exactly zero, so both amplitudes vanish for every $\Omega$ within the rigid-rotor model.

The correction equations are $U_A+U_B=-0.0200-0.0100i$ and $-0.500U_A+0.500U_B=-0.00600+0.00200i$. Solving gives $U_A=-0.00400-0.00700i$ and $U_B=-0.0160-0.00300i\,\mathrm{kg\,m}$. CM:191.title: Planar gravity-gradient libration of a dumbbell satellite
CM:191.objective: Extract the exact gravity-gradient attitude equation and compare its small-libration period with the orbital period.
CM:191.statement: A slender dumbbell satellite is in a circular orbit of mean motion $n$. Let $\theta$ be its small in-plane angle from the local radial direction. Starting from the quadrupole gravity-gradient potential $U(\theta)=-(3/2)n^2(I_t-I_r)\cos^2\theta$ and rotational kinetic energy $I_n\dot\theta^2/2$, derive the exact angular equation and its small-libration frequency when the planar inertia relation gives $(I_t-I_r)/I_n=1$. Compare the libration period with the orbital period.
permittedResults: Differentiate the supplied attitude potential before linearizing.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Form the attitude equation from the supplied potential and rotational inertia. Next: Linearize only after obtaining the exact sine-cosine torque. Finally: Compare periods and check the equilibrium curvature sign.

milestones.criterion: Differentiation of the cosine-squared potential includes the factor two and the correct restoring sign.
The stated inertia ratio reduces the linear frequency to $\sqrt3n$.
Curvature classifies radial alignment as stable and gives $T_{lib}=T_{orbit}/\sqrt3$.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates $\cos^2\theta$ without the factor two.
commonErrors.consequence: Missing the derivative factor two lowers the torque and frequency by a spurious factor of $\sqrt2$.

commonErrors.description: Uses orbital mean motion $n$ itself as the libration frequency.
commonErrors.consequence: Orbital rotation supplies the scale $n$ but the gravity-gradient curvature changes the libration frequency.

hintTree.content: Form the attitude equation from the supplied potential and rotational inertia.
Linearize only after obtaining the exact sine-cosine torque.
Compare periods and check the equilibrium curvature sign.

CM:191.canonicalSolution: $I_n\ddot\theta=-dU/d\theta=-3n^2(I_t-I_r)\sin\theta\cos\theta$. With the stated inertia ratio, $\ddot\theta+3n^2\sin\theta\cos\theta=0$. For small angle, $\sin\theta\cos\theta\simeq\theta$, so $\omega_{lib}=\sqrt3n$. Therefore $T_{lib}=2\pi/(\sqrt3n)=T_{orbit}/\sqrt3$. The radial alignment is stable because $U''(0)=3n^2(I_t-I_r)>0$ under the stated ordering; the tangential alignment has the opposite curvature.

graderFixtures.proofText: $I_n\ddot\theta=-dU/d\theta=-3n^2(I_t-I_r)\sin\theta\cos\theta$. With the stated inertia ratio, $\ddot\theta+3n^2\sin\theta\cos\theta=0$. For small angle, $\sin\theta\cos\theta\simeq\theta$, so $\omega_{lib}=\sqrt3n$. Therefore $T_{lib}=2\pi/(\sqrt3n)=T_{orbit}/\sqrt3$. The radial alignment is stable because $U''(0)=3n^2(I_t-I_r)>0$ under the stated ordering; the tangential alignment has the opposite curvature.
Differentiate $\cos^2\theta$ as $-\sin\theta\cos\theta$, missing its factor two. This gives $\omega_{lib}=\sqrt{3/2}n$ and $T_{lib}=\sqrt{2/3}T_{orbit}$.

CM:192.title: Oblique spinning-rod impact through effective mass
CM:192.objective: Reduce an oblique spinning-rod collision to a scalar contact effective mass and verify restitution after coupled translation and rotation.
CM:192.statement: A uniform slender rod of mass $M$ and length $2a$ lies in a vertical plane at angle $\gamma$ above horizontal. Its lower-left endpoint, with center-to-contact vector $\mathbf r=(-a\cos\gamma,-a\sin\gamma)$, strikes a fixed smooth horizontal plane. Before impact the center vertical velocity is $V_y^-$ and the counterclockwise spin is $\omega^-$. Derive the contact normal speed, effective inverse mass, normal impulse for restitution coefficient $e$, and post-impact $(V_y^+,\omega^+)$. Show angular momentum about contact is conserved during impact. Evaluate for $M=4.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $a=0.750\,\mathrm m$, $\gamma=30.0^\circ$, $V_y^-=-2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $\omega^-=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $e=0.500$, using $I_C=Ma^2/3$.
permittedResults: With upward normal and $r_x=-a\cos\gamma$, the signed contact speed is $g^-=V_y^-+\omega^-r_x<0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Write the pre-impact contact velocity from rigid-body kinematics in the declared axes. Next: Propagate one normal impulse through both center translation and angular impulse to obtain the contact effective mass. Finally: Apply restitution, recompute the contact speed numerically, and verify angular momentum about contact.

milestones.criterion: Rigid-body kinematics gives $g^-=V_y^-+\omega^-r_x$ at the actual endpoint.
Impulse updates produce $\mathcal K=1/M+r_x^2/I_C$ and $J=-(1+e)g^-/\mathcal K$.
The numerical post-impact state reconstructs $g^+=-eg^-$ and preserves angular momentum about contact.

commonErrors.description: Applies restitution to the center velocity instead of the velocity of the oblique spinning contact point.
commonErrors.consequence: Applying restitution at the center ignores pre-impact spin and predicts the wrong normal impulse.

commonErrors.description: Drops the rotational term $r_x^2/I_C$ from the effective inverse mass.
commonErrors.consequence: Omitting rotational compliance overestimates the impulse because all contact-speed change is assigned to translation.

hintTree.content: Write the pre-impact contact velocity from rigid-body kinematics in the declared axes.
Propagate one normal impulse through both center translation and angular impulse to obtain the contact effective mass.
Apply restitution, recompute the contact speed numerically, and verify angular momentum about contact.

CM:192.canonicalSolution: An upward impulse $J$ gives $V_y^+=V_y^-+J/M$ and $\omega^+=\omega^-+r_xJ/I_C$. Hence $g^+=g^-+J\mathcal K$ with $\mathcal K=1/M+r_x^2/I_C>0$. Restitution $g^+=-eg^-$ gives $J=-(1+e)g^-/\mathcal K$. Because the plane impulse acts at contact, its moment about contact vanishes; with gravity negligible, angular momentum about that point is unchanged. Numerically $I_C=0.750\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, $r_x=-0.6495\,\mathrm m$, $g^-=-2.6495\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $\mathcal K=0.8125\,\mathrm{kg^{-1}}$. Thus $J=4.891\,\mathrm{N\,s}$, $V_y^+=-0.777\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $\omega^+=-3.236\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The reconstructed $g^+=1.3248\,\mathrm{m/s}=-eg^-$ checks every sign.

CM:193.title: Euler-top quadrature from invariant elimination
CM:193.objective: Eliminate two squared Euler-top components from the invariant pair and reduce the remaining motion to an explicit cubic quadrature.
CM:193.statement: Let $I_1<I_2<I_3$, $A=2T$, $B=L^2$, and $y=\omega_2^2$. Eliminate $\omega_1^2$ and $\omega_3^2$ from the two invariants, then derive a first-order cubic equation $(\dot y)^2=P_3(y)$. State the quadrature for one oscillation between adjacent nonnegative turning roots. No special-function name may replace the derivation.
permittedResults: Use Euler's second equation only after solving the two linear invariant equations.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Solve the pair of invariant equations linearly for the other two squared components. Next: Square the second Euler equation only after multiplying by $2\omega_2$. Finally: Identify allowed roots, write the round-trip quadrature, and check dimensions.

milestones.criterion: Linear algebra is applied to $\omega_1^2$ and $\omega_3^2$ with the denominators and moment order intact.
Differentiating $y=\omega_2^2$ supplies $2\omega_2$ before Euler's second equation is squared.
The cubic, its allowed adjacent roots, round-trip period integral, and $\mathrm{s^{-6}}$ dimensions are all consistent.

commonErrors.description: Eliminates unsquared angular-velocity components linearly from quadratic invariants.
commonErrors.consequence: Quadratic invariants do not support linear elimination of signed angular velocities, so that route creates false branches.

commonErrors.description: Forgets the factor $2\omega_2$ when differentiating $y=\omega_2^2$.
commonErrors.consequence: Losing $2\omega_2$ changes the polynomial degree and the temporal dimensions of the reduced equation.

hintTree.content: Solve the pair of invariant equations linearly for the other two squared components.
Square the second Euler equation only after multiplying by $2\omega_2$.
Identify allowed roots, write the round-trip quadrature, and check dimensions.

CM:193.canonicalSolution: Invariant elimination gives $\omega_1^2=[I_3A-B-I_2(I_3-I_2)y]/[I_1(I_3-I_1)]$ and $\omega_3^2=[B-I_1A-I_2(I_2-I_1)y]/[I_3(I_3-I_1)]$. Since $\dot y=2\omega_2\dot\omega_2=2[(I_3-I_1)/I_2]\omega_1\omega_2\omega_3$, squaring yields $P_3(y)=4y[I_3A-B-I_2(I_3-I_2)y][B-I_1A-I_2(I_2-I_1)y]/(I_1I_2^2I_3)$. If $y_-$ and $y_+$ are adjacent allowed roots, the oscillation period is $2\int_{y_-}^{y_+}dy/\sqrt{P_3(y)}$. Dimensional inspection gives $(\dot y)^2$ units $\mathrm{s^{-6}}$ on both sides.

CM:194.title: Dzhanibekov flip time on the Euler separatrix
CM:194.objective: Construct the Euler-separatrix model of a Dzhanibekov flip and quantify its logarithmically diverging near-endpoint flip time.
CM:194.statement: To model a Dzhanibekov, or tennis-racket, flip for $I_1<I_2<I_3$, consider the torque-free separatrix with $2T=L^2/I_2$ and define $\Omega=L/I_2>0$. Verify a heteroclinic solution with $\omega_2=\Omega\tanh(\sigma t)$ and transverse components proportional to $\operatorname{sech}(\sigma t)$. Derive $\sigma$, the two transverse amplitudes, and the time to go from $\omega_2=-\Omega(1-\delta)$ to $+\Omega(1-\delta)$. Evaluate it for $(I_1,I_2,I_3)=(1,2,3)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, $\Omega=10.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $\delta=0.0100$.
permittedResults: Use both invariants to determine transverse amplitudes before applying Euler's second equation.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Use the separatrix energy relation in both quadratic invariants. Next: Match the hyperbolic-function ansatz to Euler's equations to determine amplitudes and growth scale. Finally: Solve the two threshold times, evaluate them, and identify the logarithmic divergence.

milestones.criterion: Both invariants fix the transverse $\operatorname{sech}$ amplitudes with the correct moment ratios.
Euler's equation supplies $\sigma=\Omega\sqrt{(I_3-I_2)(I_2-I_1)/(I_1I_3)}$.
The threshold-to-threshold time reduces to $\ln[(2-\delta)/\delta]/\sigma$ and evaluates to $0.917$ s.

commonErrors.description: Calls the exact heteroclinic separatrix a finite-period orbit.
commonErrors.consequence: A heteroclinic orbit approaches equilibria asymptotically, so assigning it a finite period erases the logarithmic delay.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\sigma=\Omega$ independent of all principal moments.
commonErrors.consequence: Ignoring principal moments gives the wrong local growth scale and therefore the wrong flip-time estimate.

hintTree.content: Use the separatrix energy relation in both quadratic invariants.
Match the hyperbolic-function ansatz to Euler's equations to determine amplitudes and growth scale.
Solve the two threshold times, evaluate them, and identify the logarithmic divergence.

CM:194.canonicalSolution: The invariant relations give $\omega_1=\Omega\sqrt{I_2(I_3-I_2)/[I_1(I_3-I_1)]}\,\operatorname{sech}(\sigma t)$ and $\omega_3=\Omega\sqrt{I_2(I_2-I_1)/[I_3(I_3-I_1)]}\,\operatorname{sech}(\sigma t)$, up to consistent signs. Euler's second equation then gives $\sigma=\Omega\sqrt{(I_3-I_2)(I_2-I_1)/(I_1I_3)}$. The requested interval is $\Delta t=2\operatorname{artanh}(1-\delta)/\sigma=\ln[(2-\delta)/\delta]/\sigma$. Numerically $\sigma=10/\sqrt3=5.7735\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $\Delta t=\ln199/5.7735=0.917\,\mathrm s$. As $\delta\to0$, the time diverges logarithmically; the exact separatrix is not periodic.

CM:195.title: Heavy-top nutation separatrix and double-root test
CM:195.objective: Characterize a heavy-top nutation separatrix as an unstable double turning root and prove its logarithmic approach time locally.
CM:195.statement: For the heavy symmetric-top effective potential $U_{eff}(\theta)=(p_\phi-p_\psi\cos\theta)^2/(2I\sin^2\theta)+p_\psi^2/(2I_3)+Mg\ell\cos\theta$, prove that a nutation separatrix occurs when the energy line has a double root at an unstable stationary angle $\theta_s$. Derive the two algebraic conditions and show the travel time to $\theta_s$ diverges logarithmically when $U_{eff}''(\theta_s)<0$.
permittedResults: Near the stationary angle, expand $E-U_{eff}$ through quadratic order.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: State both energy equality and vanishing derivative at the proposed separatrix angle. Next: Expand the effective potential locally and insert it into the nutation energy equation. Finally: Compare the logarithmic double-root time with an ordinary simple turning point.

milestones.criterion: Both $E_s=U_{eff}(\theta_s)$ and $U_{eff}'(\theta_s)=0$ are imposed at the candidate root.
Negative curvature turns the local energy difference into a positive quadratic in displacement.
The resulting $dq/|q|$ time integral is contrasted with the integrable square-root behavior of a simple turning point.

commonErrors.description: Identifies every ordinary turning point as a separatrix.
commonErrors.consequence: An ordinary simple root produces a finite reflection time and therefore is not automatically a separatrix.

commonErrors.description: Uses a stable minimum with positive curvature to claim logarithmic approach.
commonErrors.consequence: Expansion about a stable minimum has the wrong curvature sign for asymptotic approach at the same energy.

hintTree.content: State both energy equality and vanishing derivative at the proposed separatrix angle.
Expand the effective potential locally and insert it into the nutation energy equation.
Compare the logarithmic double-root time with an ordinary simple turning point.

CM:195.canonicalSolution: A double turning root requires $E_s=U_{eff}(\theta_s)$ and $U_{eff}'(\theta_s)=0$. If the stationary point is unstable, $U_{eff}''(\theta_s)<0$. Writing $q=\theta-\theta_s$ gives $E_s-U_{eff}(\theta)=-(1/2)U_{eff}''(\theta_s)q^2+O(q^3)$. From $I\dot\theta^2/2=E_s-U_{eff}$, $dt\sim\sqrt{I/[-U_{eff}''(\theta_s)]}\,dq/|q|$. Its integral diverges as $\ln|q|^{-1}$. A simple turning root would instead give an integrable inverse-square-root singularity, so stationarity is essential.

CM:196.title: Routh reduction of the heavy symmetric top
CM:196.objective: Perform a genuine partial Legendre transform of the heavy top at fixed axial momentum and verify the reduced dynamics.
CM:196.statement: For the heavy symmetric-top Lagrangian in problem CM:185, hold $p_\psi$ fixed and eliminate the cyclic rate $\dot\psi$. Derive the Routhian $\mathcal R=L-p_\psi\dot\psi$ as a function of $(\theta,\phi,\dot\theta,\dot\phi;p_\psi)$. Verify that its $\phi$ momentum is still $p_\phi$ and that its reduced Euler-Lagrange equation for $\theta$ matches the full equation after elimination.
permittedResults: Solve $p_\psi=I_3(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)$ before performing the partial Legendre transform.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Solve the cyclic momentum relation exactly. Next: Perform the partial Legendre transform rather than mere substitution into the Lagrangian. Finally: Check the surviving cyclic momentum and compare the reduced tilt equation term by term.

milestones.criterion: The axial rate is solved from $p_\psi$ before forming $\mathcal R=L-p_\psi\dot\psi$.
The Routhian retains the gyroscopic $p_\psi\dot\phi\cos\theta$ term and has the correct negative axial constant.
Its surviving $\phi$ momentum and $\theta$ equation agree with the full eliminated system.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes the eliminated rate into $L$ but omits the $-p_\psi\dot\psi$ term.
commonErrors.consequence: Substitution into $L$ alone is not Routh reduction and leaves the cyclic sector with the wrong sign.

commonErrors.description: Drops the gyroscopic term $p_\psi\dot\phi\cos\theta$ as a total derivative.
commonErrors.consequence: The gyroscopic term depends on $\theta$ and affects reduced motion; discarding it is not a harmless boundary change.

hintTree.content: Solve the cyclic momentum relation exactly.
Perform the partial Legendre transform rather than mere substitution into the Lagrangian.
Check the surviving cyclic momentum and compare the reduced tilt equation term by term.

CM:196.canonicalSolution: The eliminated rate is $\dot\psi=p_\psi/I_3-\dot\phi\cos\theta$. Substitution into $\mathcal R=L-p_\psi\dot\psi$ gives $\mathcal R=\tfrac12I(\dot\theta^2+\dot\phi^2\sin^2\theta)+p_\psi\dot\phi\cos\theta-p_\psi^2/(2I_3)-Mg\ell\cos\theta$. Its momentum is $\partial\mathcal R/\partial\dot\phi=I\dot\phi\sin^2\theta+p_\psi\cos\theta=p_\phi$. Differentiating with respect to $\theta$ produces the same centrifugal, gyroscopic, and gravitational terms as the full $\theta$ equation with the eliminated rate. The negative constant $-p_\psi^2/(2I_3)$ does not affect reduced trajectories.

CM:197.title: Two-impulse rest-to-rest attitude maneuver
CM:197.objective: Optimize a bounded-torque rest-to-rest principal-axis maneuver and compute its switching data and impulse budget.
CM:197.statement: A spacecraft rotates about one principal axis with moment $I$. It starts and ends at rest and must rotate through angle $\Theta>0$. An actuator can apply torques $+\tau$ and $-\tau$ of fixed magnitude, switching once. Derive the minimum-time symmetric maneuver, switch time, peak angular speed, total time, and angular impulse magnitude of each burn. Evaluate for $I=120\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, $\tau=24.0\,\mathrm{N\,m}$, and $\Theta=\pi/2$.
permittedResults: With bounded torque and no speed limit, accelerate at full torque then decelerate at full opposite torque.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Use the torque bound to identify full positive and negative acceleration arcs. Next: Integrate angular speed and angle on both symmetric phases. Finally: Evaluate the switch quantities and verify zero final angular momentum.

milestones.criterion: Time symmetry splits the rotation into equal acceleration and deceleration phases.
The relation $\Theta=at_s^2$ yields the switch time, peak speed, and total time with correct factors.
The numerical impulses are equal and opposite, returning angular momentum to zero after a $\pi/2$ turn.

commonErrors.description: Accelerates for the whole maneuver and assumes the spacecraft can stop without a second impulse.
commonErrors.consequence: A single positive burn cannot satisfy the final-rest boundary condition, regardless of its displacement time.

commonErrors.description: Sets each half-phase displacement equal to $at_s^2$ instead of $at_s^2/2$.
commonErrors.consequence: Doubling each half-phase displacement underestimates the switch time and leaves the integrated angle inconsistent.

hintTree.content: Use the torque bound to identify full positive and negative acceleration arcs.
Integrate angular speed and angle on both symmetric phases.
Evaluate the switch quantities and verify zero final angular momentum.

The peak speed is $at_s=\sqrt{\tau\Theta/I}$ and total time is $2t_s$. Each burn has angular impulse $\tau t_s=\sqrt{I\tau\Theta}$. Opposite impulses give zero final angular momentum.

CM:198.title: Small-angle stability of a rolling convex body
CM:198.objective: Relate local contact curvature to the quadratic rocking stability and frequency of a rolling convex body.
CM:198.statement: A smooth convex body rocks without slip in a vertical plane about an equilibrium contact. Its center of mass is height $h$ above contact, the local radius of curvature of the boundary is $\rho$, and the central moment about the out-of-plane axis is $I_C$. Show that to quadratic order the center height changes by $(\rho-h)\theta^2/2$ and the kinetic energy is $(I_C+Mh^2)\dot\theta^2/2$. Derive the stability condition and small-rocking frequency. Apply it to an elliptical cross-section with horizontal semi-axis $a$ and vertical semi-axis $b$, for which $\rho=a^2/b$ at the bottom.
permittedResults: Use rolling geometry only to second order around the equilibrium contact.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Expand both rolling geometry and kinetic energy consistently to quadratic order. Next: Build the small-angle Lagrangian and read the curvature sign and frequency. Finally: Insert the ellipse curvature and check broad, tall, and circular limits.

milestones.criterion: Geometry gives center-height change $(\rho-h)\theta^2/2$ under the declared displacement.
The effective inertia includes both $I_C$ and the center translation term $Mh^2$.
The sign of $\rho-h$ classifies ellipse orientations and the circular limit becomes neutral.

commonErrors.description: Uses $h-\rho$ instead of $\rho-h$ and reverses broad-versus-tall stability.
commonErrors.consequence: Reversing the height-curvature difference swaps stable broad bodies with unstable tall ones.

commonErrors.description: Omits the translational contribution $Mh^2$ from the effective inertia.
commonErrors.consequence: Dropping $Mh^2$ makes the predicted frequency too high by ignoring center-of-mass kinetic energy.

hintTree.content: Expand both rolling geometry and kinetic energy consistently to quadratic order.
Build the small-angle Lagrangian and read the curvature sign and frequency.
Insert the ellipse curvature and check broad, tall, and circular limits.

CM:198.canonicalSolution: The quadratic Lagrangian is $L=(I_C+Mh^2)\dot\theta^2/2-Mg(\rho-h)\theta^2/2$ up to constants. Hence $(I_C+Mh^2)\ddot\theta+Mg(\rho-h)\theta=0$. Stability requires $\rho>h$, with frequency $\omega=\sqrt{Mg(\rho-h)/(I_C+Mh^2)}$; equality is neutral at this order and $\rho<h$ is unstable. For the ellipse with its center at height $h=b$, $\rho-h=(a^2-b^2)/b$, so the broad orientation $a>b$ is stable and the tall orientation $a<b$ is unstable. A circle $a=b$ is neutrally indifferent, a useful limit check.

Stability requires $\rho>h$, with frequency $\omega=\sqrt{Mg(\rho-h)/(I_C+Mh^2)}$; equality is neutral at this order and $\rho<h$ is unstable. For the ellipse with its center at height $h=b$, $\rho-h=(a^2-b^2)/b$, so the broad orientation $a>b$ is stable and the tall orientation $a<b$ is unstable. A circle $a=b$ is neutrally indifferent, a useful limit check.
The height change is $(h-\rho)\theta^2/2$, so broad ellipses with $a>b$ have negative curvature energy and are unstable, while tall ellipses are stable.

CM:199.title: General frictionless rigid-body collision impulse
CM:199.objective: Derive the normal impulse between two offset rigid bodies from their full translational and rotational contact compliance.
CM:199.statement: Two free rigid bodies contact at points with center-to-contact vectors $\mathbf r_A$ and $\mathbf r_B$. Let the unit normal $\mathbf n$ point from $B$ to $A$, and let the pre-impact relative normal speed $g^-=(\mathbf v_A+\boldsymbol\omega_A\times\mathbf r_A-\mathbf v_B-\boldsymbol\omega_B\times\mathbf r_B)\cdot\mathbf n<0$. Derive the frictionless impulse magnitude $J$ for coefficient of restitution $e$, including both rotational effective-mass terms. State the positivity condition on the denominator.
permittedResults: Apply impulses $+J\mathbf n$ to $A$ and $-J\mathbf n$ to $B$, then update both spins by angular impulse.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Write linear and angular impulse updates for both bodies with one normal convention. Next: Project the resulting contact-point relative velocity onto the normal. Finally: Apply restitution, prove denominator positivity, and check the central-impact limit.

milestones.criterion: Opposite impulses update both center velocities and both angular velocities with consistent contact arms.
The effective inverse mass contains two positive translational terms and both inertia-weighted rotational terms.
Restitution gives a positive impulse for closing contact and recovers the particle limit when both arms are normal.

commonErrors.description: Uses only the reduced translational mass and omits both rotational contact responses.
commonErrors.consequence: Using only reduced translational mass ignores contact-point motion generated by angular impulse.

commonErrors.description: Applies impulses in the same direction to both bodies.
commonErrors.consequence: Impulses in the same direction violate action-reaction and create spurious net momentum in the isolated pair.

hintTree.content: Write linear and angular impulse updates for both bodies with one normal convention.
Project the resulting contact-point relative velocity onto the normal.
Apply restitution, prove denominator positivity, and check the central-impact limit.

CM:199.canonicalSolution: The velocity updates are $\Delta\mathbf v_A=J\mathbf n/m_A$, $\Delta\boldsymbol\omega_A=\mathbf I_A^{-1}(\mathbf r_A\times J\mathbf n)$, with opposite linear and corresponding angular impulses for $B$. The relative normal change is $J\mathcal K$, where $\mathcal K=1/m_A+1/m_B+(\mathbf r_A\times\mathbf n)\cdot\mathbf I_A^{-1}(\mathbf r_A\times\mathbf n)+(\mathbf r_B\times\mathbf n)\cdot\mathbf I_B^{-1}(\mathbf r_B\times\mathbf n)$. Restitution $g^+=-eg^-$ gives $J=-(1+e)g^-/\mathcal K>0$. For positive masses and positive-definite inertia on the relevant rotational subspaces, $\mathcal K>0$. If both contact arms are parallel to $\mathbf n$, the rotational terms vanish and the particle formula returns.

The relative normal change is $J\mathcal K$, where $\mathcal K=1/m_A+1/m_B+(\mathbf r_A\times\mathbf n)\cdot\mathbf I_A^{-1}(\mathbf r_A\times\mathbf n)+(\mathbf r_B\times\mathbf n)\cdot\mathbf I_B^{-1}(\mathbf r_B\times\mathbf n)$. If both contact arms are parallel to $\mathbf n$, the rotational terms vanish and the particle formula returns.
The impulse is $-(1+e)g^-/(1/m_A+1/m_B)$ for every rigid-body contact, regardless of contact offset.

CM:201.title: Regular Legendre transform of a natural Lagrangian
CM:201.objective: Convert a regular natural Lagrangian into canonical variables and verify that Hamilton and Euler-Lagrange evolution agree.
CM:201.statement: For $L(q,\dot q)=m\dot q^2/2-V(q)$ with $m>0$, compute the canonical momentum, invert the velocity-momentum relation, and construct the Hamiltonian. Verify Hamilton's equations reproduce the Euler-Lagrange equation and identify the regularity condition.
permittedResults: Use $H=p\dot q-L$ only after expressing $\dot q$ in terms of $(q,p)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Differentiate the Lagrangian with respect to velocity and check the Hessian. Next: Invert for velocity before evaluating the Legendre transform. Finally: Apply both Hamilton equations and recover the second-order equation.

milestones.criterion: The velocity Hessian $m$ is identified as invertible and gives $p=m\dot q$.
Eliminating velocity from the Legendre transform produces $H=p^2/(2m)+V(q)$.
Hamilton's two first-order equations recombine to $m\ddot q+V'(q)=0$ with energy dimensions intact.

commonErrors.description: Leaves $\dot q$ inside the alleged Hamiltonian.
commonErrors.consequence: A Hamiltonian containing unresolved velocity is not a function on canonical phase space and cannot generate the requested equations.

commonErrors.description: Uses $H=L-p\dot q$ and reverses both energy terms.
commonErrors.consequence: Reversing the Legendre transform changes kinetic and potential signs and yields dynamics opposite to the Lagrangian system.

hintTree.content: Differentiate the Lagrangian with respect to velocity and check the Hessian.
Invert for velocity before evaluating the Legendre transform.
Apply both Hamilton equations and recover the second-order equation.

CM:201.canonicalSolution: The momentum is $p=\partial L/\partial\dot q=m\dot q$, so $\dot q=p/m$. The Legendre transform is $H=p(p/m)-[p^2/(2m)-V]=p^2/(2m)+V(q)$. Hamilton's equations give $\dot q=p/m$ and $\dot p=-V'(q)$, hence $m\ddot q+V'(q)=0$, exactly Euler-Lagrange. The velocity Hessian is $\partial^2L/\partial\dot q^2=m$, which is nonzero because $m>0$; this is the required regularity. Kinetic and potential terms both have energy dimensions.

milestones.criterion: Initial data propagate through the correct sine-cosine formulas with reciprocal $m\omega$ scalings.
The matrix determinant is one and its $t=0$ value is the identity.
Substitution into the Hamiltonian cancels cross terms and proves exact energy preservation.

commonErrors.description: Uses $p=mq$ instead of $p=m\dot q$.
commonErrors.consequence: Confusing coordinate with velocity removes the canonical momentum scale and makes the phase map dimensionally inconsistent.

commonErrors.description: Chooses the same sign in both off-diagonal matrix entries.
commonErrors.consequence: Equal off-diagonal signs produce a hyperbolic matrix rather than bounded oscillator rotation.

The map matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\omega t&\sin\omega t/(m\omega)\\-m\omega\sin\omega t&\cos\omega t\end{pmatrix}$. Its determinant is one, and direct substitution cancels cross terms in $p^2/(2m)+m\omega^2q^2/2$, proving exact energy preservation. At $t=0$ it is the identity.

CM:212.statement: A particle moves in a planar potential $V(x,y)$ that is stationary in a frame rotating at constant $\boldsymbol\Omega=\Omega\mathbf e_z$. Derive the rotating-frame Hamiltonian $K=(p_x^2+p_y^2)/(2m)+V-\Omega L_z$, where $L_z=xp_y-yp_x$. Derive the velocity-momentum relation and the second-order rotating-frame equation. Identify the conserved quantity.
permittedResults: Apply Hamilton's equations to $K$ before eliminating canonical momentum.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Use the canonical angular-momentum term with its declared sign. Next: Derive both first-order equations and eliminate momentum carefully. Finally: Identify Coriolis, centrifugal, and the time-independent conserved Hamiltonian.

milestones.criterion: The $-\Omega L_z$ coupling leads to $\dot{\mathbf r}=\mathbf p/m-\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r$.
Momentum elimination yields both $-2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\dot{\mathbf r}$ and $-\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r)$.
Autonomy identifies the rotating Jacobi energy while distinguishing it from inertial energy.

commonErrors.description: Treats canonical momentum as $m\dot{\mathbf r}$ in rotating coordinates.
commonErrors.consequence: Equating canonical and mechanical momentum in rotating coordinates removes the velocity shift and corrupts both fictitious terms.

commonErrors.description: Uses $+\Omega L_z$ while retaining equations for the opposite rotation convention.
commonErrors.consequence: Changing the angular-momentum coupling sign without changing rotation convention reverses Coriolis dynamics.

CM:212.canonicalSolution: Hamilton's equations give $\dot{\mathbf r}=\mathbf p/m-\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r$, so $\mathbf p=m(\dot{\mathbf r}+\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r)$. The momentum equation is $\dot{\mathbf p}=-\nabla V-\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf p$. Differentiation and elimination produce $m\ddot{\mathbf r}=-\nabla V-2m\boldsymbol\Omega\times\dot{\mathbf r}-m\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r)$. The two extra terms are Coriolis and centrifugal contributions with the declared rotating-coordinate convention. Because $K$ has no explicit time dependence, $K$ is conserved; it is the rotating-frame Jacobi energy, not generally the inertial energy.

CM:215.objective: Reduce inverse-square motion Hamiltonianly and identify zero linear apsidal precession through the radial symplectic flow over one orbit.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Construct the polar Hamiltonian and identify the cyclic angle. Next: Find the circular fixed point and linearize both canonical radial Hamilton equations there. Finally: Compare the symplectic eigenfrequency with orbital motion and evaluate the full-period matrix exponential.

milestones.criterion: The conserved polar momentum creates the effective potential and fixes $r_c=L^2/(\mu k)$ and $E_c$.
Linearizing $(r,p_r)$ gives the displayed Hamiltonian matrix with eigenvalues $\pm i\Omega$.

commonErrors.consequence: The bare attractive potential has no finite minimum; omitting the angular barrier cannot produce the circular orbit.

Since $U_{eff}''(r_c)=k/r_c^3$, the perturbation vector $(\delta r,\delta p_r)^{\mathsf T}$ obeys $\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}=A\boldsymbol\xi$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/\mu\\-k/r_c^3&0\end{pmatrix}$. Its eigenvalues are $\pm i\sqrt{k/(\mu r_c^3)}=\pm i\Omega$. Over one circular period $2\pi/\Omega$, $e^{A(2\pi/\Omega)}=\mathbf1$, the linear no-apsidal-precession signature of the inverse-square potential.

CM:216.title: Symplectic test for a linear phase map
CM:216.objective: Apply the full symplectic matrix test to a concrete linear map and cross-check it through inversion and a Poisson bracket.
CM:216.statement: Let $(Q,P)^{\mathsf T}=M(q,p)^{\mathsf T}$ with $M=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Verify $M^{\mathsf T}JM=J$ for $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Find the inverse map and check $\{Q,P\}=1$ directly.
permittedResults: For a two-dimensional linear map, the symplectic condition is equivalent to determinant one, but verify the full matrix identity.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Compute determinant and the complete $M^{\mathsf T}JM$ product. Next: Invert the matrix using its unit determinant. Finally: Evaluate the fundamental bracket and compare with a nearby noncanonical matrix.

milestones.criterion: Direct multiplication verifies $M^{\mathsf T}JM=J$ rather than relying on matrix symmetry.
The inverse map is computed using the unit determinant.
The component bracket $2(1)-1(1)$ equals one and agrees with the matrix criterion.

commonErrors.description: Checks only that $M$ is symmetric and calls symmetry equivalent to symplecticity.
commonErrors.consequence: Symmetric matrices need not preserve the canonical two-form, so symmetry is not a substitute for the $J$ test.

commonErrors.description: Uses $M^{\mathsf T}M=I$ as the canonical condition.
commonErrors.consequence: Orthogonality preserves Euclidean length, not necessarily symplectic area; $M^{\mathsf T}M=I$ is the wrong condition.

Invert the matrix using its unit determinant.

Directly, $\{Q,P\}=Q_qP_p-Q_pP_q=2(1)-1(1)=1$. Thus the map is globally invertible and canonical. Replacing the lower-right entry by $2$ would make determinant three and fail the test.

CM:217.title: Infinitesimal canonical scaling generated by $qp$
CM:217.objective: Integrate the Poisson flow generated by $qp$ from its infinitesimal action to an exact reciprocal scaling.
CM:217.statement: Let $G(q,p)=qp$ and define an infinitesimal transformation by $\delta f=\varepsilon\{f,G\}$. Find $\delta q$ and $\delta p$, integrate the generator flow to a finite transformation, and verify the finite map preserves $dq\wedge dp$.

CM:218.title: Poisson brackets transported by Hamiltonian flow
CM:218.objective: Use the Jacobi identity to prove Poisson brackets are transported consistently by autonomous Hamiltonian flow.
CM:218.statement: For time-independent observables $f$ and $g$ and autonomous Hamiltonian $H$, prove $d\{f,g\}/dt=\{\dot f,g\}+\{f,\dot g\}=\{\{f,g\},H\}$. State the Jacobi identity step and explain why an initially canonical pair remains canonical.

The ordered Jacobi identity combines the nested terms into $\{\{f,g\},H\}$.
Initial brackets one and zero remain so, while explicitly time-dependent observables are correctly excluded.

commonErrors.consequence: Poisson brackets are not associative, so reassociating nested brackets invalidates the transport proof.

commonErrors.consequence: Only a bracket commuting with $H$ is constant; the transport equation does not freeze every observable bracket.

CM:231.title: Ermakov invariant for a time-dependent oscillator
CM:231.objective: Prove the dimensional Ermakov invariant by coupling a physical time-dependent oscillator to a positive auxiliary amplitude.
CM:231.statement: Let $q$ solve $\ddot q+\omega(t)^2q=0$. Let a positive auxiliary amplitude $\rho$ solve $\ddot\rho+\omega(t)^2\rho=c^2/\rho^3$, where $c>0$ is constant. Hence $\dot I=u\dot u+v\dot v=ucv/\rho^2-vcu/\rho^2=0$. If $q$ and $\rho$ have length units, then $c$ has units $\mathrm{m^2/s}$ and both $u$ and $v$ have units $\mathrm{m^2/s}$, so $I$ has units $\mathrm{m^4/s^2}$. Positivity prevents division by zero and selects a regular auxiliary branch; the proof applies on any interval where $\rho\ne0$.

CM:233.title: Mass-metric symplectic diagonalization of quadratic motion
CM:233.objective: Mass-normalize a positive quadratic Hamiltonian through a generalized eigenbasis while preserving the canonical one-form.

CM:234.objective: Construct canonical linear invariants for a genuinely time-dependent oscillator from normalized fundamental solutions and distinguish their quadratic invariant from instantaneous energy.

Then take $\tau>0$ and $\omega(t)^2=2/(t+\tau)^2$ on the interval $t>-\tau$. Derive the normalized $u,v$ and, for $\tau=1.00\,\mathrm s$, $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $t=\tau$, $q=0.400\,\mathrm m$, and $p=-0.600\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, evaluate the basis functions, both linear invariants, the quadratic invariant, the instantaneous energy, and $\dot H$.

CM:235.title: Jacobi constant from the rotating three-body Hamiltonian
CM:235.objective: Recover the circular restricted three-body Jacobi constant from its autonomous rotating Hamiltonian and explicit normalization.
CM:235.statement: In normalized planar circular restricted three-body coordinates, put primaries at $(-\mu,0)$ and $(1-\mu,0)$, define $r_1^2=(x+\mu)^2+y^2$ and $r_2^2=(x-1+\mu)^2+y^2$, and let $U=(1-\mu)/r_1+\mu/r_2$. commonErrors.consequence: Equating rotating canonical momenta with velocities removes coordinate shifts and loses the centrifugal contribution.

commonErrors.consequence: The Jacobi integral belongs to the rotating autonomous system and is not the test particle's inertial mechanical energy.

The rotating Hamiltonian is autonomous, so $dH/dt=0$ and $C$ is conserved wherever $r_1r_2\ne0$. The formula uses unit primary separation, unit rotation rate, and unit $G(m_1+m_2)$ with masses $1-\mu$ and $\mu$. In inertial coordinates the test particle sees moving primaries, so its mechanical energy alone need not be constant even though the rotating-frame Jacobi integral is.

Here $S=mr^2\dot\phi$ is the mechanical axial angular momentum; the sign of the axial force therefore depends on signed charge and instantaneous azimuthal motion. The parameter $\alpha$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-2}}$. At $\alpha=0$, $\mathbf B=B_0\mathbf e_z$ and $\dot p_z=0$.

CM:237.title: Euler-angle Hamiltonian of a heavy symmetric top
CM:237.objective: Legendre-transform the heavy symmetric top in Euler angles and isolate its two cyclic momenta and polar chart boundary.
CM:237.statement: A symmetric top fixed at one point has transverse moment $I_1$, axial moment $I_3$, and Euler kinetic energy $T=I_1(\dot\theta^2+\dot\phi^2\sin^2\theta)/2+I_3(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)^2/2$. The center of mass is distance $\ell$ along the body axis, $\theta$ is measured from the upward vertical, and $V=Mg\ell\cos\theta$. Derive all canonical momenta and the Hamiltonian. Identify the two conserved momenta and the coordinate-singular set.
permittedResults: First use $p_\psi$ to eliminate the repeated combination $\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta$.
The angles $\phi$ and $\psi$ are cyclic for the stated axisymmetric gravitational model.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Differentiate the full kinetic energy with respect to all three Euler rates. Next: Invert the coupled $\phi$ and $\psi$ momentum relations before taking the Legendre transform. Finally: Use cyclicity to identify constants and interpret the polar coordinate singularity.

milestones.criterion: All three momenta follow from the coupled kinetic metric, including the shared $\dot\phi$-$\dot\psi$ combination.
Rate inversion produces the standard Hamiltonian with the squared momentum difference over $\sin^2\theta$.
Only $p_\phi$ and $p_\psi$ are conserved, and regular polar states satisfy the numerator compatibility condition.

commonErrors.description: Treats all three Euler-angle momenta as independent scalar moments times their own rates.
commonErrors.consequence: Treating Euler rates as orthogonal ignores their kinetic coupling and yields an incorrect diagonal Hamiltonian.

commonErrors.description: Calls $p_\theta$ conserved even though gravity makes $\theta$ noncyclic.
commonErrors.consequence: Gravity and the kinetic metric depend on tilt, so $p_\theta$ is not a cyclic constant.

hintTree.content: Differentiate the full kinetic energy with respect to all three Euler rates.
Invert the coupled $\phi$ and $\psi$ momentum relations before taking the Legendre transform.
Use cyclicity to identify constants and interpret the polar coordinate singularity.

CM:237.canonicalSolution: $p_\theta=I_1\dot\theta$, $p_\psi=I_3(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)$, and $p_\phi=I_1\dot\phi\sin^2\theta+p_\psi\cos\theta$. Thus $\dot\phi=(p_\phi-p_\psi\cos\theta)/(I_1\sin^2\theta)$ and $\dot\psi=p_\psi/I_3-\dot\phi\cos\theta$. The Legendre transform is $H=p_\theta^2/(2I_1)+(p_\phi-p_\psi\cos\theta)^2/(2I_1\sin^2\theta)+p_\psi^2/(2I_3)+Mg\ell\cos\theta$. Since $H$ is independent of $\phi$ and $\psi$, both $p_\phi$ and $p_\psi$ are conserved. The apparent singularity at $\sin\theta=0$ is an Euler-coordinate singularity; regular physical states there require the numerator to approach zero consistently.

The Legendre transform is $H=p_\theta^2/(2I_1)+(p_\phi-p_\psi\cos\theta)^2/(2I_1\sin^2\theta)+p_\psi^2/(2I_3)+Mg\ell\cos\theta$. Since $H$ is independent of $\phi$ and $\psi$, both $p_\phi$ and $p_\psi$ are conserved. The apparent singularity at $\sin\theta=0$ is an Euler-coordinate singularity; regular physical states there require the numerator to approach zero consistently.
The top Hamiltonian is the sum of three uncoupled terms $p_i^2/(2I_i)$ because Euler angles are orthogonal coordinates.

CM:238.title: Exact shadow Hamiltonian of oscillator leapfrog
CM:238.objective: Find the exact autonomous quadratic shadow Hamiltonian whose time-step flow equals stable oscillator leapfrog.
CM:238.statement: For the kick-drift-kick oscillator map of CM:227, write $x=h\omega$ and assume $0<x<2$. With $\theta=\arccos(1-x^2/2)$, construct an autonomous quadratic Hamiltonian whose exact time-$h$ flow is exactly one leapfrog step. Prove the match and expand the shadow Hamiltonian through order $h^2$. Audit the limits $h\to0$ and $x\to2^-$.
permittedResults: The leapfrog matrix has off-diagonal entries $h/m$ and $-hm\omega^2(1-x^2/4)$.
For $H_*=(\alpha p^2+\beta q^2)/2$, the flow angle is $h\sqrt{\alpha\beta}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Express the stable symplectic matrix as the flow of a general diagonal quadratic Hamiltonian. Next: Solve its two coefficients from the exact off-diagonal matrix entries. Finally: Expand both coefficient factors and inspect the small-step and stability-boundary limits.

milestones.criterion: The stable map angle satisfies $\cos\theta=1-x^2/2$ and determines both shadow coefficients.
Exact flow entries reproduce the leapfrog diagonal and both off-diagonal terms.
The $h^2$ expansion has the stated kinetic and potential corrections and becomes singular at the stability boundary.

commonErrors.description: Uses the physical Hamiltonian itself and claims leapfrog advances it by the exact physical frequency.
commonErrors.consequence: The physical oscillator Hamiltonian generates the exact physical rotation, not the frequency-modified leapfrog map.

commonErrors.description: Expands only $1-x^2/4$ and omits the compensating factor $\theta/\sin\theta$.
commonErrors.consequence: Expanding only the explicit potential factor misses the common $\theta/\sin\theta$ correction and gives wrong $h^2$ coefficients.

hintTree.content: Express the stable symplectic matrix as the flow of a general diagonal quadratic Hamiltonian.
Solve its two coefficients from the exact off-diagonal matrix entries.
Expand both coefficient factors and inspect the small-step and stability-boundary limits.

CM:238.canonicalSolution: Because $\sin\theta=x\sqrt{1-x^2/4}$, define $H_{sh}=(\theta/\sin\theta)[p^2/(2m)+m\omega^2(1-x^2/4)q^2/2]$. Its frequency is $\sqrt{\alpha\beta}=\theta/h$. The exact time-$h$ flow therefore has diagonal entries $\cos\theta=1-x^2/2$, upper-right entry $(\alpha h/\theta)\sin\theta=h/m$, and lower-left entry $-(\beta h/\theta)\sin\theta=-hm\omega^2(1-x^2/4)$, exactly the leapfrog matrix. Since $\theta/\sin\theta=1+x^2/6+O(x^4)$, $H_{sh}=H+h^2[\omega^2p^2/(12m)-m\omega^4q^2/24]+O(h^4)$. It tends to $H$ as $h\to0$ but becomes singular as $x\to2^-$, matching the stability boundary.

The exact time-$h$ flow therefore has diagonal entries $\cos\theta=1-x^2/2$, upper-right entry $(\alpha h/\theta)\sin\theta=h/m$, and lower-left entry $-(\beta h/\theta)\sin\theta=-hm\omega^2(1-x^2/4)$, exactly the leapfrog matrix. Since $\theta/\sin\theta=1+x^2/6+O(x^4)$, $H_{sh}=H+h^2[\omega^2p^2/(12m)-m\omega^4q^2/24]+O(h^4)$. It tends to $H$ as $h\to0$ but becomes singular as $x\to2^-$, matching the stability boundary.
Symplecticity means leapfrog exactly conserves the original oscillator energy for every stable step.

CM:239.title: Stability chart for a kicked canonical oscillator
CM:239.objective: Build the ordered Floquet map of a kicked canonical oscillator and extract its exact stability chart from the trace.
CM:239.statement: In scaled canonical variables, free oscillator evolution through angle $\vartheta$ is $R=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\vartheta&\sin\vartheta\\-\sin\vartheta&\cos\vartheta\end{pmatrix}$. It is followed by an impulsive quadratic kick $P^+=P^- -\kappa Q$. Derive the stroboscopic matrix, prove it is symplectic, and obtain the exact bounded-stability condition. Specialize to $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and classify the boundaries.
permittedResults: The kick matrix is $K=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-\kappa&1\end{pmatrix}$ and the stated ordering is $M=KR$.
For determinant one, strict elliptic stability is $|\operatorname{tr}M|<2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Translate the impulse and free evolution into matrices in the declared temporal order. Next: Multiply them, verify determinant one, and compute the trace. Finally: Apply the unit-determinant eigenvalue criterion and inspect the quarter-period boundaries.

milestones.criterion: Free rotation followed by kick is represented as $M=KR$ with the correct lower row.
Determinant one verifies symplecticity and trace $2\cos\vartheta-\kappa\sin\vartheta$ controls eigenvalues.
At a quarter period the stable band is $|\kappa|<2$ with nontrivial parabolic boundaries.

commonErrors.description: Uses $RK$ while claiming to apply the free evolution before the kick.
commonErrors.consequence: Using $RK$ applies the kick at the wrong phase and changes the stroboscopic coordinates.

commonErrors.description: Tests only determinant one and concludes every kick strength is bounded.
commonErrors.consequence: Symplectic kicked maps can be hyperbolic, so determinant alone cannot bound repeated motion.

hintTree.content: Translate the impulse and free evolution into matrices in the declared temporal order.
Multiply them, verify determinant one, and compute the trace.
Apply the unit-determinant eigenvalue criterion and inspect the quarter-period boundaries.

CM:239.canonicalSolution: Multiplication gives $M=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\kappa c-s&c-\kappa s\end{pmatrix}$, where $c=\cos\vartheta$ and $s=\sin\vartheta$. Both $K$ and $R$ have determinant one, so $M$ is symplectic. Its trace is $2c-\kappa s$, and repeated stroboscopic motion is elliptic precisely when $|2\cos\vartheta-\kappa\sin\vartheta|<2$. It is hyperbolic when the magnitude exceeds two and marginal at equality. For $\vartheta=\pi/2$, the condition is $|\kappa|<2$, with parabolic boundaries at $\kappa=\pm2$ unless the matrix degenerates to $\pm\mathbf1$, which it does not here.

Both $K$ and $R$ have determinant one, so $M$ is symplectic. Its trace is $2c-\kappa s$, and repeated stroboscopic motion is elliptic precisely when $|2\cos\vartheta-\kappa\sin\vartheta|<2$. It is hyperbolic when the magnitude exceeds two and marginal at equality. For $\vartheta=\pi/2$, the condition is $|\kappa|<2$, with parabolic boundaries at $\kappa=\pm2$ unless the matrix degenerates to $\pm\mathbf1$, which it does not here.

Although free evolution occurs before the kick, multiply in the opposite order and use $M=RK$. This is valid because both factors are symplectic, so their temporal order cannot affect the stroboscopic map.

CM:240.title: Freely falling canonical frame for a constant force
CM:240.objective: Construct a freely falling canonical frame that removes a uniform force exactly and verify the cancellation numerically.
CM:240.statement: A particle has $H=p^2/(2m)-Fq$ with constants $m>0$ and $F$, and put $a=F/m$. Construct a type-2 generator that implements $Q=q-at^2/2$ and $P=p-mat$ while reducing the new Hamiltonian exactly to $K=P^2/(2m)$. Verify every time-dependent term. Then for $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $F=6.00\,\mathrm N$, $q(0)=0$, and $p(0)=8.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, find $(q,p,Q,P,K)$ at $t=2.00\,\mathrm s$.
permittedResults: Try $F_2=(q-at^2/2)(P+mat)+g(t)$ and determine $g$ by cancellation.
For the original constant force, $p(t)=p_0+Ft$ and $q(t)=q_0+p_0t/m+at^2/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Differentiate the generator to recover both requested canonical variables. Next: Compute its explicit time derivative at fixed old coordinate and new momentum, then cancel every force term. Finally: Evaluate the inertial and transformed trajectories numerically with units and verify constant $K$.

milestones.criterion: The generator produces both $Q=q-at^2/2$ and the essential momentum shift $P=p-mat$.
Its cubic time term cancels every residual force and leaves $K=P^2/(2m)$.
The computed inertial state maps to $(Q,P)=(8,8)$ and constant $K=16.0$ J.

commonErrors.description: Uses the translating coordinate but omits the momentum shift needed for a freely falling frame.
commonErrors.consequence: Translating position without boosting momentum does not match free-fall kinematics and leaves the force in the transformed equations.

commonErrors.description: Chooses the cubic generator term with coefficient $1/6$ and leaves residual explicit time dependence.
commonErrors.consequence: The coefficient $1/6$ is appropriate to a different accelerating-frame potential; here it leaves an uncancelled time function.

hintTree.content: Differentiate the generator to recover both requested canonical variables.

CM:240.canonicalSolution: Take $F_2(q,P,t)=(q-at^2/2)(P+mat)+ma^2t^3/3$. Then $p=F_{2,q}=P+mat$ and $Q=F_{2,P}=q-at^2/2$. At fixed $(q,P)$, $F_{2,t}=-atP+maq-3ma^2t^2/2+ma^2t^2$. Adding this to $(P+mat)^2/(2m)-maq$ cancels the terms in $atP$, $maq$, and $ma^2t^2$, leaving $K=P^2/(2m)$. Numerically $a=3.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$; at $t=2.00$ s, $p=20.0\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ and $q=14.0$ m, so $P=8.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, $Q=8.00$ m, and $K=16.0$ J. The transformed free motion has constant $P$ and $\ddot Q=0$.
